# Estimation and the design process {#sec-estimation-and-the-design-process}

A large software system is designed before it is built, and most of the design is decided by a few numbers: how many
requests arrive each second, how much data accumulates, how long a user may wait, how often the service may be down and
what all of it costs. These numbers are rarely known exactly when the design starts. They are estimated from
assumptions about the users, checked against the capacity of machines and networks, and revised as the design takes
shape. This chapter sets out that process and the arithmetic behind it. Its claims are of two kinds. The design process,
its requirements and its components are definitions. The results that let estimates be combined, such as how latency
budgets add up, how errors in an estimate propagate and how the availability of a system follows from that of its
parts, are propositions with proofs that use only elementary probability.

The sources are the four benchmark books of the tutorial and three section sources. The design process follows
@SystemDesignInterview2021 [Ch. 3], @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Ch. 2 and App. C], @liuSystemDesignInterview2020
[Ch. 2] and @sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024 [Ch. 1]. Architectural characteristics and decision records follow
@gandhiHeadFirstSoftware2024 [Chs. 2-3] and @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Ch. 3]. The estimates follow
@SystemDesignInterview2021 [Ch. 2] and @liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 5 and Apps. 1-4], availability follows
@tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Sec. 3.2] and @sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024 [Ch. 2], fan-out follows
@dean2013tail, and cost follows @reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022 [Ch. 4] with @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Sec. 3.8]
and @SystemDesignInterview2021 [Ch. 14]. The probability used throughout comes from
[Probability and statistics](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd).

The chapter has six sections. @sec-design-process defines a requirements specification and the design process that
turns it into an architecture. @sec-architectural-characteristics defines the architectural characteristics that a
design must trade against each other. @sec-units-and-latency fixes the units and the latency numbers of estimates and
proves how the latency budgets of a request path combine. @sec-estimating-load defines the load estimate of a service,
from requests per second to the number of servers, and proves how the errors of its factors propagate.
@sec-availability-arithmetic defines availability and proves the rules for components in series and in parallel and
for requests that fan out to many servers. @sec-estimating-cost defines the total cost of ownership and estimates it
with the same arithmetic.

A running example, a photo-sharing service, appears in every section. Users upload photos, follow other users and read
a feed of the photos of the people they follow. Its assumptions are fixed in the first section and are used
unchanged afterwards, so that the estimates of later sections can be compared.

Every definition and proposition is followed by ten examples and ten exercises, each exercise with a hidden solution
in two tabs: the argument, then a computation with its recorded output. The computations run in plain Python 3.12 with
NumPy, the standard library's `sqlite3` and, for the simulations of request paths, SimPy 4.1.2. Architecture diagrams
are written in the D2 language, and an exercise that asks for a diagram shows its source next to the drawing. Code that
would need a running service is marked as illustrative and is not run.

## The design process {#sec-design-process}

Every benchmark book begins a design in the same way: by finding out what the system must do and how well it must do
it, before drawing any component. Xu warns that answering "without a thorough understanding of the requirements is a
huge red flag" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 3, Step 1], Tan asks that every requirement "must have a number"
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 2.1], and Liu spends the first step of his framework on functional requirements,
scale and performance constraints [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 2, Step 1]. This section turns these
prescriptions into two definitions. The first says what a requirement is, precisely enough that it can be checked; the
second lists the steps that turn a set of requirements into an architecture, and the artefact each step produces. The
estimates, characteristics and availability figures of the later sections are the inputs and outputs of these steps.

For more on this topic, see @SystemDesignInterview2021 [Ch. 3], @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Secs. 2.1-2.3 and Ch. 3],
@liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 2] and @sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024 [Ch. 1, "Understanding system design"].

### Requirements

A requirement is useful to a designer only if one can tell, after the system is built, whether it holds. "The feed
should be fast" cannot be checked; "99% of feed requests are answered within 500 ms when 50 000 requests arrive per
second" can. The definition below separates what the system does from how well it does it, and it records the workload
under which the "how well" is promised, because a latency or availability target means nothing without the load at
which it is measured.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-requirements-specification}
#### Requirements specification

A **requirements specification** of a software system consists of three parts.

1. A finite set of **functional requirements**. Each names an operation $o$ that the system offers to a named actor
   (a user role or another system), its inputs, its outputs, and its effect on the data the system stores.
2. A finite set of **non-functional requirements**. Each is a triple (metric, comparison, target): the metric is a
   quantity that can be measured on the running system, such as a latency quantile $t_q$, an availability, a
   throughput, the probability of losing a stored item in a year, or a cost per month; the target is a number with a
   unit; and the comparison ($\leq$ or $\geq$) says which side is acceptable.
3. The **workload assumptions** under which the non-functional requirements are stated: the number of users $U$, the
   request rate of each operation, the sizes of the stored items and the period for which they are kept.

A statement about the system that is neither an operation with its inputs and outputs nor a measurable triple is not
yet a requirement in this sense, and the design process begins by turning it into one.
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The smallest specification with a real use is the URL shortener of Xu's eighth chapter. Its functional part has two
operations and nothing else, which makes it the standard first example of the benchmark books.

::: {#exm-req-url-shortener}
#### A URL shortener

The functional requirements are two operations offered to any client: *shorten*, with input a long URL and output a
short URL, which stores the pair; and *redirect*, with input a short URL and output an HTTP redirect to the long URL,
which reads the pair. Xu adds that "shortened URLs cannot be deleted or updated", which removes two more operations
from scope [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 8, Step 1].
:::

The running example of the chapter has three actors' worth of operations. Writing them in the form of the definition
shows at once which ones write data and which only read it.

::: {#exm-req-photoshare}
#### The photo-sharing service

The functional requirements are: *upload* (input: a photo and a caption; output: a photo identifier; effect: stores the
photo and its metadata), *follow* (input: a user to follow; effect: stores the pair), and *feed* (input: a user and a
page number; output: the ten most recent photos of the users followed, as thumbnails with captions; no effect). Upload
and follow write; feed only reads.
:::

The most common non-requirement is an adjective. Liu's example of a news feed shows how it becomes a measurable
triple, with a quantile rather than a mean as the metric.

::: {#exm-req-latency-quantile}
#### From "fast" to a latency quantile

"The feed must be fast" names no metric. Liu notes that it is "not acceptable to render the Facebook News Feed to take
more than 500 ms in p99 of the use cases" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 2, "Performance Constraints"]. As a
non-functional requirement this is the triple ($t_{0.99}$ of the feed response time, $\leq$, $500\,\mathrm{ms}$). A
quantile is chosen because a mean of $100\,\mathrm{ms}$ is compatible with one request in ten taking seconds.
:::

Availability is the second metric every specification states. Its target is a number close to one, and the
comparison runs the other way.

::: {#exm-req-availability-target}
#### An availability target

Tan defines availability as "the percentage of time a system can accept requests and return the desired response"
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 3.2]. For the photo-sharing service the triple (monthly availability of the feed,
$\geq$, $99.9\%$) allows the feed to fail for at most $0.001 \times 30 \times 24 \times 60 = 43.2$ minutes in a
30-day month.
:::

Durability is easily confused with availability, but it measures something else: whether an item, once stored, can
ever be read again. A photo service promises its users that it will not lose their photos, and that promise is a
non-functional requirement of its own.

::: {#exm-req-durability}
#### Durability

Liu's file-storage example ends with the promise "We will ensure the system has strong durability"
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 2, "Functional Requirements"]. Made measurable, it reads (probability that a given
stored photo is lost within a year, $\leq$, $10^{-11}$). With $10^{10}$ photos stored this allows an expected $0.1$
lost photos a year.
:::

The workload assumptions are the third part, and the whole of the chapter's later arithmetic rests on them. Here they
are fixed once for the running example.

::: {#exm-req-workload-assumptions}
#### Workload of the photo-sharing service

The assumptions are: $U = 10^8$ daily active users; each uploads $\nu_{\text{up}} = 0.2$ photos a day and reads
$\nu_{\text{feed}} = 50$ feed pages a day; a photo is $2\,\mathrm{MB}$ (Liu's "high" quality phone photo
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, App. 3]) with $1\,\mathrm{kB}$ of metadata, and a feed page carries ten thumbnails of
$30\,\mathrm{kB}$; photos are kept for five years in $N = 3$ replicas; and the busiest hour has three times the mean
rate. These are assumptions for the exercise, not measurements of any real service.
:::

Xu's estimation chapter states its assumptions in exactly this form before computing anything. They make a second
complete workload, used again in later sections.

::: {#exm-req-xu-twitter}
#### Xu's assumptions for a microblogging service

Xu assumes "300 million monthly active users", of whom "50% ... use Twitter daily", who "post 2 tweets per day on
average", with "10% of tweets" carrying media, and data "stored for 5 years"; he stresses that these "are not real
numbers from Twitter" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 2]. In the terms of the definition: $U = 1.5 \times 10^8$,
$\nu_{\text{post}} = 2$, a media fraction of $0.1$ and a retention of five years.
:::

Consistency requirements are often stated as a choice between system types, and Liu shows why that is the wrong level.
The user-facing version of the requirement is a bound on how stale the data may be.

::: {#exm-req-staleness}
#### Staleness instead of "AP or CP"

Instead of "I will choose AP system over CP system", Liu advises asking "can I assume that it is ok to have some delay
before the user's post shows up in other users' feed" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 2, "Performance
Constraints"]. The measurable form is (probability that a new photo appears in a follower's feed within $5\,\mathrm{s}$,
$\geq$, $0.99$).
:::

Accuracy is a separate metric again: a system may return a value that is approximately right by design. Counting is the
standard case, because exact counts at scale are expensive.

::: {#exm-req-accuracy}
#### An accuracy requirement

Tan lists accuracy among the non-functional requirements, since "a system's data may not need to be perfectly
accurate" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Ch. 3], and Liu asks whether "it is ok for rate limiters to be approximately
correct" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 2]. For the view counter of a photo the triple might be (relative error of
the displayed count, $\leq$, $1\%$), which permits counting a sample of views instead of every view.
:::

Requirements can contradict each other or the laws of physics, and a specification is only useful if it is
satisfiable. The last example combines a latency target with the distance between two data centres.

::: {#exm-req-infeasible}
#### An unsatisfiable pair of requirements

Suppose a specification demands both that every upload is confirmed only after it is stored in California and in the
Netherlands, and that uploads complete with $t_{0.99} \leq 100\,\mathrm{ms}$. Liu gives $150\,\mathrm{ms}$ as the
latency from California to the Netherlands [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, App. 3], so every confirmed upload takes at
least that long. The two requirements cannot hold together, and the design process must change one of them, for
example by confirming after the first region and copying to the second in the background.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise applies the definition directly. It asks which statements of a draft are requirements, and of which
kind.

::: {#exr-req-classify}
#### Sorting a draft

Classify each statement as a functional requirement, a non-functional requirement, a workload assumption, or not yet a
requirement: (1) "a user can delete a photo"; (2) "the service is highly available"; (3) "$t_{0.99}$ of uploads is at
most $2\,\mathrm{s}$"; (4) "there are 20 million daily active users"; (5) "the system uses a NoSQL database".
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

(1) is functional: an operation with an input (a photo identifier) and an effect (the photo is removed). (2) names no
metric target and is not yet a requirement. (3) is a non-functional triple. (4) is a workload assumption. (5) is not a
requirement at all but a design decision: it says how, not what or how well, and belongs to the later steps of the
process.

## Python

A statement is accepted as a non-functional requirement only if it contains a number with a unit; the code applies
this test, which separates (2) from (3).

```{.python .run}
import re
draft = {1: "a user can delete a photo", 2: "the service is highly available",
         3: "t_0.99 of uploads is at most 2 s", 4: "there are 20 million daily active users",
         5: "the system uses a NoSQL database"}
measurable = re.compile(r"\d+(\.\d+)?\s*(ms|s|%|million|MB|GB)\b")
for k, text in draft.items():
    print(k, "has a number with a unit" if measurable.search(text) else "no number with a unit")
```

```{.text .run-output}
1 no number with a unit
2 no number with a unit
3 has a number with a unit
4 has a number with a unit
5 no number with a unit
```
::::
:::

The second exercise repairs the commonest defect, a requirement without a number. It asks for the measurable triples
behind an informal sentence.

::: {#exr-req-make-measurable}
#### Making a sentence measurable

Rewrite "the site should be fast and always up" as two non-functional requirements, choosing reasonable targets, and
give the downtime per 30-day month that your availability target allows.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

"Fast" becomes ($t_{0.99}$ of page responses, $\leq$, $300\,\mathrm{ms}$), at the stated workload. "Always up" cannot
be met by any real system; it becomes (monthly availability, $\geq$, $99.95\%$). The allowed downtime is $0.0005$ of
a month, $0.0005 \times 43\,200\,\mathrm{min} = 21.6\,\mathrm{min}$.

## Python

The downtime allowed by a few availability targets, for a 30-day month.

```{.python .run}
month_min = 30 * 24 * 60
for target in (0.999, 0.9995, 0.9999):
    print(f"{target:.2%}: {(1 - target) * month_min:.1f} min of downtime per month")
```

```{.text .run-output}
99.90%: 43.2 min of downtime per month
99.95%: 21.6 min of downtime per month
99.99%: 4.3 min of downtime per month
```
::::
:::

The third exercise checks a derived assumption from Tan's guide to requirements. It converts a daily count into an
hourly and a per-second rate.

::: {#exr-req-derive-rate}
#### Tan's search example

Tan writes that "if a search service has 1 billion daily users, each submitting 10 search requests, there are 10
billion daily requests or 420 million hourly requests" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 2.1]. Check the hourly figure
and give the mean rate per second.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$10^9 \times 10 = 10^{10}$ requests a day; divided by 24 this is $4.17 \times 10^8$ an hour, which Tan rounds to 420
million; divided by $86\,400$ it is $1.16 \times 10^5$ requests per second.

## Python

The same three numbers.

```{.python .run}
daily = 1e9 * 10
print(f"per day {daily:.3g}, per hour {daily / 24:.3g}, per second {daily / 86400:.3g}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
per day 1e+10, per hour 4.17e+08, per second 1.16e+05
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise moves from requirements to the interface that serves them. It checks that every functional
requirement of the running example is covered by an endpoint.

::: {#exr-req-api-coverage}
#### Endpoints for the functional requirements

Propose one HTTP endpoint for each functional requirement of @exm-req-photoshare, in the style of Tan's draft API
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 2.2], and check that no requirement is left without one.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

`POST /photos` (multipart body with the photo and caption; returns the photo identifier) serves upload; `POST
/users/{id}/follow` serves follow; `GET /feed?page=k` serves feed. Each operation of the specification is the target
of exactly one endpoint, and no endpoint lacks a requirement.

## Python

The specification and the draft API as two mappings, and the set differences that would reveal a gap.

```{.python .run}
requirements = {"upload", "follow", "feed"}
api = {"POST /photos": "upload", "POST /users/{id}/follow": "follow", "GET /feed?page=k": "feed"}
print("requirements without an endpoint:", sorted(requirements - set(api.values())))
print("endpoints without a requirement:", sorted(e for e, r in api.items() if r not in requirements))
```

```{.text .run-output}
requirements without an endpoint: []
endpoints without a requirement: []
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise makes the infeasibility of @exm-req-infeasible quantitative. It bounds a round trip from below by
the speed of light in optical fibre.

::: {#exr-req-light-bound}
#### A lower bound from the speed of light

Light travels in optical fibre at about $2 \times 10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Give the least possible round-trip time between
New York and London ($5570\,\mathrm{km}$ apart) and between London and Sydney ($17\,000\,\mathrm{km}$), and say whether
a requirement of a $50\,\mathrm{ms}$ synchronous write confirmed on both sides of the Atlantic can be met.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A round trip covers twice the distance: $2 \times 5.57 \times 10^6 / (2 \times 10^8) = 55.7\,\mathrm{ms}$ for New York
to London and $170\,\mathrm{ms}$ for London to Sydney. Real routes are longer than great circles, so these are lower
bounds. A synchronous write confirmed in both New York and London needs at least one round trip, $55.7 >
50\,\mathrm{ms}$, so the requirement is unsatisfiable whatever the design.

## Python

The two lower bounds.

```{.python .run}
v = 2e8  # m/s in fibre
for route, km in [("New York - London", 5570), ("London - Sydney", 17000)]:
    print(f"{route}: round trip >= {2 * km * 1e3 / v * 1e3:.1f} ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
New York - London: round trip >= 55.7 ms
London - Sydney: round trip >= 170.0 ms
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise turns the durability target of @exm-req-durability into expected losses. It shows why such targets
have many zeros.

::: {#exr-req-durability-losses}
#### Expected losses

A service stores $10^{10}$ photos, and each is lost within a year independently with probability $q$. Give the expected
number of photos lost per year, and the probability that at least one is lost, for $q = 10^{-9}$ and $q = 10^{-11}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The number lost is binomial with $n = 10^{10}$ trials (the
[binomial distribution](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#def-binomial-distribution)),
with mean $nq$: $10$ photos for $q = 10^{-9}$ and $0.1$ for $q = 10^{-11}$. The probability of losing none is $(1 -
q)^n \approx e^{-nq}$, so at least one is lost with probability $1 - e^{-10} \approx 0.99995$ and $1 - e^{-0.1}
\approx 0.095$.

## Python

The exact binomial values, computed with logarithms to avoid underflow.

```{.python .run}
from math import exp, log1p
n = 1e10
for q in (1e-9, 1e-11):
    print(f"q = {q:g}: mean lost {n * q:g}, P(at least one) = {1 - exp(n * log1p(-q)):.5f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
q = 1e-09: mean lost 10, P(at least one) = 0.99995
q = 1e-11: mean lost 0.1, P(at least one) = 0.09516
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise checks the staleness requirement of @exm-req-staleness against a model of the delay. The model is
the simplest one with a tail.

::: {#exr-req-staleness-check}
#### Checking a staleness target

Suppose the delay before a new photo reaches a follower's feed is exponentially distributed with mean $1\,\mathrm{s}$.
Does the system meet (probability of arrival within $5\,\mathrm{s}$, $\geq$, $0.99$)? What is the largest mean delay
that meets it?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

For an exponential delay with mean $m$, $\mathbb P(T \leq 5) = 1 - e^{-5/m}$. With $m = 1$ this is $1 - e^{-5} =
0.99326 \geq 0.99$, so the target is met. It holds as long as $e^{-5/m} \leq 0.01$, that is $m \leq 5/\ln 100 =
1.086\,\mathrm{s}$.

## Python

The exact probability, a simulated check with $10^6$ delays, and the largest mean.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
delays = rng.exponential(1.0, 10**6)
print(f"exact {1 - np.exp(-5):.5f}, simulated {np.mean(delays <= 5):.5f}")
print(f"largest mean delay: {5 / np.log(100):.3f} s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
exact 0.99326, simulated 0.99349
largest mean delay: 1.086 s
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise checks whether sampling meets the accuracy requirement of @exm-req-accuracy. It uses the variance of
a binomial count.

::: {#exr-req-accuracy-sampling}
#### Counting by sampling

A photo has $M = 10^6$ views. Each view is recorded independently with probability $p = 0.01$, and the count is
estimated as $\hat M = X/p$, where $X$ is the number of recorded views. Give the relative standard deviation of $\hat
M$. Is the requirement "relative error at most $1\%$" met with high probability?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$X \sim \operatorname{Bin}(M, p)$ has mean $Mp$ and variance $Mp(1 - p)$, so $\hat M$ has mean $M$ and relative
standard deviation $\sqrt{Mp(1 - p)}/(Mp) = \sqrt{(1 - p)/(Mp)} = \sqrt{0.99/10^4} = 0.995\%$. The $1\%$ bound is about
one standard deviation, so it fails roughly a third of the time: the requirement is not met with high probability. A
sampling rate of $p = 0.1$ gives $0.30\%$, and $1\%$ is then more than three standard deviations.

## Python

The formula, and the share of $10^5$ simulated counts that miss the $1\%$ bound, for both rates.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
M = 10**6
for p in (0.01, 0.1):
    est = rng.binomial(M, p, 10**5) / p
    print(f"p = {p}: relative sd {np.sqrt((1 - p) / (M * p)):.4f}, "
          f"share with error > 1%: {np.mean(np.abs(est / M - 1) > 0.01):.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
p = 0.01: relative sd 0.0099, share with error > 1%: 0.318
p = 0.1: relative sd 0.0030, share with error > 1%: 0.001
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise looks ahead in time, as Xu's first step does when it asks for "the anticipated scales in 3 months, 6
months, and a year" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 3, Step 1]. The workload assumptions must name the horizon they
hold for.

::: {#exr-req-growth}
#### Growth of the workload

The service has $10^8$ daily active users today and grows by $10\%$ a month. How many will it have in 3, 6 and 12
months? By what factor must the capacity planned today be multiplied to last a year?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

After $k$ months the count is $10^8 \times 1.1^k$: $1.33 \times 10^8$, $1.77 \times 10^8$ and $3.14 \times 10^8$. A
design that must last a year without being rebuilt has to be sized for $1.1^{12} = 3.14$ times today's load, not for
today's.

## Python

The compound growth.

```{.python .run}
for k in (3, 6, 12):
    print(f"after {k:2d} months: {1e8 * 1.1**k:.3g} users, factor {1.1**k:.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
after  3 months: 1.33e+08 users, factor 1.33
after  6 months: 1.77e+08 users, factor 1.77
after 12 months: 3.14e+08 users, factor 3.14
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise asks for a contradiction inside a specification, of the kind @exm-req-infeasible found between a
specification and physics. The argument needs only the meaning of availability.

::: {#exr-req-dependency-cap}
#### A dependency that caps availability

A payment page must have monthly availability at least $99.99\%$, and every request to it calls an external payment
provider synchronously; the page fails whenever the provider does. The provider's contract promises $99.9\%$. Show
that the specification cannot be met as stated, and propose a change of a requirement that removes the conflict.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Whenever the provider is down, so is the page. The set of instants at which the page is up is therefore contained in
the set at which the provider is up, and the fraction of time the page is up is at most the provider's. If the provider
meets its contract exactly, it may be down $0.1\%$ of a month, which is ten times the $0.01\%$ the page is allowed. The
two requirements cannot hold together. The conflict disappears if the functional requirement changes so that the page
does not wait for the provider: it accepts the payment request, confirms receipt, and completes the payment
asynchronously, which is Tan's advice to consider "whether the immediate response can be an acknowledgment"
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 3.2].

## Python

Check on one month: with the provider down for its full allowance of $0.1\%$, the page's downtime against its own
allowance.

```{.python .run}
month_min = 30 * 24 * 60
provider_down = (1 - 0.999) * month_min
page_allowed = (1 - 0.9999) * month_min
print(f"provider may be down {provider_down:.1f} min; page may be down {page_allowed:.2f} min")
print("specification satisfiable:", provider_down <= page_allowed)
```

```{.text .run-output}
provider may be down 43.2 min; page may be down 4.32 min
specification satisfiable: False
```
::::
:::
::::

### The design process and its artefacts

With requirements defined, the benchmark books agree on the steps that follow, though not on their order or names. Xu
has four steps, Liu six, Tan a list of topics and Sinha six stages of a design. The definition below takes the union of
their steps, names the artefact each step produces, and records the one point on which they all agree: that the steps
are revisited when a later one reveals a problem.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-design-process}
#### Design process

The **design process** for a system with a requirements specification (@def-requirements-specification) is the
following sequence of steps, each of which produces an artefact.

1. **Requirements**: the specification itself, agreed with the people who need the system.
2. **Interface**: an API, with one endpoint (or message type) per functional requirement, giving its inputs and outputs.
3. **Estimates**: the request rates, data volumes, bandwidths and numbers of machines implied by the workload
   assumptions.
4. **High-level design**: an architecture diagram, whose boxes are components (clients, load balancers, services, data
   stores, caches, queues, external systems) and whose arrows are the requests between them, such that every endpoint is
   served by a path of components. It is drawn at one of the levels of the C4 model: a **context diagram** shows the
   system as one box among its actors and the external systems it uses; a **container diagram** shows the separately
   deployable units inside it; a **component diagram** shows the parts inside one container.
5. **Data model**: the schema of each data store of the diagram.
6. **Deep dives**: for each requirement that the design puts at risk (a bottleneck, a single point of failure, a target
   the estimates say cannot be met), the alternatives, the trade-off between them, and the decision taken, with its
   reason.

The steps are iterated: an artefact may be revised whenever a later step shows that it does not meet the requirements.
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Xu's interview framework is the shortest version of the process. Its four steps fit the six of the definition, with
the estimate placed inside the high-level design.

::: {#exm-process-xu-four-steps}
#### Xu's four steps

Xu's steps are: "Understand the problem and establish design scope" (step 1 of the definition), "Propose high-level
design and get buy-in" (steps 2 to 4, including "back-of-the-envelope calculations to evaluate if your blueprint fits
the scale constraints"), "Design deep dive" (steps 5 and 6) and "Wrap up", which discusses bottlenecks, failures and
"the next scale curve" and so starts a new iteration [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 3].
:::

Liu orders the steps differently and gives a reason, which is worth recording because it is a statement about
dependencies between artefacts. An estimate is an estimate of something.

::: {#exm-process-liu-order}
#### Liu's order: estimates after the interface

Liu's six steps are requirements, API, high-level diagram, data model and schema, end-to-end flow and deep dives, with
the estimate deferred: "How can you calculate the QPS without knowing which API the QPS is for? How do you know what
storage capacity you're calculating for without knowing the schema?" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 2]. In the
terms of the definition, the request rates depend on step 2 and the storage on step 5, so step 3 can only be
completed after them; the order of the definition is a first pass.
:::

The first diagram of a design is the context diagram, in which the system is a single box. Tan's appendix on the C4
model draws an internet bank this way; the running example has a simpler context.

::: {#exm-process-context}
#### The context of the photo-sharing service

The context diagram has one box for the photo-sharing service, one actor (a user, through the web or mobile app) and
one external system, the content delivery network that serves photos near the users. Tan's example is an internet
banking system between its customers, an e-mail system and a mainframe [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, App. C, Fig. C.1];
at this level nothing inside the system is shown.
:::

A container diagram opens the box. For the running example it shows the classic three tiers, clients, stateless
application servers and data stores, together with the asynchronous path that makes thumbnails.

::: {#exm-process-three-tier}
#### A container diagram

@fig-three-tier is the container diagram of the photo-sharing service. Clients call the application servers through a
load balancer; the servers read and write photo metadata in a database, read hot data from a cache, store photos in an
object store and announce each upload on a queue, from which workers make thumbnails. Photos are read through the
content delivery network, which fetches from the object store on a miss. Every endpoint of @exr-req-api-coverage is
served by a path of arrows, as the definition requires.

![Container diagram of the photo-sharing service: clients, a load balancer, application servers, cache, metadata
database, queue, thumbnail workers, object store and a content delivery network.](figures/three_tier.svg){#fig-three-tier width=100%}
:::

The second step fixes the interface. Tan advises spending little time on it and listing the endpoints every system has
before the specific ones.

::: {#exm-process-api}
#### The interface

Beside `POST /photos`, `POST /users/{id}/follow` and `GET /feed?page=k`, Tan lists endpoints common to nearly all
systems: a health check `GET /health`, signup and login, and user management [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 2.2.1].
They are named and declared out of scope, so that the design concentrates on the three operations of the specification.
:::

The data model of step 5 is a schema per store. For the running example it is three tables, and their sizes feed back
into the estimates of step 3.

::: {#exm-process-data-model}
#### The data model

The metadata database holds `users(user_id, name, created_at)`, `photos(photo_id, user_id, caption, object_key,
created_at)` and `follows(follower_id, followee_id, created_at)`. Following Liu's advice to assign "each column to a
rough memory" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5], a photo row is about $8 + 8 + 100 + 40 + 4 = 160$ bytes with
8-byte identifiers and a 4-byte timestamp, well inside the $1\,\mathrm{kB}$ of metadata assumed in
@exm-req-workload-assumptions.
:::

Liu's fifth step traces each operation through the diagram before any deep dive. The trace is a check that the
diagram is complete, done by hand.

::: {#exm-process-flow}
#### An end-to-end flow

An upload in @fig-three-tier goes: client, load balancer, application server; the server stores the photo in the object
store, inserts a row in `photos`, puts a message on the queue and returns the identifier; later a worker reads the
message, makes thumbnails and stores them. A feed request goes: load balancer, application server, cache (or database
on a miss), and returns thumbnail URLs that the client fetches through the content delivery network. Liu's purpose for
this step is "to ensure there is at least a working solution" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 2, Step 5].
:::

Xu's own example of the high-level step is a news feed, and it shows that a design is often drawn as several flows
rather than one diagram. Each flow is the path of one group of endpoints.

::: {#exm-process-news-feed-flows}
#### Two flows of a news feed

"At the high level, the design is divided into two flows: feed publishing and news feed building": publishing writes a
post "into cache/database" and populates it "into friends' news feed", and building aggregates "friends' posts in a reverse
chronological order" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 3, Step 2]. In the photo-sharing service the same split separates the
upload flow from the feed flow of @exm-process-flow. The two flows have different loads, $231$ against $57\,870$ requests a
second on average, and can be scaled separately.
:::

A deep dive starts from a risk. The first risk of any diagram with one database is that the database is a single point
of failure, and the deep dive records the alternatives and the decision.

::: {#exm-process-deep-dive}
#### A deep dive on a single point of failure

In @fig-three-tier one metadata database serves every request, so its failure stops the service. The alternatives are a
standby replica that takes over on failure, several replicas that all serve reads, or partitioning the data so a
failure stops only part of the service. The decision, a primary with two replicas serving reads, is recorded with its
reason: it removes the single point of failure and also absorbs the read-heavy feed load. Its cost is that a reader may
see a replica that lags the primary, which the staleness requirement of @exm-req-staleness allows.
:::

The last example is an iteration of the process, in which the estimate of step 3 forces a change to step 4. Xu's wrap-up
step asks for exactly this.

::: {#exm-process-iteration}
#### An iteration forced by an estimate

The feed is read $U\nu_{\text{feed}} = 5 \times 10^9$ times a day, about $5.8 \times 10^4$ times a second and three times
that in the busiest hour. Liu's table gives a few hundred reads per second for a database and tens of thousands for
memory [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, App. 2], so the design without a cache would need hundreds of database replicas.
The cache in @fig-three-tier is the result of this iteration: the estimate showed that step 4 did not meet the load,
and step 4 was revised. Xu's question "if your current design supports 1 million users, what changes do you need to
make to support 10 million users?" starts the same loop [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 3, Step 4].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise orders the artefacts of the design process by their dependencies. It is the argument of
@exm-process-liu-order made mechanical, so that a program can check it.

::: {#exr-process-order}
#### Ordering the artefacts

Each artefact depends on others: the interface on the requirements; the request rates on the interface and the
workload; the storage estimate on the data model and the workload; the diagram on the interface; the data model on the
diagram; the deep dives on the estimates and the diagram. Give an order of the steps in which every artefact comes
after the ones it depends on.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The dependencies form a directed graph without cycles, and any topological order works. One is: requirements,
interface, diagram, request rates, data model, storage estimate, deep dives. It places the request-rate estimate after
the interface and the storage estimate after the data model, which is Liu's order; Xu's order, with all estimates
before the diagram, violates the dependency of the storage estimate on the data model.

## Python

A topological sort of the dependency graph with the standard library.

```{.python .run}
from graphlib import TopologicalSorter
deps = {"interface": {"requirements"}, "request rates": {"interface", "requirements"},
        "diagram": {"interface"}, "data model": {"diagram"},
        "storage estimate": {"data model", "requirements"},
        "deep dives": {"request rates", "storage estimate", "diagram"}}
print(" -> ".join(TopologicalSorter(deps).static_order()))
```

```{.text .run-output}
requirements -> interface -> request rates -> diagram -> data model -> storage estimate -> deep dives
```
::::
:::

The second exercise checks the completeness condition of step 4 on a diagram given as a graph. It is the hand trace of
@exm-process-flow done by a search.

::: {#exr-process-paths}
#### Every endpoint has a path

Write the arrows of @fig-three-tier as a directed graph, and check that the upload and feed endpoints reach every store
they need: upload must reach the metadata database, the object store and the queue; feed must reach the cache and the
database.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

From the client the arrows lead to the load balancer and the application servers, and from there to the cache, the
database, the object store and the queue. Every required store is reachable, so both endpoints have a path. A missing
arrow, for example from the servers to the queue, would make the upload flow incomplete, and the search would show it.

## Python

A breadth-first search from the client over the arrows of the diagram.

```{.python .run}
from collections import deque
arrows = {"client": ["lb", "cdn"], "lb": ["app"], "app": ["cache", "db", "objects", "queue"],
          "queue": ["workers"], "workers": ["objects"], "cdn": ["objects"]}
def reachable(start):
    seen, todo = {start}, deque([start])
    while todo:
        for nxt in arrows.get(todo.popleft(), []):
            if nxt not in seen:
                seen.add(nxt)
                todo.append(nxt)
    return seen
r = reachable("client")
for endpoint, needs in [("upload", {"db", "objects", "queue"}), ("feed", {"cache", "db"})]:
    print(endpoint, "complete" if needs <= r else f"missing {needs - r}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
upload complete
feed complete
```
::::
:::

The third exercise asks for a diagram, so its solution shows the diagram's source with the drawing. The system is Xu's
URL shortener of @exm-req-url-shortener.

::: {#exr-process-url-shortener-diagram}
#### A container diagram for the URL shortener

Draw a container diagram for the URL shortener, with a load balancer, web servers, an identifier generator, a cache and a
database, and check that both endpoints are served. Xu estimates $1160$ writes and $11\,600$ reads per second
[@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 8]; say which arrow carries most of the load.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The user calls the load balancer, which forwards to the web servers. *Shorten* takes a new identifier from the
generator and writes the pair to the database (and the cache); *redirect* reads the cache and, on a miss, the database,
then answers with a redirect. Reads are ten times as frequent as writes, so the arrow from the web servers to the cache
carries most of the load, and the cache is what keeps the database's read rate low.

## Python

The diagram is written in D2; the code checks its two flows and the share of reads.

```{.python .run}
arrows = {("user", "lb"), ("lb", "web"), ("web", "ids"), ("web", "cache"), ("web", "db")}
flows = {"shorten": [("user", "lb"), ("lb", "web"), ("web", "ids"), ("web", "db")],
         "redirect": [("user", "lb"), ("lb", "web"), ("web", "cache"), ("web", "db")]}
for name, needed in flows.items():
    missing = set(needed) - arrows
    print(name, "served" if not missing else f"missing {missing}")
writes, reads = 1160, 11600
print(f"share of requests that read: {reads / (reads + writes):.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
shorten served
redirect served
share of requests that read: 0.909
```

The D2 source of the diagram:

```d2
...@../../../_filters/d2-theme

direction: right

user: User {
  shape: person
}

shortener: URL shortener {
  lb: Load balancer
  web: Web servers {
    style.multiple: true
  }
  ids: ID generator
  cache: Cache {
    shape: cylinder
  }
  db: URL database {
    shape: cylinder
  }

  lb -> web
  web -> ids: next ID
  web -> cache: "short -> long"
  web -> db: "read on miss, write"
}

user -> shortener.lb: "POST shorten, GET short URL"
shortener.lb -> user: "short URL, or 301 redirect" {
  style.stroke-dash: 3
}
```

![Container diagram of the URL shortener: a load balancer, web servers, an identifier generator, a cache and a URL
database.](figures/url_shortener.svg){#fig-url-shortener width=90%}
::::
:::

The fourth exercise looks for single points of failure in a diagram, the risk behind @exm-process-deep-dive. A
component is one when removing it disconnects a client from a store that some endpoint needs.

::: {#exr-process-spof}
#### Finding single points of failure

In @fig-three-tier, treat the application servers as one box and the database as one box. Which components, if removed,
cut the client off from the metadata database? What changes if the load balancer is duplicated?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Every path from the client to the database passes through the load balancer, the application tier and the database, so
removing any one of these three boxes cuts it. The application tier is a group of interchangeable machines, and only the
loss of the whole group cuts the path, so the real single points of failure are the load balancer and the database. With
two load balancers the search finds only the application tier and the database, and @exm-process-deep-dive removes the
database.

## Python

For each component, remove it and test whether the database is still reachable from the client; then repeat with two
load balancers.

```{.python .run}
def cuts(arrows, target="db"):
    nodes = {n for n in arrows} | {m for v in arrows.values() for m in v}
    out = []
    for x in sorted(nodes - {"client"}):
        seen, todo = {"client"}, ["client"]
        while todo:
            for m in arrows.get(todo.pop(), []):
                if m != x and m not in seen:
                    seen.add(m)
                    todo.append(m)
        if target not in seen:
            out.append(x)
    return out
one_lb = {"client": ["lb"], "lb": ["app"], "app": ["db", "cache"]}
two_lb = {"client": ["lb1", "lb2"], "lb1": ["app"], "lb2": ["app"], "app": ["db", "cache"]}
print("one load balancer:", cuts(one_lb))
print("two load balancers:", cuts(two_lb))
```

```{.text .run-output}
one load balancer: ['app', 'db', 'lb']
two load balancers: ['app', 'db']
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise sizes the data model of @exm-process-data-model, which is the input of the storage estimate. It uses
Liu's table of field sizes.

::: {#exr-process-row-sizes}
#### Sizes of the rows

Using Liu's sizes (Int 4 bytes, BigInt 8, Timestamp 4, one byte per character [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, App. 3]),
give the size of a `follows` row and of a `photos` row with a 100-character caption and a 40-character object key. If
every user follows 200 others, how large is the `follows` table for $10^8$ users?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A `follows` row is two BigInts and a Timestamp, $8 + 8 + 4 = 20$ bytes; a `photos` row is $8 + 8 + 100 + 40 + 4 = 160$
bytes. The table has $2 \times 10^{10}$ rows, so $4 \times 10^{11}$ bytes, $400\,\mathrm{GB}$, before indexes and
replicas: enough to rule out a single small database but not to dominate a photo service's storage.

## Python

The row sizes and the table size.

```{.python .run}
size = {"Int": 4, "BigInt": 8, "Timestamp": 4}
follows = 2 * size["BigInt"] + size["Timestamp"]
photos = 2 * size["BigInt"] + 100 + 40 + size["Timestamp"]
print(f"follows row {follows} B, photos row {photos} B")
print(f"follows table: {1e8 * 200 * follows / 1e9:.0f} GB")
```

```{.text .run-output}
follows row 20 B, photos row 160 B
follows table: 400 GB
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise concerns the interface again. A client that retries an upload after a timeout may store the same
photo twice unless the endpoint is designed for retries.

::: {#exr-process-idempotent}
#### An idempotent upload

Liu recommends idempotent APIs [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "API Design"]. Explain how a client-generated
upload key makes `POST /photos` idempotent, and show the difference for a client that sends each of five uploads twice.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The client generates a random key for each upload and sends it with every attempt. The server stores the key with the
photo and, if a request arrives with a key it has seen, returns the stored identifier instead of storing again. Repeating
a request then has the same effect as sending it once, which is the definition of idempotence. Without the key, ten
requests store ten photos; with it, five.

## Python

A dictionary stands for the store; each of five uploads is sent twice, with and without keys.

```{.python .run}
import random, uuid
rng = random.Random(3)
store_plain, store_keyed = [], {}
for i in range(5):
    key = uuid.UUID(int=rng.getrandbits(128))
    for attempt in range(2):
        store_plain.append(f"photo {i}")
        store_keyed.setdefault(key, f"photo {i}")
print("without keys:", len(store_plain), "photos stored")
print("with keys:   ", len(store_keyed), "photos stored")
```

```{.text .run-output}
without keys: 10 photos stored
with keys:    5 photos stored
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise builds the data model in a real database engine and runs the feed query against it. It is the
first use of SQLite in the tutorial.

::: {#exr-process-sqlite-feed}
#### The feed query

Create the three tables of @exm-process-data-model in SQLite, with an index on `photos(user_id, created_at)`, insert a
small social graph, and write the query that returns the most recent photos of the users that user 1 follows.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The feed is a join of `follows` with `photos` on the followee, filtered by the follower and ordered by time:
`SELECT p.photo_id, p.user_id FROM follows f JOIN photos p ON p.user_id = f.followee_id WHERE f.follower_id = 1 ORDER BY
p.created_at DESC LIMIT 10`. The index lets the database find each followee's photos without scanning the table. This
"pull" form of the feed is what the cache of @exm-process-iteration saves the database from repeating.

## Python

An in-memory database with three users; user 1 follows users 2 and 3, and the query returns their photos newest first.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE users(user_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, created_at INTEGER);
CREATE TABLE photos(photo_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, user_id INTEGER, caption TEXT, object_key TEXT, created_at INTEGER);
CREATE TABLE follows(follower_id INTEGER, followee_id INTEGER, created_at INTEGER,
                     PRIMARY KEY (follower_id, followee_id));
CREATE INDEX photos_by_user ON photos(user_id, created_at);
INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 'ana', 0), (2, 'ben', 0), (3, 'chen', 0);
INSERT INTO follows VALUES (1, 2, 1), (1, 3, 1);
INSERT INTO photos VALUES (10, 2, 'sea', 'k10', 100), (11, 3, 'hill', 'k11', 105),
                          (12, 1, 'me', 'k12', 110), (13, 2, 'boat', 'k13', 120);
""")
feed = db.execute("""SELECT p.photo_id, p.user_id, p.caption FROM follows f
                     JOIN photos p ON p.user_id = f.followee_id
                     WHERE f.follower_id = 1 ORDER BY p.created_at DESC LIMIT 10""").fetchall()
print(feed)
```

```{.text .run-output}
[(13, 2, 'boat'), (11, 3, 'hill'), (10, 2, 'sea')]
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise is a deep dive in numbers. It asks how good a cache must be for the database behind it to keep up.

::: {#exr-process-cache-hit-ratio}
#### How good must the cache be?

Feed requests arrive at $1.74 \times 10^5$ per second at peak, and a fraction $h$ of them is answered by the cache. The
database replicas can serve $10^4$ reads per second together. What hit ratio $h$ is needed? What if the database
capacity doubles?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The database receives the misses, $(1 - h) \times 1.74 \times 10^5$ per second, which must not exceed $10^4$; so $1 - h
\leq 0.0575$ and $h \geq 0.9425$. With twice the capacity, $h \geq 0.885$. The deep dive's decision depends on whether a
hit ratio of $94\%$ is plausible for the feed, which is a question about the workload, not about the cache.

## Python

The required hit ratio for the two capacities.

```{.python .run}
peak = 1.74e5
for capacity in (1e4, 2e4):
    print(f"database capacity {capacity:.0f}/s: hit ratio >= {1 - capacity / peak:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
database capacity 10000/s: hit ratio >= 0.9425
database capacity 20000/s: hit ratio >= 0.8851
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise is about iteration. When an assumption changes, the artefacts that depend on it must be revisited,
and they are found by following the dependencies forwards.

::: {#exr-process-revisit}
#### What to revisit when an assumption changes

The product team adds one-minute videos of $90\,\mathrm{MB}$ (Liu's 1080p figure [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, App.
3]) beside photos. With the dependencies of @exr-process-order, plus "workload" on which the request rates and the
storage estimate depend, which artefacts must be revisited?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The change is to the workload assumptions (object sizes) and, since videos need new endpoints, to the functional
requirements. Everything that depends on either, directly or through other artefacts, must be revisited: the interface,
the request rates, the diagram, the data model, the storage estimate and the deep dives. In a design of this size a
change of requirements touches every artefact; a change of the workload alone would leave the interface, the diagram and
the data model in place.

## Python

The artefacts downstream of a change, found by following the dependency graph forwards.

```{.python .run}
deps = {"interface": {"requirements"}, "request rates": {"interface", "workload"},
        "diagram": {"interface"}, "data model": {"diagram"},
        "storage estimate": {"data model", "workload"},
        "deep dives": {"request rates", "storage estimate", "diagram"}}
def downstream(changed):
    out, grew = set(), True
    while grew:
        new = {a for a, d in deps.items() if d & (changed | out)} - out
        out |= new
        grew = bool(new)
    return sorted(out)
print("workload only:          ", downstream({"workload"}))
print("workload and requirements:", downstream({"workload", "requirements"}))
```

```{.text .run-output}
workload only:           ['deep dives', 'request rates', 'storage estimate']
workload and requirements: ['data model', 'deep dives', 'diagram', 'interface', 'request rates', 'storage estimate']
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise is Xu's wrap-up question in numbers. It scales the load of every tier by ten and asks which tier
first needs more than one machine.

::: {#exr-process-next-scale}
#### The next scale curve

In its first year, before it reaches the workload of @exm-req-workload-assumptions, the photo-sharing service sends, at
peak, $2 \times 10^4$ requests per second to the load balancer,
$2 \times 10^4$ to the application tier, $1.7 \times 10^4$ to the cache and $1.2 \times 10^3$ to the database. One
machine handles $10^5$ per second as a load balancer, $2 \times 10^3$ as an application server, $10^5$ as a cache and
$2 \times 10^3$ as a database. How many machines does each tier need today and at ten times the load, and which tier
changes its design rather than its size?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Today: one load balancer, $10$ application servers, one cache and one database. At ten times the load: $2$ load
balancers, $100$ application servers, $2$ cache machines and $6$ databases. The stateless tiers only grow. The database
goes from one machine to six, and a database cannot simply be copied when it also takes writes: its data must be
replicated or partitioned, which is a change of design. Xu's question "what changes do you need to make to support 10
million users?" is answered by this tier.

## Python

The number of machines per tier, $\lceil\text{load}/\text{capacity}\rceil$, at both scales.

```{.python .run}
from math import ceil
tiers = {"load balancer": (2e4, 1e5), "application": (2e4, 2e3), "cache": (1.7e4, 1e5), "database": (1.2e3, 2e3)}
for name, (load, cap) in tiers.items():
    print(f"{name:13s}: today {ceil(load / cap):3d}, at 10x {ceil(10 * load / cap):3d}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
load balancer: today   1, at 10x   2
application  : today  10, at 10x 100
cache        : today   1, at 10x   2
database     : today   1, at 10x   6
```
::::
:::
::::

## Architectural characteristics and trade-offs {#sec-architectural-characteristics}

Non-functional requirements say how well a system must work; architectural characteristics are the subset of them that
decide its shape. Gandhi, Richards and Ford separate the two by asking whether a property "require[s] special
structural support to succeed" [@gandhiHeadFirstSoftware2024, Ch. 2, p. 47]: every system must be reasonably secure,
but security becomes architectural only when it forces a component, a boundary or a protocol of its own. The same
authors state the two laws that govern decisions about such properties: that everything in software architecture is a
trade-off, and that "why is more important than how" [@gandhiHeadFirstSoftware2024, Ch. 3, pp. 90 and 96]. Tan's
chapter on non-functional requirements lists the characteristics a system design discusses, from scalability and
availability to cost and complexity, and repeats that they are "commonly traded off against each other"
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Ch. 3]. This section defines the notion and works through the trade-offs, which the later
sections then quantify.

For more on this topic, see @gandhiHeadFirstSoftware2024 [Chs. 2-3], @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Secs. 1.1 and 3.1-3.8]
and @saltzer1984end.

### Architectural characteristics

The definition below follows Gandhi, Richards and Ford's three-part definition. Each part excludes something: the
first excludes the domain functions, which are the functional requirements; the second excludes properties that good
code alone achieves; and the third excludes properties nobody needs, which an architect could support only at the cost
of the ones that matter.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-architectural-characteristic}
#### Architectural characteristic

An **architectural characteristic** of a system is a property of it that satisfies three conditions:

1. it is not a domain requirement: it does not say which operations the system performs, but how well, by a criterion
   that can be stated for any domain (performance, scalability, availability, durability, consistency, security,
   cost, maintainability, and so on);
2. it influences the structure of the system: meeting it requires a decision about components, their number, placement
   or connections (for example replication, partitioning, a cache or a separate service), not only careful coding of a
   given structure;
3. it is critical or important to the success of the system, as shown by the requirements specification
   (@def-requirements-specification) or by knowledge of its domain.

A **trade-off** between two characteristics is a design decision that improves one of them and degrades the other.
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Performance is the first characteristic in most lists and the one most often missing from requirements documents. It
meets all three conditions in the running example.

::: {#exm-char-performance}
#### Performance of the feed

The feed's latency target of @exm-req-latency-quantile is not a domain function (condition 1). It cannot be met by a
single database at the load of @exm-process-iteration, so it shapes the structure by adding a cache (condition 2). It
is important because a slow feed loses users (condition 3). Gandhi, Richards and Ford note that performance "often
doesn't appear in requirements documents" [@gandhiHeadFirstSoftware2024, Ch. 2, p. 46], which is why the design
process asks for it.
:::

Security shows how condition 2 separates a characteristic from good practice. The same property can be one or the
other, depending on the effort it needs.

::: {#exm-char-security}
#### When security is a characteristic

"Security is a concern in virtually every project, and all systems must take baseline precautions during design and
coding. However, security becomes an architectural characteristic when the architect needs to make a special effort to
accommodate it" [@gandhiHeadFirstSoftware2024, Ch. 2, p. 47]. For the photo-sharing service, encrypted connections and
hashed passwords are baseline; storing private photos in a separately keyed store with its own access service is
structural, and makes security a characteristic.
:::

Different domains need different characteristics, though some, like scalability, are needed almost everywhere. Gandhi,
Richards and Ford compare a bank and an auction site.

::: {#exm-char-bank-auction}
#### A bank and an auction site

The bank needs auditability, data integrity and security; the auction site needs usability, reliability and the
consistent ordering of bids; both need scalability, for many concurrent users [@gandhiHeadFirstSoftware2024, Ch. 2,
p. 44]. Condition 3 is what differs: auditability is critical to a bank and irrelevant to most auction sites.
:::

Scalability has two forms with very different structures, and Tan explains why system design means the second. The
difference is condition 2 itself.

::: {#exm-char-vertical-horizontal}
#### Vertical and horizontal scaling

Vertical scaling buys a bigger machine; it changes no structure but has three costs: "monetary cost increases faster
than the upgraded hardware's performance", there are "technological limits", and it "may require downtime". Horizontal
scaling spreads load "across multiple hosts" and requires a load balancer and stateless servers
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 3.1]. Only the second is a structural decision, and it is what the word "scalable"
means in system design.
:::

Availability and consistency are the standard pair in tension. Tan's advice is to establish which of them the system
really needs before designing for both.

::: {#exm-char-availability-consistency}
#### Availability against consistency

"Do not assume that strong consistency and low latency are required" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 3.2]. A request
that must read the latest write needs the replica that holds it, so it fails when that replica is unreachable; a request
that may read a slightly stale copy can be served by any replica. Choosing the second for the feed, as
@exm-req-staleness allows, trades consistency for availability.
:::

Cost trades against almost everything else, and Tan lists three typical cases. Each has a structural lever, as
condition 2 requires.

::: {#exm-char-cost}
#### Cost as a characteristic

Tan's examples are "higher cost for lower complexity by vertical scaling instead of horizontal scaling", "lower
availability for improved costs by decreasing the redundancy of a system (such as the number of hosts, or the
replication factor in a database)", and "higher latency for improved costs by using a data center in a cheaper location
that is further away from users" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 3.8]. The levers are the size of machines, the number
of replicas and the placement of data centres.
:::

Gandhi, Richards and Ford illustrate the first law with a choice between two messaging structures. The answer depends
on which characteristic matters more, and so on the business.

::: {#exm-char-queue-topic}
#### A queue or a topic

A trading service must tell several downstream services about each trade. Point-to-point queues, one per consumer,
keep each consumer's access separately controlled; one topic that every consumer reads lets new consumers join without
changing the producer. "If security is paramount, we should probably go with queues", but a business whose "biggest
priority" is extensibility should "pick the topic option": "it depends!" [@gandhiHeadFirstSoftware2024, Ch. 3, p. 90].
:::

Condition 3 is the filter against over-engineering, and the same authors put a number on it. Their advice is to keep
the list short and to rank it.

::: {#exm-char-limit}
#### Keeping the list short

"Every architectural characteristic the system must support adds complexity", so architects "should try to pick as few
architectural characteristics as possible" [@gandhiHeadFirstSoftware2024, Ch. 2, p. 48]. Their worked analysis limits
the list "to seven characteristics" and then marks "the top three most important" (p. 70). For the photo-sharing
service the three might be availability, performance of the feed and durability of photos.
:::

The second law asks that each decision be recorded with its reason. The record has a fixed form, the architectural
decision record.

::: {#exm-char-adr}
#### A decision record for the feed cache

"An ADR has seven sections: Title, Status, Context, Decision, Consequences, Governance, and finally Notes"
[@gandhiHeadFirstSoftware2024, Ch. 3, p. 97]. For the cache of @exm-process-iteration: *Title*: cache the feed in memory.
*Status*: accepted. *Context*: $1.7 \times 10^5$ feed reads per second at peak against a few hundred per database
machine. *Decision*: a cache in front of the metadata database, refreshed on upload. *Consequences*: feeds may be a few
seconds stale; one more component to operate. *Governance*: a dashboard of the hit ratio, alerting below $90\%$.
*Notes*: author and date.
:::

The last example is the classic argument about where in a layered system a property should be implemented. Saltzer,
Reed and Clark show that the answer is a trade-off of performance, not a question of correctness.

::: {#exm-char-end-to-end}
#### The end-to-end argument

To copy a file reliably from one host to another, the file-transfer program must in the end compare a checksum of the
file at both ends and retry if they differ, whatever the network guarantees, because errors can also occur on the disks
and in the hosts' memories. Reliability inside the network therefore cannot replace the end-to-end check; it only
reduces how often the check fails. "The amount of effort to put into reliability measures within the data communication
system is seen to be an engineering tradeoff based on performance, rather than a requirement for correctness"
[@saltzer1984end, "End-to-end caretaking" and "Performance aspects"].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise applies the three conditions of the definition to five candidate properties. Each candidate fails a
different condition, or none of them.

::: {#exr-char-classify}
#### Which are characteristics?

For the photo-sharing service, decide which of these are architectural characteristics: (a) "users can follow other
users"; (b) "photos are never lost" (with the target of @exm-req-durability); (c) "the code follows a style guide";
(d) "the service survives the loss of a data centre"; (e) "the service runs on a mainframe for regulatory audits", for a
service with no such regulation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

(a) is a domain function and fails condition 1. (b) is a characteristic: it is not a domain function, it forces
replication of stored photos (condition 2), and it is critical. (c) fails condition 2: it is achieved by careful coding
of any structure. (d) is a characteristic: it forces copies in several data centres and a way to switch between them.
(e) fails condition 3: without the regulation it is important to nobody.

## Python

The three conditions as a table; a candidate is a characteristic when it meets all three.

```{.python .run}
candidates = {"(a) follow users": (False, False, True), "(b) photos never lost": (True, True, True),
              "(c) style guide": (True, False, True), "(d) survive loss of a data centre": (True, True, True),
              "(e) mainframe without regulation": (True, True, False)}
for name, conditions in candidates.items():
    print(f"{name:34s} {'characteristic' if all(conditions) else 'not a characteristic'}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
(a) follow users                   not a characteristic
(b) photos never lost              characteristic
(c) style guide                    not a characteristic
(d) survive loss of a data centre  characteristic
(e) mainframe without regulation   not a characteristic
```
::::
:::

The second exercise counts how fast the work of trading characteristics off grows with their number. It is the
arithmetic behind the advice of @exm-char-limit.

::: {#exr-char-pairs}
#### How many trade-offs?

If every pair of chosen characteristics may have to be traded off against each other, how many pairs must be analysed
for 3, 7 and 20 characteristics?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

There are $\binom k2 = k(k - 1)/2$ pairs: $3$, $21$ and $190$. The work grows quadratically, so going from seven to
twenty characteristics multiplies it by about nine, which is one reason to keep the list to seven.

## Python

The binomial coefficients.

```{.python .run}
from math import comb
for k in (3, 7, 20):
    print(f"{k:2d} characteristics: {comb(k, 2):3d} pairs")
```

```{.text .run-output}
 3 characteristics:   3 pairs
 7 characteristics:  21 pairs
20 characteristics: 190 pairs
```
::::
:::

The third exercise makes Tan's first objection to vertical scaling precise. It compares a price that grows faster than
capacity with the linear price of adding machines.

::: {#exr-char-vertical-cost}
#### Where vertical scaling stops paying

Suppose a machine with $k$ cores costs $100\,k^{1.5}$ per month, and the work is perfectly divisible. Compare the
cost of $64$ cores as one machine and as eight machines of $8$ cores, and find the largest single machine that costs at
most twice as much per core as an $8$-core machine.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

One $64$-core machine costs $100 \times 64^{1.5} = 51\,200$; eight $8$-core machines cost $8 \times 100 \times 8^{1.5} =
18\,102$. The cost per core is $100\,k^{0.5}$, which is at most twice that of $k = 8$ when $k^{0.5} \leq 2 \times
8^{0.5}$, that is $k \leq 32$. Beyond that the structure must change to horizontal scaling, with the load balancer and
stateless servers it requires.

## Python

The two costs and the cost per core for a range of sizes.

```{.python .run}
price = lambda k: 100 * k**1.5
print(f"one 64-core machine {price(64):.0f}, eight 8-core machines {8 * price(8):.0f}")
for k in (8, 16, 32, 64):
    print(f"{k:2d} cores: {price(k) / k:6.1f} per core, ratio to 8 cores {price(k) / k / (price(8) / 8):.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
one 64-core machine 51200, eight 8-core machines 18102
 8 cores:  282.8 per core, ratio to 8 cores 1.00
16 cores:  400.0 per core, ratio to 8 cores 1.41
32 cores:  565.7 per core, ratio to 8 cores 2.00
64 cores:  800.0 per core, ratio to 8 cores 2.83
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise prices the second of Tan's cost trade-offs of @exm-char-cost, the replication factor. It shows the
size of the saving that lower redundancy buys.

::: {#exr-char-replication-cost}
#### The price of a replica

Storing one petabyte of photos costs $20$ per terabyte per month for each copy. Give the monthly cost with replication
factors $N = 2$ and $N = 3$, and the yearly saving of the lower factor.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

One petabyte is $1000$ terabytes, so each copy costs $20\,000$ a month: $40\,000$ for $N = 2$ and $60\,000$ for $N = 3$.
The lower factor saves $20\,000$ a month, $240\,000$ a year, and the price is a lower durability and availability of the
data, which the requirements must be able to afford.

## Python

The monthly costs and the yearly saving.

```{.python .run}
tb, price = 1000, 20
cost = {N: N * tb * price for N in (2, 3)}
print(cost, "yearly saving:", 12 * (cost[3] - cost[2]))
```

```{.text .run-output}
{2: 40000, 3: 60000} yearly saving: 240000
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise prices the third trade-off of @exm-char-cost, a cheaper but farther data centre. The added latency
comes from distance, as in @exr-req-light-bound.

::: {#exr-char-farther-dc}
#### A cheaper, farther data centre

A data centre $3000\,\mathrm{km}$ farther from the users costs $15\%$ less. By how much does it lengthen a request that
makes two sequential round trips between client and data centre, at $2 \times 10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in fibre? Is it
compatible with a budget of $100\,\mathrm{ms}$ that currently has $40\,\mathrm{ms}$ to spare?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Each round trip adds $2 \times 3 \times 10^6 / (2 \times 10^8) = 30\,\mathrm{ms}$ at least, so two add $60\,\mathrm{ms}$.
That exceeds the $40\,\mathrm{ms}$ to spare, so the cheaper location breaks the latency requirement unless one round
trip is removed (for example by reusing connections), in which case $30\,\mathrm{ms}$ fits.

## Python

The added time for one and two round trips.

```{.python .run}
extra_rtt_ms = 2 * 3000e3 / 2e8 * 1e3
for trips in (1, 2):
    added = trips * extra_rtt_ms
    print(f"{trips} round trip(s): +{added:.0f} ms, fits in 40 ms: {added <= 40}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
1 round trip(s): +30 ms, fits in 40 ms: True
2 round trip(s): +60 ms, fits in 40 ms: False
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise writes a decision record. The check that comes with it is the one a team would automate: that a
record has all seven sections.

::: {#exr-char-write-adr}
#### Writing a decision record

Write an architectural decision record for the choice of @exm-char-availability-consistency, serving feeds from read
replicas that may lag the primary, in the seven sections of @exm-char-adr.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

*Title*: serve feeds from read replicas. *Status*: accepted. *Context*: feed reads outnumber writes by about $250$ to
one; one primary cannot serve them; the staleness requirement allows $5\,\mathrm{s}$. *Decision*: two read replicas
behind the cache; writes go to the primary. *Consequences*: a user may not see a just-uploaded photo of a friend for a
few seconds; replica lag must be monitored. *Governance*: alert when replica lag exceeds $2\,\mathrm{s}$. *Notes*:
alternatives considered were partitioning by user (deferred) and a single larger machine (rejected: a single point of
failure). The *why* is the context and the rejected alternatives, which is what the second law asks to keep.

## Python

The record as a mapping, and a check that it has the seven sections in order.

```{.python .run}
SECTIONS = ["Title", "Status", "Context", "Decision", "Consequences", "Governance", "Notes"]
adr = {"Title": "Serve feeds from read replicas", "Status": "accepted",
       "Context": "reads/writes about 250; staleness up to 5 s allowed",
       "Decision": "two read replicas behind the cache", "Consequences": "feeds may lag by seconds",
       "Governance": "alert when replica lag > 2 s", "Notes": "rejected: one larger machine (single point of failure)"}
print("complete and ordered:", list(adr) == SECTIONS)
```

```{.text .run-output}
complete and ordered: True
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise quantifies the end-to-end argument of @exm-char-end-to-end. It computes how the number of attempts
of an end-to-end retry grows with the size of the file.

::: {#exr-char-end-to-end-retries}
#### End-to-end retries on a lossy network

Saltzer, Reed and Clark consider "a network that is somewhat unreliable, dropping one message of each hundred messages
sent", and note that the probability that all packets arrive "decreases exponentially with the file length"
[@saltzer1984end, "Performance aspects"]. If a file of $k$ packets is resent whole until every packet arrives, with
packets lost independently, give the expected number of attempts for $k = 10$, $100$ and $1000$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

An attempt succeeds when all $k$ packets arrive, with probability $0.99^k$ by independence. The attempts are independent
trials, so their number is geometric with mean $1/0.99^k$: $1.11$, $2.73$ and $2.3 \times 10^4$. A thousand-packet file
practically never gets through whole, so some reliability in the lower layer pays for itself, though it is not needed
for correctness.

## Python

The expected numbers of attempts, and a simulation of the case $k = 100$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
for k in (10, 100, 1000):
    print(f"k = {k:4d}: expected attempts {1 / 0.99**k:.3g}")
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
attempts = rng.geometric(0.99**100, 10**5)
print(f"simulated mean for k = 100: {attempts.mean():.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
k =   10: expected attempts 1.11
k =  100: expected attempts 2.73
k = 1000: expected attempts 2.32e+04
simulated mean for k = 100: 2.727
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise adds the lower-layer reliability that @exr-char-end-to-end-retries shows is worth having. Each hop
now retries a lost packet itself, which costs bandwidth but rescues long files.

::: {#exr-char-hop-retries}
#### Retries in the lower layer

Let each packet be retried by the network until it arrives, so that the end-to-end check fails only on corruption that
the network cannot see, with probability $10^{-6}$ per packet. Give the expected number of end-to-end attempts for
$k = 1000$ and the expected number of packet transmissions per packet delivered when each transmission is lost with
probability $0.01$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

An end-to-end attempt now fails with probability $1 - (1 - 10^{-6})^{1000} \approx 10^{-3}$, so the expected number of
attempts is $1/(1 - 10^{-6})^{1000} = 1.001$. Each packet needs a geometric number of transmissions with success
probability $0.99$, mean $1/0.99 = 1.0101$: one percent more bandwidth buys an end-to-end success rate of $99.9\%$
instead of $4 \times 10^{-5}$. The end-to-end check stays, as the argument requires, but rarely fires.

## Python

The two expectations.

```{.python .run}
k = 1000
print(f"end-to-end attempts: {1 / (1 - 1e-6)**k:.4f}")
print(f"transmissions per packet: {1 / 0.99:.4f}")
print(f"P(whole file in one attempt) without hop retries: {0.99**k:.1e}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
end-to-end attempts: 1.0010
transmissions per packet: 1.0101
P(whole file in one attempt) without hop retries: 4.3e-05
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise turns a trade-off analysis into numbers. It weighs three designs against the ranked characteristics
of @exm-char-limit and asks how robust the winner is.

::: {#exr-char-weighted}
#### A weighted comparison

Score three designs from $1$ to $5$ on availability, feed performance and durability, with weights $0.5$, $0.3$ and
$0.2$: design A (one region, cache) scores $(3, 5, 4)$; B (two regions, cache) $(5, 4, 5)$; C (two regions, no cache)
$(5, 2, 5)$. Which design wins, and how far must the weight of performance rise before A beats B, with the other two
weights in their original proportion?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The weighted sums are $0.5 \cdot 3 + 0.3 \cdot 5 + 0.2 \cdot 4 = 3.8$ for A, $4.7$ for B and $4.1$ for C, so B wins. With
