performance weight $w$ and the others $\frac58(1 - w)$ and $\frac38(1 - w)$, A scores $5w + (1 - w)(\frac{15}8 +
\frac{12}8) = 5w + 3.375(1 - w)$ and B scores $4w + 5(1 - w)$. A beats B when $w > 1.625(1 - w)$, that is $w >
0.619$. The ranking of the designs is robust unless performance is weighted more than everything else together.

## Python

The scores, and the break-even weight found by solving the linear equation.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
scores = {"A": np.array([3, 5, 4]), "B": np.array([5, 4, 5]), "C": np.array([5, 2, 5])}
w = np.array([0.5, 0.3, 0.2])
print({k: round(float(v @ w), 2) for k, v in scores.items()})
weights = lambda p: np.array([5 / 8 * (1 - p), p, 3 / 8 * (1 - p)])
diff = lambda p: (scores["A"] - scores["B"]) @ weights(p)
p0 = -diff(0) / (diff(1) - diff(0))
print(f"A beats B when the performance weight exceeds {p0:.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
{'A': 3.8, 'B': 4.7, 'C': 4.1}
A beats B when the performance weight exceeds 0.619
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise drops the weights, which are the weakest part of @exr-char-weighted, and keeps only the designs that
no other design beats on every characteristic. These are the designs among which a real trade-off has to be made.

::: {#exr-char-pareto}
#### The designs worth arguing about

Six designs have (monthly cost, $t_{0.99}$ in ms, availability): $(10, 300, 0.999)$, $(14, 200, 0.999)$, $(20, 200,
0.9999)$, $(25, 150, 0.9995)$, $(30, 120, 0.9999)$, $(32, 150, 0.9999)$. Lower cost and latency and higher availability
are better. Find the designs that are not dominated, that is, for which no other design is at least as good on all three
and better on one.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The last design, $(32, 150, 0.9999)$, is dominated by $(30, 120, 0.9999)$, which is cheaper, faster and as available. No
other design is dominated: the first is the cheapest, the second is faster than the first at a higher cost, the third
adds a nine, the fourth is faster than the third at a higher cost and lower availability, and the fifth is the fastest.
Five designs remain, and choosing among them is the trade-off: no ranking of the designs follows from the
characteristics alone, which is the first law.

## Python

A direct test of dominance between every pair of designs.

```{.python .run}
designs = [(10, 300, 0.999), (14, 200, 0.999), (20, 200, 0.9999), (25, 150, 0.9995), (30, 120, 0.9999),
           (32, 150, 0.9999)]
def dominates(a, b):
    at_least = a[0] <= b[0] and a[1] <= b[1] and a[2] >= b[2]
    return at_least and a != b
front = [d for d in designs if not any(dominates(e, d) for e in designs)]
print("not dominated:", front)
```

```{.text .run-output}
not dominated: [(10, 300, 0.999), (14, 200, 0.999), (20, 200, 0.9999), (25, 150, 0.9995), (30, 120, 0.9999)]
```
::::
:::
::::

## Units, powers of two and latency numbers {#sec-units-and-latency}

An estimate is only as good as its units. Xu's tips for estimation end with "Label your units", because "when you write
down '5', does it mean 5 KB or 5 MB?" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 2], and Liu reports candidates who were off "by a
magnitude of 1,000 because they confused GB with TB" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Common Mistakes"]. This
section fixes the units of the tutorial and the reference latencies that estimates start from, and then proves the rule
by which the latencies of the stages of a request combine into the latency of the request. The rule is simple for means
and subtle for quantiles, and the quantiles are what requirements are written in.

Sizes are counted in bytes ($\mathrm B$) and rates on networks in bits ($\mathrm b$), with $1\,\mathrm B = 8\,\mathrm b$.
Decimal prefixes are powers of ten, $1\,\mathrm{kB} = 10^3\,\mathrm B$, $1\,\mathrm{MB} = 10^6\,\mathrm B$, up to
$1\,\mathrm{PB} = 10^{15}\,\mathrm B$, which is how Liu's conversion table pairs "thousand" with KB and "quadrillion" with
PB [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, App. 1]. Binary prefixes are powers of two, $1\,\mathrm{KiB} = 2^{10}\,\mathrm B =
1024\,\mathrm B$ and $1\,\mathrm{GiB} = 2^{30}\,\mathrm B$; Xu's table of data volumes uses powers of two
[@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 2, "Power of two"]. The two agree to $2.4\%$ at the kilo level and drift apart by the
same factor at each step, $7.4\%$ at giga and $12.6\%$ at peta. A day has $86\,400\,\mathrm s$ and a 30-day month
$2.592 \times 10^6\,\mathrm s$.

The reference latencies below are Liu's, which follow the numbers Dean published for Google's machines and Xu
reproduces [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, App. 3; @SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 2]. They change with hardware, by
factors rather than orders of magnitude, and their use is to compare designs, not to predict a measurement.

| Operation | Latency |
|---|---|
| main-memory reference | $100\,\mathrm{ns}$ |
| read $1\,\mathrm{MB}$ sequentially from memory | $10\,\mu\mathrm s$ |
| random read from an SSD | $15\,\mu\mathrm s$ |
| read $1\,\mathrm{MB}$ sequentially from an SSD | $200\,\mu\mathrm s$ |
| round trip within a data centre | $0.5\,\mathrm{ms}$ |
| disk seek | $2\,\mathrm{ms}$ |
| read $1\,\mathrm{MB}$ sequentially from a disk | $1\,\mathrm{ms}$ |
| round trip California to Virginia | $60\,\mathrm{ms}$ |
| round trip California to the Netherlands | $150\,\mathrm{ms}$ |

Xu draws the lessons that "memory is fast but the disk is slow", that one should "avoid disk seeks if possible", and
that it "takes time to send data between" data centres in different regions [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 2]. Dean
and Barroso give the user's side: systems that respond "within 100ms" feel "more fluid and natural" than those that take
longer [@dean2013tail, p. 74]. The proposition below says how such numbers add up along a request.

For more on this topic, see @SystemDesignInterview2021 [Ch. 2], @liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Apps. 1-3],
@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024 [Ch. 2, "Latency"] and @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Sec. 3.4].

### Latency budgets of a request path

A request that passes through several stages one after another takes the sum of their times, and a designer who must
meet a target for the whole request splits it into a **budget** for each stage. For means the split is exact, because
expectations add. For quantiles it is not: the 99th percentile of a sum is not the sum of the 99th percentiles. The
proposition shows what can be said instead, with and without independence between the stages. It uses the union bound
and independence from
[Probability and statistics](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#prp-probability-rules).

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-latency-budget}
#### Latency budgets of sequential stages

Let a request pass through stages $1, \dots, k$ one after another, stage $i$ taking time $T_i \geq 0$, where $T_1, \dots,
T_k$ are random variables on one probability space, and let $T = T_1 + \dots + T_k$.

(a) If every $\mathbb E[T_i]$ is finite, then $\mathbb E[T] = \mathbb E[T_1] + \dots + \mathbb E[T_k]$.

(b) If $\mathbb P(T_i > \tau_i) \leq \varepsilon_i$ for each $i$, then
$$
\mathbb P(T > \tau_1 + \dots + \tau_k) \leq \varepsilon_1 + \dots + \varepsilon_k,
$$
whatever the dependence between the stages.

(c) If moreover $T_1, \dots, T_k$ are independent, then $\mathbb P(T \leq \tau_1 + \dots + \tau_k) \geq (1 -
\varepsilon_1)\cdots(1 - \varepsilon_k)$, which is at least $1 - \varepsilon_1 - \dots - \varepsilon_k$.

(d) For levels $q, q_1, \dots, q_k \in (0, 1)$ with $(1 - q_1) + \dots + (1 - q_k) \leq 1 - q$, the quantiles satisfy
$t_q(T) \leq t_{q_1}(T_1) + \dots + t_{q_k}(T_k)$.
:::

::::

*Proof.* (a) Expectation is linear.

(b) If $T_i \leq \tau_i$ for every $i$, then $T \leq \sum_i\tau_i$. Taking complements, the event $\{T > \sum_i\tau_i\}$
is contained in $\bigcup_i\{T_i > \tau_i\}$, whose probability is at most $\sum_i\mathbb P(T_i > \tau_i) \leq
\sum_i\varepsilon_i$ by monotonicity and the union bound. No independence is used.

(c) The event $\{T \leq \sum_i\tau_i\}$ contains $\bigcap_i\{T_i \leq \tau_i\}$, whose probability is $\prod_i\mathbb
P(T_i \leq \tau_i) \geq \prod_i(1 - \varepsilon_i)$ by independence. The last inequality, $\prod_i(1 - \varepsilon_i)
\geq 1 - \sum_i\varepsilon_i$ for $\varepsilon_i \in [0, 1]$, holds for $k = 1$, and if it holds for $k - 1$ factors then
$\prod_{i \leq k}(1 - \varepsilon_i) \geq (1 - \sum_{i < k}\varepsilon_i)(1 - \varepsilon_k) \geq 1 - \sum_{i \leq
k}\varepsilon_i$, because the dropped product $\varepsilon_k\sum_{i < k}\varepsilon_i$ is non-negative (when $1 -
\sum_{i<k}\varepsilon_i < 0$ the claim is trivial).

(d) Write $\tau_i = t_{q_i}(T_i) = \inf\{t : \mathbb P(T_i \leq t) \geq q_i\}$. A distribution function is
right-continuous, so the infimum is attained: $\mathbb P(T_i \leq \tau_i) \geq q_i$, that is $\mathbb P(T_i > \tau_i)
\leq 1 - q_i$. By (b), $\mathbb P(T > \sum_i\tau_i) \leq \sum_i(1 - q_i) \leq 1 - q$, so $\mathbb P(T \leq
\sum_i\tau_i) \geq q$, and $t_q(T) \leq \sum_i\tau_i$ by the definition of $t_q(T)$ as an infimum. $\square$

Part (d) is the rule a budget can rely on: to promise a $99$th percentile for the whole request, give each of $k$ stages
a budget at the level $1 - 0.01/k$, for example the $99.75$th percentile for four stages. Parts (b) and (d) are what
remains true when the stages share machines, networks or garbage-collection pauses, as Dean and Barroso stress they do
[@dean2013tail, p. 75]; part (c) is sharper but needs independence.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest use of part (a) adds fixed costs. Liu's table gives the cost of reading a megabyte from each kind of storage
as the sum of a seek and a sequential read.

::: {#exm-budget-read-one-mb}
#### Reading a megabyte

Liu adds a disk seek of $2\,\mathrm{ms}$ to a sequential read of $1\,\mathrm{ms}$ for a total of $3\,\mathrm{ms}$ from
disk, an SSD random read of $15\,\mu\mathrm s$ to $200\,\mu\mathrm s$ for about $0.2\,\mathrm{ms}$, and a memory reference
to $10\,\mu\mathrm s$ for $0.01\,\mathrm{ms}$ [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, App. 3]. Fetching the megabyte from another
machine in the same data centre adds a round trip of $0.5\,\mathrm{ms}$, so a remote memory read ($0.51\,\mathrm{ms}$) is
faster than a local disk read ($3\,\mathrm{ms}$): the reason caches are separate machines.
:::

The request path of the running example has six stages with budgets that add up to its target. The diagram is the
artefact a deep dive on latency produces.

::: {#exm-budget-request-path}
#### A budget for the feed

@fig-request-path splits the feed's target of $200\,\mathrm{ms}$ at the $99$th percentile into six budgets: the network
round trip, the load balancer, the application, the cache, the database on a miss and the serialisation of the response.
The budgets sum to $200\,\mathrm{ms}$. By part (d) they guarantee the target only if each is set at a level $q_i$ with
$\sum_i(1 - q_i) \leq 0.01$, for example the $99.83$th percentile of each of the six stages.

![The stages of a feed request with a latency budget for each, summing to the target for the whole
request.](figures/request_path.svg){#fig-request-path width=100%}
:::

Some budgets are set by geography before any software runs. A request that needs two round trips across an ocean cannot
meet a budget smaller than both together.

::: {#exm-budget-ocean}
#### Two round trips across the Atlantic

A client in California that opens a new encrypted connection to a server in the Netherlands needs at least one round
trip to set up the connection and one for the request, $2 \times 150 = 300\,\mathrm{ms}$ by part (a) with Liu's figure
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, App. 3]. A budget of $200\,\mathrm{ms}$ is impossible; reusing connections or serving
from a nearby region are the only remedies.
:::

Part (b) is the tool when nothing is known about dependence. It turns per-stage percentiles into a guarantee for the
whole path, at a loss that grows with the number of stages.

::: {#exm-budget-union}
#### Three stages at their 99th percentiles

If each of three stages exceeds its $99$th percentile $\tau_i$ with probability $0.01$, part (b) gives $\mathbb P(T >
\tau_1 + \tau_2 + \tau_3) \leq 0.03$. The sum of the three $99$th percentiles is therefore a $97$th-percentile bound for
the request, not a $99$th.
:::

Part (c) improves the bound when the stages are independent. For small $\varepsilon_i$ the improvement is tiny, which
is why the union bound costs so little in practice.

::: {#exm-budget-independent}
#### The same stages, independent

With independence, $\mathbb P(T \leq \tau_1 + \tau_2 + \tau_3) \geq 0.99^3 = 0.970299$, against $0.97$ from part (b).
The two bounds differ by the second-order terms $\sum_{i<j}\varepsilon_i\varepsilon_j = 3 \times 10^{-4}$ minus a
third-order one.
:::

The sum of the percentiles is a bound, and for independent stages it is a generous one. Two exponential stages make the
gap explicit.

::: {#exm-budget-not-additive}
#### Percentiles do not add

Let $T_1$, $T_2$ be independent exponential with mean $1$. Each has $t_{0.99} = \ln 100 = 4.605$, so the sum of the
percentiles is $9.21$. The sum $T$ has density $te^{-t}$ and $\mathbb P(T > t) = (1 + t)e^{-t}$, which equals $0.01$ at
$t = 6.638$. The true percentile is $28\%$ below the sum of percentiles, because both stages are rarely slow together.
:::

Dependence between the stages can close that gap. If the stages are always slow together, their percentiles add exactly,
and the sum of the percentiles is no longer generous.

::: {#exm-budget-comonotone}
#### Stages that are slow together

If both stages are slowed by the same cause, say $T_1 = T_2 = X$ with $X$ exponential of mean $1$, then $T = 2X$ and
$t_{0.99}(T) = 2\ln 100 = 9.21$, exactly the sum of the percentiles. The bound of part (d), with $q_1 = q_2 = 0.995$,
gives $2\ln 200 = 10.6$, which is still valid, as it must be whatever the dependence.
:::

The union bound itself can be attained, so part (b) cannot be improved without assumptions. The extreme case is stages
whose slow moments never overlap.

::: {#exm-budget-disjoint}
#### When the union bound is exact

Suppose a background job pauses exactly one of three stages at a time, each for $1\%$ of requests, never two at once,
and a paused stage exceeds its budget while an unpaused one stays within it. The events $\{T_i > \tau_i\}$ are disjoint,
so $\mathbb P(\text{some stage exceeds its budget}) = 0.03$ exactly. If any one overrun is enough to exceed the total
budget, the bound of part (b) is attained.
:::

Part (a) also explains a classic slow page. A page that issues many dependent queries one after another pays their
latencies in sequence.

::: {#exm-budget-sequential-queries}
#### Twenty queries in a row

A page that loads a list and then issues one database query per item, twenty in sequence, each taking $2\,\mathrm{ms}$
on average, spends $40\,\mathrm{ms}$ in queries by part (a). One query that fetches all twenty items in a join takes
about the time of one, a few milliseconds. Removing sequential stages is often cheaper than speeding each of them up.
:::

The last example compares two designs by their summed stages. Xu's conclusions from the latency numbers include
"compress data before sending it over the internet if possible" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 2]; part (a) says when.

::: {#exm-budget-compress}
#### Whether to compress

Sending $1\,\mathrm{MB}$ over a $100\,\mathrm{Mb/s}$ link takes $8 \times 10^6/10^8 = 80\,\mathrm{ms}$. Compressing it
to a third at $200\,\mathrm{MB/s}$ takes $5\,\mathrm{ms}$, sending the third takes $26.7\,\mathrm{ms}$, and decompressing
it back to a megabyte at $500\,\mathrm{MB/s}$ takes $2\,\mathrm{ms}$ (assumed speeds). The compressed path has three
stages totalling $33.7\,\mathrm{ms}$ against one of $80\,\mathrm{ms}$. Within a data centre, at $10\,\mathrm{Gb/s}$, the transfer takes
$0.8\,\mathrm{ms}$ and compression no longer pays.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise practises the units of the section. It is the kind of conversion Liu's "common mistakes" are about.

::: {#exr-budget-units}
#### Converting units

Express $1\,\mathrm{TB}$ in $\mathrm{TiB}$, $10\,\mathrm{Gb/s}$ in $\mathrm{GB/s}$, $2^{40}\,\mathrm B$ in
$\mathrm{TB}$, and the number of seconds in a year of 365 days as a power of ten to two significant digits.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$10^{12}/2^{40} = 0.909\,\mathrm{TiB}$; $10\,\mathrm{Gb/s} = 10/8 = 1.25\,\mathrm{GB/s}$; $2^{40}\,\mathrm B =
1.0995\,\mathrm{TB}$; a year is $3.15 \times 10^7\,\mathrm s$, close to $\pi \times 10^7$.

## Python

The four conversions.

```{.python .run}
print(f"1 TB = {1e12 / 2**40:.3f} TiB")
print(f"10 Gb/s = {10 / 8:.2f} GB/s")
print(f"2^40 B = {2**40 / 1e12:.4f} TB")
print(f"one year = {365 * 86400:.3g} s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
1 TB = 0.909 TiB
10 Gb/s = 1.25 GB/s
2^40 B = 1.0995 TB
one year = 3.15e+07 s
```
::::
:::

The second exercise applies part (a) to a page with several sequential stages. Only the means are needed, and the question
is which stage is worth improving.

::: {#exr-budget-mean}
#### Mean latency of a page

A page needs a round trip of $60\,\mathrm{ms}$ (California to Virginia), $3\,\mathrm{ms}$ at the load balancer, three
sequential service calls of mean $12$, $8$ and $25\,\mathrm{ms}$, and $4\,\mathrm{ms}$ to render. What is its mean
latency, and which change helps more: halving the slowest service call, or serving the page from California?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

By part (a) the mean is $60 + 3 + 12 + 8 + 25 + 4 = 112\,\mathrm{ms}$. Halving the slowest call saves $12.5\,\mathrm{ms}$;
serving from California replaces the $60\,\mathrm{ms}$ round trip by a local one of a few milliseconds and saves about
$55\,\mathrm{ms}$. The network dominates.

## Python

The two alternatives, with a local round trip of $5\,\mathrm{ms}$.

```{.python .run}
stages = {"network": 60, "load balancer": 3, "call A": 12, "call B": 8, "call C": 25, "render": 4}
base = sum(stages.values())
print("mean:", base, "ms")
print("halve call C:", base - stages["call C"] / 2, "ms")
print("serve locally:", base - stages["network"] + 5, "ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
mean: 112 ms
halve call C: 99.5 ms
serve locally: 57 ms
```
::::
:::

The third exercise is the budgeting rule stated after the proof. It asks what each stage must promise for the whole to
meet its target.

::: {#exr-budget-allocate}
#### Splitting a percentile target

The feed must have $t_{0.99} \leq 200\,\mathrm{ms}$, and its four stages get budgets $\tau_i$ that sum to
$200\,\mathrm{ms}$. At what percentile must each stage meet its budget for part (d) to guarantee the target, if all
stages get the same level? And if the network, which is the least controllable, is allowed to exceed its budget for
$0.4\%$ of requests while the others share the rest equally?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Part (d) needs $\sum_i(1 - q_i) \leq 0.01$. With equal levels, $1 - q_i = 0.0025$, so each stage must meet its budget at
its $99.75$th percentile. If the network has $1 - q_1 = 0.004$, the other three share $0.006$, so $1 - q_i = 0.002$ and
they must meet their budgets at the $99.8$th percentile.

## Python

The levels for the two splits.

```{.python .run}
total = 0.01
print("equal split:", [round(1 - total / 4, 4)] * 4)
rest = (total - 0.004) / 3
print("network first:", [round(1 - 0.004, 4)] + [round(1 - rest, 4)] * 3)
```

```{.text .run-output}
equal split: [0.9975, 0.9975, 0.9975, 0.9975]
network first: [0.996, 0.998, 0.998, 0.998]
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise asks for a proof of part (b) for two stages without the union bound. It uses inclusion-exclusion
instead, and the check simulates dependent stages.

::: {#exr-budget-two-stage-proof}
#### Two stages by inclusion-exclusion

Prove part (b) for $k = 2$ from the formula $\mathbb P(A \cup B) = \mathbb P(A) + \mathbb P(B) - \mathbb P(A \cap B)$,
and identify the term the bound throws away.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Let $A = \{T_1 > \tau_1\}$ and $B = \{T_2 > \tau_2\}$. If $T_1 + T_2 > \tau_1 + \tau_2$ then $T_1 > \tau_1$ or $T_2 >
\tau_2$, so $\{T > \tau_1 + \tau_2\} \subseteq A \cup B$ and $\mathbb P(T > \tau_1 + \tau_2) \leq \mathbb P(A) + \mathbb
P(B) - \mathbb P(A \cap B) \leq \varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2$. The bound discards $\mathbb P(A \cap B)$, the probability
that both stages overrun, and the inclusion $\{T > \tau_1 + \tau_2\} \subseteq A \cup B$, which is strict when one stage
overruns by less than the other's slack.

## Python

Check on two dependent stages, $T_1 = X + Y_1$ and $T_2 = X + Y_2$ with a shared exponential part $X$: the empirical
probability of exceeding the summed $99$th percentiles against the bound $0.02$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
X = rng.exponential(1.0, 10**6)
T1, T2 = X + rng.exponential(2.0, 10**6), X + rng.exponential(0.5, 10**6)
tau1, tau2 = np.quantile(T1, 0.99), np.quantile(T2, 0.99)
A, B = T1 > tau1, T2 > tau2
print(f"P(T > tau1 + tau2) = {np.mean(T1 + T2 > tau1 + tau2):.4f}")
print(f"P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B) = {A.mean() + B.mean() - (A & B).mean():.4f}; bound 0.02")
```

```{.text .run-output}
P(T > tau1 + tau2) = 0.0040
P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B) = 0.0191; bound 0.02
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise measures how loose part (d) is for independent, identical stages. It generalises
@exm-budget-not-additive from two stages to many.

::: {#exr-budget-erlang}
#### Many exponential stages

For $k$ independent exponential stages of mean $1$, compare $t_{0.99}(T)$ with $k\,t_{0.99}(T_1) = k\ln 100$ and with
the bound of part (d) at $q_i = 1 - 0.01/k$, for $k = 1, 2, 5, 10$. The sum $T$ has $\mathbb P(T > t) =
e^{-t}\sum_{j<k}t^j/j!$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Part (d) with $q_i = 1 - 0.01/k$ gives $k\ln(100k)$, and the sum of the plain percentiles is $k\ln 100$. The true
percentile solves $e^{-t}\sum_{j<k}t^j/j! = 0.01$. The output shows that it grows much more slowly than either: for ten
stages the true $t_{0.99}$ is less than half of $k\ln 100$. Budgets built from the sum of percentiles are safe, and for
independent stages they are wasteful by a factor that grows with $k$.

## Python

The true percentile by bisection, against the two sums.

```{.python .run}
from math import exp, factorial, log
def tail(t, k):
    return exp(-t) * sum(t**j / factorial(j) for j in range(k))
def quantile(k, q=0.99):
    lo, hi = 0.0, 100.0
    for _ in range(100):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        lo, hi = (mid, hi) if tail(mid, k) > 1 - q else (lo, mid)
    return lo
for k in (1, 2, 5, 10):
    print(f"k = {k:2d}: true {quantile(k):6.2f}, k ln 100 = {k * log(100):6.2f}, bound (d) = {k * log(100 * k):6.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
k =  1: true   4.61, k ln 100 =   4.61, bound (d) =   4.61
k =  2: true   6.64, k ln 100 =   9.21, bound (d) =  10.60
k =  5: true  11.60, k ln 100 =  23.03, bound (d) =  31.07
k = 10: true  18.78, k ln 100 =  46.05, bound (d) =  69.08
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise checks part (d) on a request path with skewed stages. It uses lognormal latencies, whose long right
tail is typical of measured services.

::: {#exr-budget-simulate-path}
#### A simulated request path

Let four independent stages have lognormal latencies with medians $5$, $20$, $10$ and $40\,\mathrm{ms}$ and log-standard
deviation $0.8$. Estimate $t_{0.99}$ of the request by simulation, and compare it with the sum of the stages' $99$th
percentiles and with the guaranteed bound of part (d) at $q_i = 0.9975$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A lognormal stage with median $m$ and log-standard deviation $s$ has $t_q = m\,e^{s z_q}$ with $z_q$ the standard
Gaussian quantile. The simulated request percentile lies below both sums: the sum of the $99$th percentiles is a valid
bound here only because the stages are independent, and the bound of part (d) is valid always and larger still.

## Python

$10^6$ simulated requests; the stage percentiles are exact.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from statistics import NormalDist
rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
medians, s = np.array([5, 20, 10, 40]), 0.8
T = (medians * np.exp(s * rng.standard_normal((10**6, 4)))).sum(axis=1)
z = NormalDist().inv_cdf
print(f"simulated t_0.99 of the request: {np.quantile(T, 0.99):.1f} ms")
print(f"sum of stage t_0.99: {(medians * np.exp(s * z(0.99))).sum():.1f} ms")
print(f"bound (d), stages at 0.9975: {(medians * np.exp(s * z(0.9975))).sum():.1f} ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
simulated t_0.99 of the request: 321.7 ms
sum of stage t_0.99: 482.3 ms
bound (d), stages at 0.9975: 708.5 ms
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise returns to the lower bound set by distance. It asks how many sequential round trips a budget
allows between two cities.

::: {#exr-budget-round-trips}
#### Round trips in a budget

A request from Sydney is served in London ($17\,000\,\mathrm{km}$), in Singapore ($6300\,\mathrm{km}$) or in Sydney
itself ($50\,\mathrm{km}$ to the data centre). At $2 \times 10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}$, how many sequential round trips fit in
a budget of $100\,\mathrm{ms}$ in each case?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A round trip takes at least $2d/v$: $170\,\mathrm{ms}$ to London, $63\,\mathrm{ms}$ to Singapore and $0.5\,\mathrm{ms}$
locally. By part (a) the number of round trips is at most $\lfloor 100/(2d/v)\rfloor$: none to London, one to Singapore
and two hundred locally. A requirement of $100\,\mathrm{ms}$ for Australian users forces a presence in or near
Australia.

## Python

The bound for each location.

```{.python .run}
from math import floor
for city, km in [("London", 17000), ("Singapore", 6300), ("Sydney", 50)]:
    rtt = 2 * km * 1e3 / 2e8 * 1e3
    print(f"{city:9s}: round trip >= {rtt:6.1f} ms, at most {floor(100 / rtt)} in 100 ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
London   : round trip >=  170.0 ms, at most 0 in 100 ms
Singapore: round trip >=   63.0 ms, at most 1 in 100 ms
Sydney   : round trip >=    0.5 ms, at most 200 in 100 ms
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise contrasts sequential stages with parallel ones. Two calls that do not depend on each other need not
wait for each other.

::: {#exr-budget-parallel}
#### Two calls in sequence or in parallel

A page makes two independent calls, each exponential with mean $30\,\mathrm{ms}$. Give the mean time spent on them when
they run in sequence and when they run in parallel, the page waiting for both.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

In sequence the mean is $60\,\mathrm{ms}$ by part (a). In parallel the page waits for $\max(T_1, T_2)$, and $\mathbb
P(\max \leq t) = (1 - e^{-t/30})^2$; its mean is $\mathbb E[T_1] + \mathbb E[T_2] - \mathbb E[\min(T_1, T_2)] = 30 + 30 -
15 = 45\,\mathrm{ms}$, since the minimum of two independent exponentials of rate $1/30$ is exponential of rate $2/30$.
Parallel calls save a quarter here, not a half, because the page waits for the slower one.

## Python

The means, from $10^6$ simulated pairs.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
T1, T2 = rng.exponential(30, 10**6), rng.exponential(30, 10**6)
print(f"sequence: {np.mean(T1 + T2):.2f} ms; parallel: {np.mean(np.maximum(T1, T2)):.2f} ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
sequence: 59.94 ms; parallel: 44.95 ms
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise shows that the sum of the percentiles is not even an upper bound when stages are independent and
their distributions have atoms. Part (d) needs the stricter levels for a reason.

::: {#exr-budget-subadditivity-fails}
#### When the sum of percentiles is too small

Let $T_1$ and $T_2$ be independent, each equal to $1$ with probability $0.008$ and $0$ otherwise. Show that
$t_{0.99}(T_1) = t_{0.99}(T_2) = 0$ but $t_{0.99}(T_1 + T_2) = 1$. What does part (d) give?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\mathbb P(T_i \leq 0) = 0.992 \geq 0.99$, so $t_{0.99}(T_i) = 0$. The sum is $0$ only when both are $0$, with
probability $0.992^2 = 0.984064 < 0.99$, so $t_{0.99}(T_1 + T_2) \geq 1$; and $\mathbb P(T_1 + T_2 \leq 1) = 1 -
0.008^2 = 0.999936 \geq 0.99$, so it equals $1$. The sum of the percentiles, $0$, is smaller than the percentile of the
sum. Part (d) with $q_1 = q_2 = 0.995$ uses $t_{0.995}(T_i) = 1$, since $\mathbb P(T_i \leq 0) = 0.992 < 0.995$, and gives
the valid bound $2$.

## Python

The exact distribution of the sum, and the quantiles from their definition.

```{.python .run}
from itertools import product
p = 0.008
law = {}
for a, b in product((0, 1), repeat=2):
    law[a + b] = law.get(a + b, 0) + (p if a else 1 - p) * (p if b else 1 - p)
def t(q, dist):
    acc = 0
    for value in sorted(dist):
        acc += dist[value]
        if acc >= q:
            return value
single = {0: 1 - p, 1: p}
print("t_0.99 of one stage:", t(0.99, single), "; of the sum:", t(0.99, law))
print("t_0.995 of one stage:", t(0.995, single))
```

```{.text .run-output}
t_0.99 of one stage: 0 ; of the sum: 1
t_0.995 of one stage: 1
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise uses the proposition to make a design decision. A cache changes the distribution of one stage, and
the question is whether the change lets the request meet its target with a guarantee.

::: {#exr-budget-cache-decision}
#### Does the cache meet the target?

A feed request has three stages besides data access: network, lognormal with median $30\,\mathrm{ms}$; application,
lognormal with median $15\,\mathrm{ms}$; serialisation, lognormal with median $5\,\mathrm{ms}$; all with log-standard
deviation $0.5$. Data access is a database query (lognormal, median $40\,\mathrm{ms}$, log-standard deviation $0.7$), or,
with a cache, a cache read (median $1\,\mathrm{ms}$, log-standard deviation $0.3$) on a hit and the cache read followed
by the query on a miss, with hit ratio $0.9$. The target is $t_{0.99} \leq 200\,\mathrm{ms}$. Decide by simulation
whether each design meets it, and whether part (d) guarantees it without assuming independence.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

For the guarantee, part (d) at $q_i = 0.9975$ adds the four stage percentiles. Without a cache the database stage alone
has $t_{0.9975} = 40e^{0.7 \times 2.807} = 286\,\mathrm{ms}$, so no guarantee is possible, and the simulation shows the
request percentile itself above $200\,\mathrm{ms}$. With the cache, the data-access stage is slow only on the $10\%$ of
misses, so its $99.75$th percentile is the $97.5$th percentile of a miss, about $40e^{0.7 \times 1.96} + 1 =
158\,\mathrm{ms}$; the sum of the four stage bounds then decides whether the guarantee holds, and the simulation gives
the actual percentile. The output shows that with the cache the simulated $t_{0.99}$, about $167\,\mathrm{ms}$, meets the
target while the bound of part (d), about $363\,\mathrm{ms}$, does not: the design meets the requirement if its stages are
close to independent, as simulated, but part (d) alone cannot promise it. Without the cache neither holds.

## Python

Simulation of $10^6$ requests per design, and the bound of part (d) from the empirical stage percentiles.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(8)
n = 10**6
lognormal = lambda median, s: median * np.exp(s * rng.standard_normal(n))
other = [lognormal(30, 0.5), lognormal(15, 0.5), lognormal(5, 0.5)]
db = lognormal(40, 0.7)
hit = rng.random(n) < 0.9
cached = lognormal(1, 0.3) + np.where(hit, 0.0, db)
for name, data in [("no cache", db), ("cache", cached)]:
    T = sum(other) + data
    bound = sum(np.quantile(x, 0.9975) for x in other + [data])
    print(f"{name:8s}: simulated t_0.99 = {np.quantile(T, 0.99):6.1f} ms, guaranteed bound (d) = {bound:6.1f} ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
no cache: simulated t_0.99 =  266.4 ms, guaranteed bound (d) =  487.1 ms
cache   : simulated t_0.99 =  167.2 ms, guaranteed bound (d) =  363.3 ms
```
::::
:::
::::

## Estimating load: requests, storage, bandwidth and servers {#sec-estimating-load}

Xu quotes Dean's definition of the subject of this section: "back-of-the-envelope calculations are estimates you create
using a combination of thought experiments and common performance numbers to get a good feel for which designs will
meet your requirements" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 2]. The commonly asked estimates, in Xu's list, are "QPS, peak
QPS, storage, cache, number of servers", and Liu writes down the formulas for the first ones
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Types of Back-of-the-Envelope Calculations"]. Liu also says what the estimate is
for: "One of the purposes of back-of-the-envelope math is to justify a design", and an estimate with which nothing is
done is a "common mistake" (same chapter, "What is the Purpose?" and "Common Mistakes"). This section collects the
formulas into one definition and then proves how the errors of the assumptions propagate into the result, which says
how far an estimate can be trusted.

For more on this topic, see @SystemDesignInterview2021 [Chs. 2, 8 and 14], @liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 5 and
Apps. 1-4] and @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Secs. 2.1 and 3.1].

### The load estimate

The definition below takes the workload assumptions of a requirements specification and returns the numbers that the
high-level design must accommodate. Each formula is a product of assumptions, divided by a constant that converts days
into seconds; the number of servers is the only one with a rounding, and the only one that needs a measured capacity.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-load-estimate}
#### Load estimate

Let the workload assumptions (@def-requirements-specification) give $U$ daily active users and, for each operation $o$,
the mean number $\nu_o$ of requests per active user per day and the mean payload $s_o$ in bytes. Let $\kappa \geq 1$ be
the peak factor, $N$ the replication factor and $\Delta$ the retention period in days of the stored data, and, for a
tier of identical servers, $\mu$ the rate one server can serve within its latency budget and $\rho_{\max} \in (0, 1]$ the
utilisation at which it is planned to run. The **load estimate** consists of:

1. the mean request rate of each operation, $\lambda_o = U\nu_o/86\,400\,\mathrm{s}$, and its peak rate $\kappa\lambda_o$;
2. the mean bandwidth of each operation, $\beta_o = \lambda_os_o$ in bytes per second, and its peak $\kappa\beta_o$;
3. the stored volume after the retention period, $D = N\Delta\sum_oU\nu_os_o$, the sum running over the operations
   that store their payload;
4. the number of servers of a tier that receives the operations $O$, $c = \lceil\kappa\sum_{o \in O}\lambda_o/(\rho_{\max}
   \mu)\rceil$.
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Xu's worked example is the template for the definition. Its numbers are worth recomputing, because the rounding is part
of the method.

::: {#exm-load-xu-twitter}
#### Xu's microblogging estimate

With $U = 1.5 \times 10^8$ and $\nu_{\text{post}} = 2$, item 1 gives $\lambda = 3 \times 10^8/86\,400 = 3472$ posts per
second, which Xu rounds to "~3500", and a "Peek QPS = 2 * QPS = ~7000", so $\kappa = 2$. Media storage is "150 million *
2 * 10% * 1 MB = 30 TB per day" and "~55 PB" over five years [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 2]: item 3 with $N = 1$,
$s = 1\,\mathrm{MB}$ for the tenth of posts that carry media, and $\Delta = 1825$ days.
:::

Tan's search example of @exr-req-derive-rate stops at the request rate. Completing it with a payload gives the
bandwidth, which shows that a high request rate does not by itself mean a high bandwidth.

::: {#exm-load-tan-search}
#### Search traffic

$10^{10}$ searches a day are $\lambda = 1.16 \times 10^5$ per second. If a result page is $50\,\mathrm{kB}$, item 2 gives
$\beta = 5.8 \times 10^9\,\mathrm{B/s}$, about $46\,\mathrm{Gb/s}$ on average: a large rate of small responses.
:::

Liu's worked example multiplies the factors in scientific notation and includes the replication factor. Its result is a
daily volume, the input of item 3.

::: {#exm-load-liu-photos}
#### Liu's photo volume

Liu takes $2 \times 10^8$ daily active users, $10\%$ of whom post, $10$ photos each of $10\,\mathrm{MB}$, and a
replication factor of $3$, and groups the powers of ten: $10^8 \times 10^7 \times 10^1 = 10^{16}$ times $0.1 \times 3
\times 2 = 0.6$, so $6 \times 10^{15}\,\mathrm B$, "6 Petabytes" a day [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5,
"Back-of-the-Envelope Calculation Techniques"].
:::

The running example now gets its request rates. Its two operations differ by a factor of $250$, which decides the
shape of its design.

::: {#exm-load-photoshare-rates}
#### Request rates of the photo-sharing service

With the assumptions of @exm-req-workload-assumptions, uploads arrive at $\lambda_{\text{up}} = 10^8 \times
0.2/86\,400 = 231$ per second, $694$ at peak, and feed requests at $\lambda_{\text{feed}} = 5 \times 10^9/86\,400 =
57\,870$ per second, $1.74 \times 10^5$ at peak. The service is read-heavy, $250$ reads per write, which is why
@fig-three-tier has a cache and replicas but a single write path.
:::

Item 3 gives the storage of the running example. The photos dominate, and the metadata is a rounding error, a point
made precise in the next unit.

::: {#exm-load-photoshare-storage}
#### Storage of the photo-sharing service

Each day stores $2 \times 10^7$ photos of $2\,\mathrm{MB} + 1\,\mathrm{kB}$, so $4.0 \times 10^{13}\,\mathrm B =
40\,\mathrm{TB}$, and $120\,\mathrm{TB}$ with $N = 3$. Over $\Delta = 1825$ days, $D = 2.19 \times 10^{17}\,\mathrm
B$, about $219\,\mathrm{PB}$. The metadata alone is $2 \times 10^{10}\,\mathrm B$ a day, $0.05\%$ of the total.
:::

Item 2 gives the bandwidths. Liu warns that "bandwidth is usually measured in bits per second not bytes per second"
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, App. 2], so both are given.

::: {#exm-load-photoshare-bandwidth}
#### Bandwidth of the photo-sharing service

Uploads bring in $231 \times 2\,\mathrm{MB} = 463\,\mathrm{MB/s}$, $3.7\,\mathrm{Gb/s}$ on average and $11\,\mathrm{Gb/s}$
at peak. Feed pages of ten $30\,\mathrm{kB}$ thumbnails send out $57\,870 \times 300\,\mathrm{kB} = 17.4\,\mathrm{GB/s}$,
$139\,\mathrm{Gb/s}$ on average and $417\,\mathrm{Gb/s}$ at peak. Liu's machines have network cards of $10$ to
$25\,\mathrm{Gb/s}$ [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, App. 2], so the outgoing traffic needs many machines' worth of
network, which the content delivery network of @fig-three-tier provides.
:::

Item 4 needs a measured capacity and a planned utilisation. Running servers well below full load leaves room for bursts
and for the latency that grows as a server fills.

::: {#exm-load-servers}
#### Application servers

The application tier receives $694 + 1.74 \times 10^5 \approx 1.74 \times 10^5$ requests per second at peak. With $\mu
= 2000$ requests per second per server and $\rho_{\max} = 0.6$, item 4 gives $c = \lceil 1.74 \times 10^5/1200\rceil
= 146$ servers. At $\rho_{\max} = 0.9$ the same load needs $97$; the difference buys headroom.
:::

The cache is the estimate Xu's list adds after storage. Its size is the size of the data that is read often, which is
a fraction of what is stored.

::: {#exm-load-cache-size}
#### Cache size

If almost all feed reads concern photos from the last seven days, the cache needs their metadata: $7 \times 2 \times
10^7 \times 1\,\mathrm{kB} = 140\,\mathrm{GB}$. Liu's table gives $64$ to $1024\,\mathrm{GB}$ of memory per machine
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, App. 2], so the hot metadata fits on one or two machines, replicated for availability;
the photos themselves stay in the content delivery network.
:::

The capacity $\mu$ is the one input of the definition that cannot be assumed: Liu's table is only "a rough guideline"
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, App. 2]. It is measured with a load generator against one server, and the code below is
illustrative: it needs a running server and is not run.

::: {#exm-load-measure-capacity}
#### Measuring the capacity of one server

A load test raises the offered rate step by step and records the rate at which the server's $99$th-percentile latency
crosses its budget; that rate is $\mu$. A sketch with the `locust` load generator, whose results would depend on the
machine and are therefore not recorded:

```{.python .illustrative}
# Illustrative: needs a running feed server at FEED_URL and the locust package; not run, no recorded output.
from locust import HttpUser, constant_throughput, task

class FeedReader(HttpUser):
    wait_time = constant_throughput(10)  # each simulated user sends 10 requests per second

    @task
    def read_feed(self):
        self.client.get("/feed?page=1", name="feed")

# locust -f this_file.py --host $FEED_URL --users 200 --spawn-rate 20 --run-time 5m
# Repeat with more users until the 99th percentile of "feed" exceeds its budget; mu is the rate just below.
```
:::

The last example adds the headroom for failures. A tier spread over three zones must still carry the peak when a whole
zone is lost.

::: {#exm-load-zone-headroom}
#### Surviving the loss of a zone

If the $146$ servers of @exm-load-servers are spread over three zones and one zone fails, the remaining two must carry
the peak alone: each zone needs $\lceil 1.74 \times 10^5/(2 \times 1200)\rceil = 73$ servers, $219$ in all, $50\%$ more
than without the failure requirement. With $z$ zones the factor is $z/(z - 1)$, so more, smaller zones cost less
headroom.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise is a direct use of item 1. Its numbers are small enough to do without a calculator.

::: {#exr-load-rates}
#### Rates of a small service

A service has $10^7$ daily active users who post $5$ times a day, with a peak factor of $2$. Give the mean and peak post
rates per second, using $86\,400$ and Liu's shortcut of $10^5$ seconds a day.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$5 \times 10^7$ posts a day are $579$ per second, $1157$ at peak. With $10^5$ seconds, $500$ and $1000$: about $14\%$ lower,
the error of the shortcut.

## Python

Both conversions.

```{.python .run}
daily = 1e7 * 5
for seconds in (86400, 1e5):
    print(f"{seconds:.0f} s/day: mean {daily / seconds:.0f}/s, peak {2 * daily / seconds:.0f}/s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
86400 s/day: mean 579/s, peak 1157/s
100000 s/day: mean 500/s, peak 1000/s
```
::::
:::

The second exercise checks a published estimate. Item 3 makes the retention period appear exactly once, and the
published figure counts it twice.

::: {#exr-load-xu-url}
#### Checking an estimate

Xu's URL shortener assumes $10^8$ new URLs a day for ten years, so "365 billion records" of $100$ bytes, and concludes
"365 billion * 100 bytes * 10 years = 365 TB" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 8]. Recompute the storage with item 3
($N = 1$) and find the slip.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Item 3 gives $D = 3650 \times 10^8 \times 100\,\mathrm B = 3.65 \times 10^{13}\,\mathrm B = 36.5\,\mathrm{TB}$. The
"365 billion" records already include the ten years, so multiplying by "10 years" again counts them twice; the correct
figure is $36.5\,\mathrm{TB}$. The slip does not change Xu's design, which is the point of estimating to an order of
magnitude, but it changes the number of disks by ten.

## Python

The volume with the retention counted once and twice.

```{.python .run}
records = 1e8 * 365 * 10
print(f"records: {records:.3g}")
print(f"storage: {records * 100 / 1e12:.1f} TB; with the years counted twice: {records * 100 * 10 / 1e12:.0f} TB")
```

```{.text .run-output}
records: 3.65e+11
storage: 36.5 TB; with the years counted twice: 365 TB
```
::::
:::

The third exercise estimates the storage that Xu leaves out of his microblogging example. The text of the posts turns out
to matter much less than the media.

::: {#exr-load-tweet-text}
#### The text of the posts

Xu sizes a post as "tweet_id 64 bytes", "text 140 bytes" and "media 1 MB" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 2]. Estimate
the storage of identifiers and text for $3 \times 10^8$ posts a day over five years, without replication, and compare it
with the $55\,\mathrm{PB}$ of media.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Each post has $64 + 140 = 204$ bytes of identifier and text, so a day stores $6.1 \times 10^{10}\,\mathrm B =
61\,\mathrm{GB}$ and five years $112\,\mathrm{TB}$, about $0.2\%$ of the media. That is why Xu estimates "only ...
media storage".

## Python

The text volume and its share.

```{.python .run}
text = 3e8 * 204 * 1825
media = 30e12 * 1825
print(f"text: {text / 1e12:.0f} TB over five years; media: {media / 1e15:.1f} PB; share {text / media:.2%}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
text: 112 TB over five years; media: 54.8 PB; share 0.20%
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise converts the egress of @exm-load-photoshare-bandwidth into network cards. It is the estimate that
justifies a content delivery network.

::: {#exr-load-nics}
#### How many network cards?

The feed sends $417\,\mathrm{Gb/s}$ at peak. How many $25\,\mathrm{Gb/s}$ cards would carry it at $60\%$ utilisation?
If a content delivery network serves $95\%$ of the thumbnail bytes, how many are needed at the origin?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Item 4 with bandwidth in place of requests: $\lceil 417/(0.6 \times 25)\rceil = 28$ cards. With $95\%$ served at the
edge, the origin sends $20.8\,\mathrm{Gb/s}$, which needs $\lceil 20.8/15\rceil = 2$ cards.

## Python

Both counts.

```{.python .run}
from math import ceil
peak = 3 * 57870 * 300e3 * 8 / 1e9
print(f"peak egress {peak:.0f} Gb/s; cards {ceil(peak / (0.6 * 25))}; at the origin {ceil(0.05 * peak / (0.6 * 25))}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
peak egress 417 Gb/s; cards 28; at the origin 2
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise varies the planned utilisation of item 4. It shows how quickly the number of servers grows as the
planned utilisation is lowered.

::: {#exr-load-utilisation}
#### Servers against utilisation

For the peak of @exm-load-servers and $\mu = 2000$, give $c$ for $\rho_{\max} = 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9$. By what factor
does halving the idle capacity (from $0.5$ to $0.75$) reduce the number of servers?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$c = \lceil 87.15/\rho_{\max}\rceil$: $175$, $146$, $125$, $109$ and $97$. Going from $0.5$ to $0.75$ divides $c$
by $1.5$, to $117$. The saving is real, but a server at $75\%$ has less room for bursts, which queueing theory
quantifies.

## Python

The counts for each utilisation.

```{.python .run}
from math import ceil
peak = 3 * (57870 + 231.5)
for rho in (0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.75, 0.8, 0.9):
    print(f"rho_max = {rho:.2f}: {ceil(peak / (rho * 2000))} servers")
```

```{.text .run-output}
rho_max = 0.50: 175 servers
rho_max = 0.60: 146 servers
rho_max = 0.70: 125 servers
rho_max = 0.75: 117 servers
rho_max = 0.80: 109 servers
rho_max = 0.90: 97 servers
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise sizes the metadata database. A store larger than one machine must be split, and the number of parts
follows from item 3.

::: {#exr-load-shards}
#### Partitions of the metadata

Over five years the photo-sharing service stores $2 \times 10^7$ metadata rows of $1\,\mathrm{kB}$ a day. How many
partitions of at most $8\,\mathrm{TB}$ (Liu's medium database [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, App. 2]) does it need,
and how many machines with $N = 3$ replicas of each?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

One copy is $2 \times 10^{10}\,\mathrm B \times 1825 = 36.5\,\mathrm{TB}$, so $\lceil 36.5/8\rceil = 5$ partitions and
$15$ machines. The metadata needs a partitioned database even though it is a negligible share of the bytes.

## Python

The partitions and machines.

```{.python .run}
from math import ceil
one_copy = 2e7 * 1e3 * 1825 / 1e12
parts = ceil(one_copy / 8)
print(f"{one_copy:.1f} TB, {parts} partitions, {3 * parts} machines")
```

```{.text .run-output}
36.5 TB, 5 partitions, 15 machines
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise is Xu's video service. Its storage and its outgoing bandwidth come from the same assumptions and
differ by a large factor.

::: {#exr-load-video}
#### A video service

Xu assumes $5 \times 10^6$ daily active users who watch $5$ videos a day, $10\%$ of whom upload one video a day, of
$300\,\mathrm{MB}$ on average [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 14]. Give the daily storage of uploads, the mean
outgoing bandwidth in $\mathrm{Gb/s}$, and the ratio of bytes sent to bytes stored.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Uploads store $5 \times 10^5 \times 300\,\mathrm{MB} = 150\,\mathrm{TB}$ a day, Xu's figure. Viewers fetch $2.5 \times
10^7 \times 300\,\mathrm{MB} = 7.5\,\mathrm{PB}$ a day, $8.7 \times 10^{10}\,\mathrm{B/s}$, or $694\,\mathrm{Gb/s}$.
Fifty bytes are sent for every byte stored, which is why Xu's cost estimate is about the content delivery network.

## Python

Storage, bandwidth and the ratio.

```{.python .run}
stored = 5e6 * 0.1 * 300e6
sent = 5e6 * 5 * 300e6
print(f"stored {stored / 1e12:.0f} TB/day; sent {sent / 1e15:.1f} PB/day = {sent * 8 / 86400 / 1e9:.0f} Gb/s; "
      f"ratio {sent / stored:.0f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
stored 150 TB/day; sent 7.5 PB/day = 694 Gb/s; ratio 50
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise estimates a peak factor from data rather than assuming it. Liu suggests $5$ to $10$ times the mean
for weekend nights of a ride-sharing service [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5]; a daily cycle is the common case.

::: {#exr-load-peak-factor}
#### A peak factor from hourly counts

Requests per hour follow a daily cycle $\lambda(h) = \bar\lambda(1 + 0.6\cos(2\pi(h - 20)/24))$ with Poisson noise, for
$\bar\lambda = 3.6 \times 10^5$ requests per hour. Simulate a week of hourly counts and estimate $\kappa$ as the busiest
hour over the mean hour.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Without noise the busiest hour is $h = 20$ with $1.6\bar\lambda$, so $\kappa = 1.6$. The noise of a Poisson count of
mean $5.8 \times 10^5$ is about $760$, a relative $0.13\%$, so the estimate from a week is $1.60$ to within a few
thousandths. Peaks within the hour are higher than the hourly peak, so a design should use the peak of the finest
interval that matters to it.

## Python

A week of hourly counts with a fixed seed.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
h = np.arange(7 * 24)
counts = rng.poisson(3.6e5 * (1 + 0.6 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * (h - 20) / 24)))
print(f"kappa estimated from a week: {counts.max() / counts.mean():.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
kappa estimated from a week: 1.6038
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise measures a payload size $s_o$ instead of assuming it. SQLite reports the number and size of the pages
it uses, so the bytes per row of a table, indexes included, can be read off.

::: {#exr-load-sqlite-row-size}
#### Bytes per row, measured

Insert $10^4$ rows into the `photos` table of @exr-process-sqlite-feed, with $100$-character captions and $40$-character
keys, first without and then with the index on `(user_id, created_at)`. Compare the bytes per row with the $160$ bytes
of @exr-process-row-sizes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The measured size per row is larger than the sum of the fields, because each row carries a header and each page has
free space, and the index adds its own copy of the indexed columns and the row identifier. The output shows the
overhead; an estimate should round the field sum up rather than down, as Liu's advice to round $68$ bytes to $100$ does
[@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5].

## Python

An in-memory database, measured with `PRAGMA page_count` and `PRAGMA page_size`.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3
def bytes_per_row(with_index):
    db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    db.execute("CREATE TABLE photos(photo_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, user_id INTEGER, caption TEXT, "
               "object_key TEXT, created_at INTEGER)")
    if with_index:
        db.execute("CREATE INDEX photos_by_user ON photos(user_id, created_at)")
    rows = [(i, 1 + i % 997, "c" * 100, f"{i:040d}", 1_700_000_000 + i) for i in range(10**4)]
    db.executemany("INSERT INTO photos VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", rows)
    pages, size = db.execute("PRAGMA page_count").fetchone()[0], db.execute("PRAGMA page_size").fetchone()[0]
    return pages * size / len(rows)
print(f"without index: {bytes_per_row(False):.0f} B/row; with index: {bytes_per_row(True):.0f} B/row")
```

```{.text .run-output}
without index: 165 B/row; with index: 181 B/row
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise is a complete estimate of a new service, with every item of the definition. It is the kind of
estimate a design starts from.

::: {#exr-load-chat}
#### A chat service

A chat service has $5 \times 10^7$ daily active users who send $40$ messages a day of $100$ bytes; each message is
delivered to one recipient, who is connected while active. The peak factor is $4$, messages are kept for one year in
$3$ replicas, a chat server handles $5000$ messages per second at $\rho_{\max} = 0.7$, and a connection server holds
$10^6$ open connections [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, App. 2]. Give the peak message rate, the bandwidth of sends,
the storage after a year, the chat servers, and the connection servers if a third of the daily users are connected at
the peak.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$\lambda = 2 \times 10^9/86\,400 = 23\,148$ messages per second, $92\,593$ at peak. Sends carry $2.3\,\mathrm{MB/s}$
on average, $9.3\,\mathrm{MB/s}$ at peak: bandwidth is not a concern. A year stores $3 \times 365 \times 2 \times 10^{11}
\,\mathrm B = 219\,\mathrm{TB}$. Chat servers: $\lceil 92\,593/3500\rceil = 27$. Connections: $1.67 \times 10^7$ at
the peak, so $17$ connection servers. The estimate points the design at storage and connections, not at bandwidth.

## Python

All five items.

```{.python .run}
from math import ceil
U, nu, s, kappa = 5e7, 40, 100, 4
lam = U * nu / 86400
print(f"mean {lam:.0f}/s, peak {kappa * lam:.0f}/s")
print(f"send bandwidth: mean {lam * s / 1e6:.1f} MB/s, peak {kappa * lam * s / 1e6:.1f} MB/s")
print(f"storage after a year: {3 * 365 * U * nu * s / 1e12:.0f} TB")
print(f"chat servers: {ceil(kappa * lam / (0.7 * 5000))}")
print(f"connection servers: {ceil(U / 3 / 1e6)}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
mean 23148/s, peak 92593/s
send bandwidth: mean 2.3 MB/s, peak 9.3 MB/s
storage after a year: 219 TB
chat servers: 27
connection servers: 17
```
::::
:::
::::

### How far an estimate can be trusted

Every factor of a load estimate is an assumption, and some are guesses: the share of users who post, the size of a
photo, the peak factor. Xu's advice is to use "round numbers and approximation to your advantage", because "precision
is not expected" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 2]. The proposition below says how much precision is lost. Products
multiply the error factors of their terms, sums inherit the worst error factor of their terms, and independent errors
grow much more slowly than the worst case. Part (c) uses the variance of a sum of independent random variables, from
[Probability and statistics](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#def-variance).

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-estimate-error}
#### Propagation of estimation errors

Let $x_1, \dots, x_k > 0$ be true values and $\hat x_1, \dots, \hat x_k > 0$ estimates of them with $x_i/\phi_i \leq
\hat x_i \leq \phi_ix_i$, for error factors $\phi_i \geq 1$.

(a) For a product of powers $x = x_1^{e_1}\cdots x_k^{e_k}$ with exponents $e_i \in \{1, -1\}$, the estimate $\hat x =
\hat x_1^{e_1}\cdots\hat x_k^{e_k}$ satisfies $x/\Phi \leq \hat x \leq \Phi x$ with $\Phi = \phi_1\cdots\phi_k$, and both
bounds are attained.

(b) For a sum $x = x_1 + \dots + x_k$, the estimate $\hat x = \hat x_1 + \dots + \hat x_k$ satisfies $x/\phi \leq \hat x
\leq \phi x$ with $\phi = \max_i\phi_i$.

(c) If the log-errors $L_i = \ln(\hat x_i/x_i)$ are independent random variables with mean $0$ and standard deviations
$\sigma_i$, the log-error $L = \ln(\hat x/x)$ of the product $x = x_1\cdots x_k$ has mean $0$ and standard deviation
$\sqrt{\sigma_1^2 + \dots + \sigma_k^2}$.
:::

::::

*Proof.* (a) Taking logarithms, $\ln\hat x - \ln x = \sum_ie_i\ln(\hat x_i/x_i)$, and each term lies in $[-\ln\phi_i,
\ln\phi_i]$ because $|e_i| = 1$. The sum lies in $[-\ln\Phi, \ln\Phi]$, which is the claim. Choosing $\hat x_i =
\phi_i^{e_i}x_i$ for every $i$ makes every term equal to $\ln\phi_i$ and $\hat x = \Phi x$; choosing $\hat x_i =
\phi_i^{-e_i}x_i$ gives $\hat x = x/\Phi$.

(b) $\hat x = \sum_i\hat x_i \leq \sum_i\phi_ix_i \leq \phi\sum_ix_i = \phi x$, and likewise $\hat x \geq
\sum_ix_i/\phi_i \geq x/\phi$.

(c) $L = \sum_iL_i$, so $\mathbb E[L] = 0$ by linearity. Independent variables with finite variances are uncorrelated,
so $\operatorname{Var}(L) = \sum_i\operatorname{Var}(L_i) + \sum_{i \neq j}\operatorname{Cov}(L_i, L_j) =
\sum_i\sigma_i^2$. $\square$

Part (a) is the worst case, reached when every guess errs in the same direction; part (c) is the typical case of
unrelated guesses, in which the logarithmic errors add in quadrature. Part (b) explains why the small terms of a sum can
be guessed carelessly. The three parts together say which assumption to refine first: the factor with the largest
$\phi_i$ in a product, and the largest term in a sum.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example is the conversion of days into seconds, which every estimate contains. Liu replaces it by a round
number, and part (a) says what that costs.

::: {#exm-error-seconds}
#### Rounding the seconds of a day

Liu divides by $10^5$ instead of $86\,400$ [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5]. This is one factor with $\phi =
10^5/86\,400 = 1.157$, so every rate computed this way is $14\%$ low, always in the same direction; it is a bias, not a
random error, and can be corrected at the end by multiplying by $1.157$.
:::

Binary and decimal prefixes give a second systematic factor. It is small, but it compounds with the size of the prefix.

::: {#exm-error-prefixes}
#### Confusing TB and TiB

Reading a capacity of $100\,\mathrm{TiB}$ as $100\,\mathrm{TB}$ underestimates it by $\phi = 2^{40}/10^{12} = 1.0995$.
In a product with factors of $2$ elsewhere this is negligible; in a sum of a few such terms, by part (b), it is the whole
error.
:::

Xu's tip on rounding replaces a division by an easier one. Part (a) applies to quotients as well as products.

::: {#exm-error-xu-rounding}
#### Xu's rounded division

Xu suggests simplifying "99987 / 9.1" to "100,000 / 10" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 2]. The numerator is rounded up by
$\phi_1 = 1.00013$ and the denominator up by $\phi_2 = 1.0989$; the denominator enters with $e_2 = -1$, so the two
errors pull in opposite directions, and the result $10^4$ is below the true $10\,987.6$ by a factor of $1.0988$, inside
the bound $\Phi = 1.0990$.
:::

Xu's microblogging estimate has four guessed factors. If each is right to within a factor of two, part (a) gives the
worst case.

::: {#exm-error-twitter-worst}
#### The worst case of four guesses

The media storage of @exm-load-xu-twitter is $U \times \nu \times 0.1 \times 1\,\mathrm{MB}$. If each of the four factors
is known within a factor of $2$, the $30\,\mathrm{TB}$ a day is known within $\Phi = 2^4 = 16$: anywhere from $1.9$ to
$480\,\mathrm{TB}$.
:::

Part (c) replaces the worst case by the typical one. For four unrelated guesses the typical error factor is the square
root of the worst.

::: {#exm-error-twitter-typical}
#### The typical case of four guesses

If each log-error has standard deviation $\ln 2$, part (c) gives $\sigma = \sqrt 4\ln 2 = 2\ln 2$ for the product, so a
one-standard-deviation error factor of $e^{2\ln 2} = 4$, not $16$. For $k$ guesses of equal quality the typical factor is
$\phi^{\sqrt k}$ against the worst $\phi^k$.
:::

Part (b) is why the metadata of a photo can be guessed carelessly. The storage of the running example is a sum
dominated by one term.

::: {#exm-error-sum-dominated}
#### A careless guess that does not matter

The daily storage of @exm-load-photoshare-storage is $40\,\mathrm{TB}$ of photos plus $0.02\,\mathrm{TB}$ of metadata. If
the metadata guess is off by a factor of $5$ and the photo size by $1.2$, part (b) bounds the error by $5$, but the
actual error is at most $\frac{1.2 \times 40 + 5 \times 0.02}{40.02} = 1.202$: the bound of part (b) is attained only
when the worst term is also the largest.
:::

The bounds of part (a) are attained, and the example makes the extreme case concrete. It is the case of an analyst who is
optimistic about every factor.

::: {#exm-error-attained}
#### Every guess too high

An estimate of upload traffic as $U \times \nu_{\text{up}} \times s_{\text{up}}$ with $U$ guessed $1.5$ times too high,
$\nu_{\text{up}}$ $2$ times and $s_{\text{up}}$ $1.3$ times is too high by $1.5 \times 2 \times 1.3 = 3.9$, which is
$\Phi$. Errors of one sign are common when the same optimism drives every guess, which is what part (c) assumes away.
:::

Liu's advice on sizes is a deliberate error. Part (a) says it is harmless when the other factors are less certain.

::: {#exm-error-liu-rounding}
#### Rounding a row size

"If the sum is 68 bytes, round it to 100 or 50 bytes, no one cares" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5]. Rounding to
$100$ is a factor $1.47$, to $50$ a factor $1.36$. Against a guessed user count good to a factor of $2$ it adds little
to the worst case, $2.94$ instead of $2$, and less to the typical one, $\exp\sqrt{\ln^22 + \ln^21.47} = 2.21$.
:::

Order-of-magnitude estimates round every factor to a power of ten. Their error is fixed by part (c) once the rounding
error is modelled.

::: {#exm-error-powers-of-ten}
#### Rounding to powers of ten

Rounding a factor to the nearest power of ten makes its $\log_{10}$-error uniform on $[-\frac12, \frac12]$ when the
factor's leading digits are spread evenly, with standard deviation $1/\sqrt{12} = 0.289$ decades. Five such factors have,
by part (c), $\sqrt 5 \times 0.289 = 0.645$ decades, a typical factor of $4.4$, against the worst case of $10^{2.5} =
316$.
:::

The last example applies the proposition to a decision, which Liu says is what an estimate is for. A decision is safe
when it is the same at both ends of the interval of part (a).

::: {#exm-error-decision}
#### A robust decision

The peak upload rate of $694$ per second is a product of $U$, $\nu_{\text{up}}$ and $\kappa$. If $U$ is known within
$1.2$, $\nu_{\text{up}}$ within $3$ and $\kappa$ within $1.5$, then $\Phi = 5.4$ and the rate lies between $129$ and
$3750$ per second. A primary database taking $10^4$ writes a second handles every value in the interval, so "one write
primary suffices" is a robust decision; "one machine of $2000$ writes a second suffices" is not.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise computes an interval from part (a) for a rate estimated from two guessed factors. It is the
computation behind @exm-error-decision.

::: {#exr-error-interval}
#### An interval for a rate

A rate is estimated as $U\nu/86\,400$ with $U = 2 \times 10^7$ known within $1.5$ and $\nu = 3$ known within $2$.
Give the estimate and its interval.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$\hat\lambda = 6 \times 10^7/86\,400 = 694$ per second, and $\Phi = 3$, so the true rate lies in $[231, 2083]$ per second.
The constant $86\,400$ is exact and contributes no factor.

## Python

The estimate and the interval.

```{.python .run}
lam = 2e7 * 3 / 86400
Phi = 1.5 * 2
print(f"estimate {lam:.0f}/s, interval [{lam / Phi:.0f}, {lam * Phi:.0f}]/s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
estimate 694/s, interval [231, 2083]/s
```
::::
:::

The second exercise looks at the shortcut of @exm-error-seconds in Liu's own text. Liu prints the number of seconds in a
day as "84,600 (24 x 60 x 60)" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5].

::: {#exr-error-seconds}
#### Liu's seconds

Compute $24 \times 60 \times 60$, the relative error of the printed $84\,600$, and the error factor of $10^5$ against the
correct and against the printed value.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$24 \times 60 \times 60 = 86\,400$; the printed value transposes two digits and is $2.1\%$ low. Against $86\,400$, $10^5$
is a factor $1.157$; against $84\,600$ it would be $1.182$. Either way the shortcut's error dwarfs the typo, and both are
far below the errors of the guessed factors.

## Python

The three numbers.

```{.python .run}
s = 24 * 60 * 60
print(s, f"printed value off by {1 - 84600 / s:.2%}; 1e5/86400 = {1e5 / s:.3f}; 1e5/84600 = {1e5 / 84600:.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
86400 printed value off by 2.08%; 1e5/86400 = 1.157; 1e5/84600 = 1.182
```
::::
:::

The third exercise asks for the proof that the bound of part (a) cannot be improved for any choice of factors. The
check computes the extremes by brute force.

::: {#exr-error-attained-proof}
#### The bound is sharp

Show that for every choice of $\phi_1, \dots, \phi_k \geq 1$ and exponents $e_i$, there are estimates within the
allowed intervals with $\hat x = \Phi x$, and that no smaller factor than $\Phi$ bounds $\hat x/x$ for all allowed
estimates.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

Take $\hat x_i = \phi_i x_i$ when $e_i = 1$ and $\hat x_i = x_i/\phi_i$ when $e_i = -1$; each is in its interval. Then
$\hat x_i^{e_i} = \phi_ix_i^{e_i}$ in both cases, so $\hat x = \prod_i\phi_ix_i^{e_i} = \Phi x$. If some $\Phi' < \Phi$
bounded $\hat x/x$ for all allowed estimates, it would bound it for this choice, giving $\Phi \leq \Phi'$, a
contradiction.

## Python

Check on three factors with $\phi = (1.5, 2, 1.3)$ and exponents $(1, -1, 1)$: the largest ratio over all corners of the
box of estimates is $\Phi = 3.9$.

```{.python .run}
from itertools import product
phi, e = (1.5, 2.0, 1.3), (1, -1, 1)
x = (7.0, 3.0, 11.0)
ratio = lambda xh: __import__("math").prod((a / b) ** k for a, b, k in zip(xh, x, e))
corners = [tuple(xi * f**s for xi, f, s in zip(x, phi, signs)) for signs in product((-1, 1), repeat=3)]
print(f"largest ratio {max(map(ratio, corners)):.4f}, smallest {min(map(ratio, corners)):.4f}, "
      f"Phi = {1.5 * 2 * 1.3:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
largest ratio 3.9000, smallest 0.2564, Phi = 3.9000
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise asks for the proof of part (b) and the case of equality. It shows that a sum is never less accurate
than its least accurate term.

::: {#exr-error-sum-equality}
#### Equality in the sum bound

Prove that in part (b) the upper bound $\hat x = \phi x$ is attained only if every term with $x_i > 0$ has $\phi_i =
\phi$ and $\hat x_i = \phi x_i$, and give an example.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

In the chain $\hat x = \sum_i\hat x_i \leq \sum_i\phi_ix_i \leq \phi\sum_ix_i$, equality in the first step needs $\hat
x_i = \phi_ix_i$ for each $i$, and in the second $\phi_ix_i = \phi x_i$, that is $\phi_i = \phi$ since $x_i > 0$. So
$\hat x = \phi x$ forces every term to be overestimated by the maximal factor. Example: two terms $x_1 = x_2 = 1$ with
$\phi_1 = \phi_2 = 2$ and $\hat x_1 = \hat x_2 = 2$ give $\hat x = 4 = 2x$. If instead $\phi_2 = 1.1$, the best possible
is $\hat x = 3.1 < 4$.

## Python

Check on the example: the largest $\hat x/x$ over the corners of the box, for $\phi = (2, 2)$ and $(2, 1.1)$.

```{.python .run}
from itertools import product
for phi in ((2, 2), (2, 1.1)):
    x = (1.0, 1.0)
    best = max(sum(xi * f**s for xi, f, s in zip(x, phi, signs)) / sum(x) for signs in product((-1, 1), repeat=2))
    print(f"phi = {phi}: largest ratio {best:.3f}, bound {max(phi)}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
phi = (2, 2): largest ratio 2.000, bound 2
phi = (2, 1.1): largest ratio 1.550, bound 2
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise checks part (c) by simulation. It also asks for a probability, which part (c) alone does not give.

::: {#exr-error-quadrature}
#### Independent errors, simulated

Let four factors have independent log-errors, Gaussian with mean $0$ and standard deviation $\ln 2$. Simulate the error
of the product, compare its standard deviation with $2\ln 2$, and give the probability that the product is off by more
than a factor of $4$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

By part (c) the log-error of the product has standard deviation $2\ln 2 = 1.386$; a sum of independent Gaussians is
Gaussian, so the product is off by more than $4 = e^{2\ln 2}$ exactly when $|L|$ exceeds one standard deviation, with
probability $2(1 - \Phi(1)) = 0.317$. Even unrelated guesses of quality "factor of two" give an estimate that is off by
a factor of four a third of the time.

## Python

$10^6$ simulated products.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(10)
L = rng.normal(0, np.log(2), (10**6, 4)).sum(axis=1)
print(f"sd {L.std():.4f} (predicted {2 * np.log(2):.4f}); P(off by > 4) = {np.mean(np.abs(L) > np.log(4)):.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
sd 1.3849 (predicted 1.3863); P(off by > 4) = 0.3165
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise asks where to spend the effort of refining an estimate. Part (c) gives the answer as a reduction of the
variance of the log-error.

::: {#exr-error-refine}
#### Which assumption to refine

An estimate is a product of three factors with log-error standard deviations $\ln 3$, $\ln 1.5$ and $\ln 1.2$. Which
factor, if measured exactly, reduces the typical error factor most, and to what?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The variances are $(\ln 3)^2 = 1.207$, $0.164$ and $0.033$; the total is $1.404$, a typical factor of $e^{1.185} =
3.27$. Removing the first leaves $0.198$, a factor of $1.56$; removing the second leaves $1.240$, a factor of $3.05$;
removing the third leaves $1.371$, a factor of $3.23$. Refine the worst guess first: the others barely matter.

## Python

The typical factor after removing each term in turn.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
var = np.log([3, 1.5, 1.2]) ** 2
print(f"all three: factor {np.exp(np.sqrt(var.sum())):.2f}")
for i in range(3):
    print(f"factor {i + 1} measured exactly: {np.exp(np.sqrt(var.sum() - var[i])):.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
all three: factor 3.27
factor 1 measured exactly: 1.56
factor 2 measured exactly: 3.05
factor 3 measured exactly: 3.23
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise applies part (a) to a quotient: the number of servers is a load divided by a capacity, and both are
estimated.

::: {#exr-error-quotient}
#### Errors in a quotient

The peak load of @exm-load-servers is known within a factor of $2$ and the capacity $\mu$ within $1.5$. Give the
interval for the number of servers before rounding, and explain why measuring $\mu$ is worth more than refining the load
when the load is known within $1.2$ instead.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$c$ before rounding is $145$, and by part (a) with $e = (1, -1)$ it lies within $\Phi = 3$: between $48$ and $435$. If the
load is known within $1.2$, then $\Phi = 1.8$, and the capacity contributes $\ln 1.5 = 0.405$ of the $\ln 1.8 = 0.588$:
most of the remaining error, which a load test removes.

## Python

The two intervals.

```{.python .run}
c = 1.74e5 / 1200
for phi_load in (2, 1.2):
    Phi = phi_load * 1.5
    print(f"load within {phi_load}: servers in [{c / Phi:.0f}, {c * Phi:.0f}]")
```

```{.text .run-output}
load within 2: servers in [48, 435]
load within 1.2: servers in [81, 261]
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise computes the distribution behind @exm-error-powers-of-ten exactly enough to answer a question about
it. It asks how often an order-of-magnitude estimate is within one order of magnitude.

::: {#exr-error-decades}
#### Within an order of magnitude

If each of $k$ factors is rounded to the nearest power of ten with a $\log_{10}$-error uniform on $[-\frac12, \frac12]$,
independently, what is the probability that the product is within a factor of $10$ of the truth, for $k = 2, 4, 8$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The $\log_{10}$-error of the product is a sum of $k$ independent uniforms on $[-\frac12, \frac12]$, with standard
deviation $\sqrt{k/12}$. For $k = 2$ it lies in $[-1, 1]$ always, so the probability is $1$. For larger $k$ the sum
spreads, and its distribution (the Irwin-Hall distribution, shifted) gives the probabilities in the output: about $92\%$
for four factors and $77\%$ for eight, against worst cases of two and four orders of magnitude.

## Python

$10^6$ simulated sums for each $k$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
for k in (2, 4, 8):
    S = rng.uniform(-0.5, 0.5, (10**6, k)).sum(axis=1)
    print(f"k = {k}: P(within a factor of 10) = {np.mean(np.abs(S) <= 1):.4f}, sd {np.sqrt(k / 12):.3f} decades")
```

```{.text .run-output}
k = 2: P(within a factor of 10) = 1.0000, sd 0.408 decades
k = 4: P(within a factor of 10) = 0.9167, sd 0.577 decades
k = 8: P(within a factor of 10) = 0.7743, sd 0.816 decades
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise turns @exm-error-decision into a rule. It asks for the largest error factor at which a decision stays
the same.

::: {#exr-error-decision-threshold}
#### How wrong may the estimate be?

A design with one write primary is adequate when the peak write rate is at most $10^4$ per second. The estimate is
$\hat\lambda = 694$ per second. What is the largest $\Phi$ for which the decision is robust? With three factors of equal
error, what may each factor's error be?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The decision is robust when $\Phi\hat\lambda \leq 10^4$, so $\Phi \leq 14.4$. With three equal factors, $\phi^3 \leq 14.4$,
so $\phi \leq 2.43$: each assumption may be off by a factor of two and the decision still stands.

## Python

The two thresholds.

```{.python .run}
Phi = 1e4 / 694
print(f"largest Phi {Phi:.1f}; per factor {Phi ** (1 / 3):.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
largest Phi 14.4; per factor 2.43
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise drops the independence of part (c). When one optimist makes every guess, the errors are correlated,
and the typical case moves towards the worst.

::: {#exr-error-correlated}
#### Correlated errors

Let the log-errors $L_1, \dots, L_k$ have mean $0$, standard deviation $\sigma$ each, and correlation $r$ between every
two of them. Show that $L = \sum_iL_i$ has standard deviation $\sigma\sqrt{k + k(k - 1)r}$, and compare $k = 4$,
$\sigma = \ln 2$ for $r = 0, 0.5, 1$ with the worst case of part (a) when each factor is within $2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

$\operatorname{Var}(L) = \sum_i\operatorname{Var}(L_i) + \sum_{i \neq j}\operatorname{Cov}(L_i, L_j) = k\sigma^2 + k(k -
1)r\sigma^2$, since $\operatorname{Cov}(L_i, L_j) = r\sigma^2$. For $k = 4$, $\sigma = \ln 2$, the typical factor $e^{\sigma
\sqrt{4 + 12r}}$ is $4$ for $r = 0$, $8.95$ for $r = 0.5$ and $16$ for $r = 1$. With perfect correlation the typical case
is the worst case of part (a), $2^4 = 16$: correlated guesses lose the benefit of part (c) entirely.

## Python

Check on $k = 4$ by simulation, with correlated Gaussian log-errors built from a shared component.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(12)
k, sigma = 4, np.log(2)
for r in (0.0, 0.5, 1.0):
    shared = rng.standard_normal(10**6)[:, None]
    own = rng.standard_normal((10**6, k))
    L = (sigma * (np.sqrt(r) * shared + np.sqrt(1 - r) * own)).sum(axis=1)
    print(f"r = {r}: typical factor {np.exp(L.std()):.2f}, formula {np.exp(sigma * np.sqrt(k + k * (k - 1) * r)):.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
r = 0.0: typical factor 4.00, formula 4.00
r = 0.5: typical factor 8.95, formula 8.95
r = 1.0: typical factor 16.00, formula 16.00
```
::::
:::
::::

## Availability arithmetic {#sec-availability-arithmetic}

Availability is the requirement that every specification states and every design must be checked against. Tan gives
the standard table of "nines" and the downtime each allows [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 3.2, Table 3.1], Xu notes
that the large cloud providers "set their SLAs at 99.9% or above" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 2, "Availability
numbers"], and Sinha and Chopra list the techniques that raise it, chiefly redundancy and replication
[@sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024, Ch. 2, "Availability"]. None of them gives the arithmetic that connects the availability
of a system to that of its components. This section defines availability precisely and proves that arithmetic, which
needs only independence and the binomial distribution from
[Probability and statistics](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#def-independence).
It ends with the same arithmetic applied to latency: a request that waits for many servers is as slow as the slowest of
them, and the probability of meeting a slow one grows with their number exactly as the unavailability of a chain of
components does.

For more on this topic, see @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Secs. 3.2-3.3], @sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024 [Ch. 2],
@SystemDesignInterview2021 [Ch. 2] and @dean2013tail.

### Availability, downtime and service levels

Tan's definition, "the percentage of time a system can accept requests and return the desired response", is a fraction
of time, and the definition below makes it one. The fraction depends on the window over which it is measured, and a
service level is a promise about that fraction over a stated window; the steady-state value is its limit over long
windows.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-availability}
#### Availability

Let a system be, at each time $t \geq 0$, either **up** (it accepts requests and returns the desired responses) or
**down**, and let $X(t) = 1$ when it is up and $X(t) = 0$ when it is down. Its **availability over the window** $[0,
