\Delta]$ is the fraction of the window during which it is up,
$$
A_\Delta = \frac1\Delta\int_0^\Delta X(t)\,dt ,
$$
its **downtime** over the window is $(1 - A_\Delta)\Delta$, and its **steady-state availability** $A$ is the limit of
$A_\Delta$ as $\Delta \to \infty$, when this limit exists and is the same number for almost every history of the
system. The **number of nines** of an availability $A < 1$ is $-\log_{10}(1 - A)$. A **service level objective**
(SLO) is a non-functional requirement $A_\Delta \geq A^*$ for windows of a stated length $\Delta$; its **error budget** is
the downtime it allows, $(1 - A^*)\Delta$. A **service level agreement** (SLA) is an SLO written into a contract together
with the remedy owed when it is missed.
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example recomputes Tan's table. Its entries are the downtimes $(1 - A)\Delta$ for a year, a month, a week and a
day.

::: {#exm-avail-nines}
#### The table of nines

With a year of $365.25$ days, $A = 99.9\%$ allows $0.001 \times 8766\,\mathrm h = 8.77\,\mathrm h$ a year, $43.8$ minutes a
month, $10.1$ minutes a week and $1.44$ minutes a day; each further nine divides these by ten, down to $5.26$ minutes a
year for five nines [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 3.2, Table 3.1]. Three nines is $3$ nines and $99.95\%$ is
$-\log_{10}0.0005 = 3.3$ nines.
:::

For a single component that fails and is repaired, the steady-state availability depends only on two means. The formula
is proved in the fourth exercise below.

::: {#exm-avail-mttf}
#### Mean time to failure and to repair

A server that runs for $\mathrm{MTTF} = 30$ days on average between failures and takes $\mathrm{MTTR} = 1$ hour to
replace has $A = \mathrm{MTTF}/(\mathrm{MTTF} + \mathrm{MTTR}) = 720/721 = 0.99861$, a little under three nines. Tan
mentions both means as incident metrics, "MTTR (Mean Time to Recovery) and MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures)"
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 3.2]; the mean time between failures is $\mathrm{MTTF} + \mathrm{MTTR}$.
:::

The formula treats failure and repair symmetrically: what matters is their ratio. That makes faster repair as valuable as
rarer failure.

::: {#exm-avail-repair}
#### Repair is as good as reliability

$1 - A = \mathrm{MTTR}/(\mathrm{MTTF} + \mathrm{MTTR}) \approx \mathrm{MTTR}/\mathrm{MTTF}$ when repairs are short. Halving
the repair time of @exm-avail-mttf to $30$ minutes gives $1 - A = 0.5/720.5 = 6.9 \times 10^{-4}$, the same as doubling
the time to failure to $60$ days. Automatic failover, which cuts the repair time from an hour to seconds, is usually the
cheaper of the two.
:::

An SLA is an SLO with a remedy. Xu cites the cloud providers' SLAs as the reference point for what is achievable
[@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 2].

::: {#exm-avail-sla}
#### A service level agreement

A provider promises a monthly availability of $99.9\%$ and owes a credit of $10\%$ of the monthly fee if the month's
availability falls below it. The SLO is $A_\Delta \geq 0.999$ for $\Delta$ one month; the SLA is that SLO plus the credit.
An internal SLO is usually set stricter than the SLA, say $99.95\%$, so that the team is alerted before the contract is
breached.
:::

The error budget turns an SLO into an allowance that can be spent. Every deployment that risks an outage spends from
it.

::: {#exm-avail-error-budget}
#### An error budget

An SLO of $99.95\%$ over a 30-day month gives an error budget of $0.0005 \times 43\,200 = 21.6$ minutes. A deployment that
causes five minutes of errors spends almost a quarter of it; when the budget is spent, the team stops risky changes until
the next window.
:::

Availability can also be measured over requests rather than time. The two agree only when the load is constant, because
an outage at the busiest hour fails more requests than one at night.

::: {#exm-avail-request-based}
#### Time-based and request-based availability

A service that is down for $30$ minutes in a month has time-based availability $1 - 30/43\,200 = 99.93\%$. If the outage
falls in an hour with twice the mean load, it fails $2 \times 30/43\,200$ of the month's requests, and the request-based
availability is $99.86\%$. Tan's phrase "accept requests and return the desired response" is the request-based view.
:::

The window matters as much as the target. A single outage is a large fraction of a short window and a small fraction of a
long one.

::: {#exm-avail-window}
#### Short and long windows

A one-hour outage gives $A_\Delta = 1 - 1/720 = 99.86\%$ for a 30-day window, $1 - 1/8760 = 99.989\%$ for a year, and
$1 - 1/24 = 95.8\%$ for that day. An SLO of $99.9\%$ per month is broken by it; the same target per year is not. An SLO
must name its window.
:::

Planned downtime counts as downtime unless the specification excludes it. Tan notes that vertical scaling "may require
downtime" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 3.1], and a maintenance window caps the availability.

::: {#exm-avail-maintenance}
#### A maintenance window

Four hours of planned maintenance a quarter, about $2190$ hours, cap the availability at $1 - 4/2190 = 99.82\%$, below
three nines, whatever the reliability of the hardware. Designs that upgrade servers one at a time behind a load balancer
avoid this cap, which is one reason they are preferred.
:::

Availability is about whether a request is answered now; durability is about whether stored data can ever be read again.
Tan's definition of fault tolerance names both, "continue operating" and "the prevention of permanent harm (such as data
loss)" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 3.3].

::: {#exm-avail-durability}
#### Availability is not durability

A storage service that is down for an hour a month but never loses data has availability $99.86\%$ and perfect
durability. A cache that is always up but loses its contents on every restart has availability $1$ and no durability.
The photo-sharing service needs high durability for photos (@exm-req-durability) and high availability for the feed;
the two are separate requirements with separate mechanisms.
:::

The last example measures availability by probing, which is how it is observed in practice. The estimate has a
statistical error that the window must be long enough to make small.

::: {#exm-avail-probes}
#### Availability from probes

A monitor sends a probe every minute, $43\,200$ probes a month, and counts the successes. If the service is up a fraction
$A = 0.999$ of the time and probes hit independent instants, the count is $\operatorname{Bin}(43\,200, 0.999)$, with mean
$43\,157$ and standard deviation $6.6$: the measured availability is $0.999 \pm 0.00015$. Probes are too sparse to see an
outage of under a minute.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise extends the table of @exm-avail-nines to targets below three nines. It applies the definition of
downtime directly.

::: {#exr-avail-downtime}
#### Downtime for a target

Give the downtime per year and per 30-day month allowed by $99\%$, $99.5\%$, $99.99\%$ and $99.999\%$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Downtime is $(1 - A)\Delta$: with $\Delta = 8766\,\mathrm h$ a year and $720\,\mathrm h$ a month, $99\%$ allows $87.7\,\mathrm h$
and $7.2\,\mathrm h$; $99.5\%$ allows $43.8\,\mathrm h$ and $3.6\,\mathrm h$; $99.99\%$ allows $52.6$ and $4.3$ minutes;
$99.999\%$ allows $5.3$ minutes and $26$ seconds.

## Python

The downtimes in hours and minutes.

```{.python .run}
for A in (0.99, 0.995, 0.9999, 0.99999):
    year_h, month_h = (1 - A) * 8766, (1 - A) * 720
    print(f"{A:.3%}: {year_h:8.3f} h/year = {year_h * 60:8.1f} min; {month_h:7.3f} h/month = {month_h * 60:7.2f} min")
```

```{.text .run-output}
99.000%:   87.660 h/year =   5259.6 min;   7.200 h/month =  432.00 min
99.500%:   43.830 h/year =   2629.8 min;   3.600 h/month =  216.00 min
99.990%:    0.877 h/year =     52.6 min;   0.072 h/month =    4.32 min
99.999%:    0.088 h/year =      5.3 min;   0.007 h/month =    0.43 min
```
::::
:::

The second exercise inverts the definition of the number of nines. It is how a downtime allowance is turned back into
a target.

::: {#exr-avail-nines-from-downtime}
#### Nines from a downtime

A team can tolerate $2$ hours of downtime a year. What availability and how many nines is that? What if it is $2$ hours
a month?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$1 - A = 2/8766 = 2.28 \times 10^{-4}$, so $A = 99.977\%$, $3.64$ nines. Per month, $1 - A = 2/720 = 2.78 \times 10^{-3}$,
$A = 99.72\%$, $2.56$ nines.

## Python

Both cases.

```{.python .run}
from math import log10
for hours, window in [(2, 8766), (2, 720)]:
    u = hours / window
    print(f"{hours} h in {window} h: A = {1 - u:.5%}, nines = {-log10(u):.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
2 h in 8766 h: A = 99.97718%, nines = 3.64
2 h in 720 h: A = 99.72222%, nines = 2.56
```
::::
:::

The third exercise measures availability from an outage log and checks it against an SLO. The log is the raw material
of every availability report.

::: {#exr-avail-log}
#### An outage log

In a 30-day month a service had outages of $12$, $3$, $27$ and $5$ minutes. Give $A_\Delta$, the share of the error budget
of a $99.9\%$ SLO that was spent, and whether the SLO was met.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The downtime is $47$ minutes, so $A_\Delta = 1 - 47/43\,200 = 99.891\%$. The error budget is $43.2$ minutes, so $109\%$ of
it was spent and the SLO was missed, by less than four minutes.

## Python

The availability and the budget.

```{.python .run}
outages = [12, 3, 27, 5]
month = 30 * 24 * 60
down = sum(outages)
budget = (1 - 0.999) * month
print(f"A = {1 - down / month:.4%}; budget spent {down / budget:.0%}; SLO met: {down <= budget}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
A = 99.8912%; budget spent 109%; SLO met: False
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise proves the formula of @exm-avail-mttf. The proof uses the strong law of large numbers for the
alternating up and down periods.

::: {#exr-avail-mttf-proof}
#### Availability from the two means

Let a component alternate up periods $U_1, U_2, \dots$ and down periods $V_1, V_2, \dots$, all independent, the $U_j$
identically distributed with mean $\mathrm{MTTF}$ and the $V_j$ with mean $\mathrm{MTTR}$, both finite and positive. Show
that the fraction of time up at the end of the $m$-th repair tends to $\mathrm{MTTF}/(\mathrm{MTTF} + \mathrm{MTTR})$ with
probability one as $m \to \infty$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

At the end of the $m$-th repair the elapsed time is $\sum_{j \leq m}(U_j + V_j)$, of which $\sum_{j \leq m}U_j$ was up, so
the fraction up is
$$
\frac{\frac1m\sum_{j \leq m}U_j}{\frac1m\sum_{j \leq m}U_j + \frac1m\sum_{j \leq m}V_j}.
$$
By the [strong law of large numbers](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/probability/index.qmd#thm-strong-law-large-numbers),
$\frac1m\sum_jU_j \to \mathrm{MTTF}$ and $\frac1m\sum_jV_j \to \mathrm{MTTR}$ with probability one, and the map $(u, v)
\mapsto u/(u + v)$ is continuous where $u + v > 0$, so the fraction tends to $\mathrm{MTTF}/(\mathrm{MTTF} +
\mathrm{MTTR})$. (Between the ends of repairs the fraction moves by at most the length of one cycle over the elapsed
time, which also tends to zero, so the limit holds for $A_\Delta$ as $\Delta \to \infty$; the distributions of $U_j$ and
$V_j$ beyond their means do not matter.)

## Python

Check on $10^5$ cycles with lognormal up times of mean $720\,\mathrm h$ and exponential repairs of mean $1\,\mathrm h$:
the simulated fraction against $720/721$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(14)
m, s = 10**5, 1.0
U = np.exp(rng.normal(np.log(720) - s**2 / 2, s, m))
V = rng.exponential(1.0, m)
print(f"simulated {U.sum() / (U.sum() + V.sum()):.6f}; formula {720 / 721:.6f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
simulated 0.998611; formula 0.998613
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise inverts the formula for a target. It asks how fast repairs must be for a component to reach four
nines.

::: {#exr-avail-mttr-target}
#### How fast must repairs be?

A component fails on average every $60$ days. What mean time to repair gives $A = 99.99\%$? And $99.999\%$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$A = \mathrm{MTTF}/(\mathrm{MTTF} + \mathrm{MTTR})$ gives $\mathrm{MTTR} = \mathrm{MTTF}(1 - A)/A$. With $\mathrm{MTTF} = 1440\,
\mathrm h$, four nines need $\mathrm{MTTR} = 0.144\,\mathrm h = 8.6$ minutes and five nines $52$ seconds: only automatic
recovery is that fast.

## Python

The two repair times.

```{.python .run}
mttf = 60 * 24
for A in (0.9999, 0.99999):
    mttr = mttf * (1 - A) / A
    print(f"A = {A}: MTTR = {mttr:.4f} h = {mttr * 60:.2f} min")
```

```{.text .run-output}
A = 0.9999: MTTR = 0.1440 h = 8.64 min
A = 0.99999: MTTR = 0.0144 h = 0.86 min
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise computes what an SLA is worth to its customer. Credits are a fraction of the fee and grow in tiers as
the availability falls.

::: {#exr-avail-credits}
#### Credits under an SLA

An SLA owes $10\%$ of the monthly fee below $99.9\%$, $25\%$ below $99\%$ and $100\%$ below $95\%$. Give the credit for
monthly downtimes of $30$ minutes, $2$ hours, $10$ hours and $2$ days, on a fee of $10\,000$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Over $43\,200$ minutes: $30$ minutes give $99.93\%$ and no credit; $2$ hours $99.72\%$, credit $1000$; $10$ hours $98.6\%$,
credit $2500$; $2$ days $93.3\%$, credit $10\,000$. The credit is bounded by the fee, while the customer's loss from two
days of downtime may not be, which is why an SLA does not replace a design for availability.

## Python

The tiers as a table.

```{.python .run}
tiers = [(0.95, 1.00), (0.99, 0.25), (0.999, 0.10)]
def credit(A, fee=10000):
    return next((share * fee for limit, share in tiers if A < limit), 0.0)
for label, minutes in [("30 min", 30), ("2 h", 120), ("10 h", 600), ("2 days", 2880)]:
    A = 1 - minutes / 43200
    print(f"{label:6s}: A = {A:.4%}, credit {credit(A):.0f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
30 min: A = 99.9306%, credit 0
2 h   : A = 99.7222%, credit 1000
10 h  : A = 98.6111%, credit 2500
2 days: A = 93.3333%, credit 10000
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise spends an error budget on deployments that sometimes fail. It is the planning question behind
@exm-avail-error-budget, answered with the binomial distribution.

::: {#exr-avail-deploys}
#### Deployments within a budget

A team deploys $40$ times a month. Each deployment fails with probability $0.05$, and a failure causes $8$ minutes of
downtime before it is rolled back. With an SLO of $99.95\%$ over a 30-day month and no other downtime, what is the
expected share of the error budget spent, and the probability that deployments alone break the SLO?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The number of failed deployments is $\operatorname{Bin}(40, 0.05)$, with mean $2$, so the expected downtime is
$16$ minutes, $74\%$ of the $21.6$-minute budget. The SLO breaks when $8F > 21.6$, that is with $F \geq 3$ failures, which
has probability $1 - \sum_{j \leq 2}\binom{40}j0.05^j0.95^{40 - j} = 0.323$. Faster rollback, to two minutes, would allow
ten failures.

## Python

The binomial probabilities.

```{.python .run}
from math import comb
n, p, budget = 40, 0.05, 0.0005 * 43200
print(f"expected share {n * p * 8 / budget:.0%}")
P = lambda j: comb(n, j) * p**j * (1 - p)**(n - j)
max_ok = int(budget // 8)
print(f"P(SLO broken) = {1 - sum(P(j) for j in range(max_ok + 1)):.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
expected share 74%
P(SLO broken) = 0.323
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise compares the two measures of @exm-avail-request-based over a day with a realistic load curve. The
difference depends on when the outage happens.

::: {#exr-avail-request-vs-time}
#### Outages at the peak and at night

The load in requests per minute over a day is $\lambda(t) = 1 + 0.6\cos(2\pi(t - 20)/24)$ in units of the mean, $t$ in
hours. A $30$-minute outage starts at 20:00 or at 08:00. Give the time-based and the request-based availability of the
day in both cases.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Time-based availability is $1 - 0.5/24 = 97.92\%$ in both cases. Request-based availability is one minus the share of the
day's requests that fall in the outage: about $1.6 \times 0.5/24$ at the peak, so $96.7\%$, and $0.4 \times 0.5/24$ at
the trough, so $99.2\%$. The same outage costs four times as many requests at the peak.

## Python

The integrals of the load over the outage, numerically.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
t = np.linspace(0, 24, 24 * 60 * 10, endpoint=False)
load = 1 + 0.6 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * (t - 20) / 24)
for start in (20.0, 8.0):
    down = (t >= start - 0.25) & (t < start + 0.25)
    print(f"outage centred at {start:4.1f} h: time-based {1 - down.mean():.4f}, "
          f"request-based {1 - load[down].sum() / load.sum():.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
outage centred at 20.0 h: time-based 0.9792, request-based 0.9667
outage centred at  8.0 h: time-based 0.9792, request-based 0.9917
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise asks how long a window must be for a probe-based measurement to tell two targets apart. It applies
the binomial model of @exm-avail-probes.

::: {#exr-avail-probe-window}
#### Telling three nines from four

Probes every minute hit independent instants. How many days of probes are needed for the measured availability of a
service with $A = 0.999$ to lie, with two standard deviations, below $0.9995$, so that it is distinguishable from a service
meeting $99.95\%$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

With $m$ probes the measured value has standard deviation $\sqrt{A(1 - A)/m}$. The requirement $0.999 + 2\sqrt{0.000999/m}
\leq 0.9995$ gives $m \geq 4 \times 0.000999/0.0005^2 = 15\,984$ probes, about $11.1$ days. A week of probes cannot reliably
separate the two levels; a month can.

## Python

The number of probes and days, and a simulation of the measured value over $12$ days.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
A, gap = 0.999, 0.0005
m = 4 * A * (1 - A) / gap**2
print(f"probes needed {m:.0f} = {m / 1440:.1f} days")
rng = np.random.default_rng(15)
measured = rng.binomial(12 * 1440, A, 10**5) / (12 * 1440)
print(f"over 12 days, share of measurements >= 0.9995: {np.mean(measured >= 0.9995):.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
probes needed 15984 = 11.1 days
over 12 days, share of measurements >= 0.9995: 0.0102
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise combines maintenance, failures and the window. It asks whether a plan meets an SLO and what to change
if it does not.

::: {#exr-avail-plan}
#### Does the plan meet the SLO?

A single database server fails every $90$ days on average with a repair of $2$ hours, and is patched for $30$ minutes every
month. The SLO is $99.9\%$ per 30-day month. Give the expected monthly downtime and the probability that a month breaks the
SLO, if failures form a Poisson process. Then redo it with patches applied to a standby that takes over, so that patching
causes $30$ seconds of downtime.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The number of failures in a month is Poisson with mean $30/90 = 1/3$. With patching in place, downtime is $30 + 120F$
minutes, expected $70$ minutes, above the $43.2$-minute budget even with no failure, so every month breaks the SLO.
With the standby, downtime is $0.5 + 120F$ minutes: a month breaks the SLO as soon as one failure occurs, with probability
$1 - e^{-1/3} = 0.283$. The plan needs both the standby for patching and a failover for failures, which brings the repair
time from hours to minutes.

## Python

The expected downtimes and the probabilities of breaking the SLO.

```{.python .run}
from math import exp
budget, mean_f = 43.2, 30 / 90
for patch in (30, 0.5):
    expected = patch + 120 * mean_f
    p_break = 1.0 if patch > budget else 1 - exp(-mean_f)
    print(f"patch downtime {patch} min: expected {expected:.1f} min, P(SLO broken) = {p_break:.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
patch downtime 30 min: expected 70.0 min, P(SLO broken) = 0.283
patch downtime 0.5 min: expected 40.5 min, P(SLO broken) = 0.283
```
::::
:::
::::

### Components in series and in parallel

A design draws a system as boxes and arrows, and its availability follows from the boxes' availabilities by two rules.
If every component is needed, as the tiers of @fig-three-tier are by a feed request, the system is up only when all are
up; if one of several replicas suffices, it is down only when all are down. With independent failures the first rule
multiplies availabilities and the second multiplies unavailabilities. The proposition proves both, the rule for quorums
of $k$ out of $n$, and what remains true without independence. The availability of each component is read, as in the
definition, as the probability that it is up at a time chosen at random.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-series-parallel-availability}
#### Availability of series and parallel systems

Let a system consist of components $1, \dots, n$, let $E_i$ be the event that component $i$ is up at a given time, with
$\mathbb P(E_i) = A_i$, and let $A$ be the probability that the system is up.

(a) (**Series**) If the system is up exactly when every component is up, and $E_1, \dots, E_n$ are independent, then $A =
A_1A_2\cdots A_n$; in particular $A \leq \min_iA_i$.

(b) (**Parallel**) If the system is up exactly when at least one component is up, and $E_1, \dots, E_n$ are independent,
then $1 - A = (1 - A_1)\cdots(1 - A_n)$; in particular $A \geq \max_iA_i$.

(c) (**$k$ out of $n$**) If the system is up exactly when at least $k$ components are up, $E_1, \dots, E_n$ are
independent and $A_i = a$ for all $i$, then
$$
A = \sum_{j = k}^n\binom nj a^j(1 - a)^{n - j}.
$$

(d) (**Without independence**) In the series case $1 - \sum_i(1 - A_i) \leq A \leq \min_iA_i$, and in the parallel case
$\max_iA_i \leq A$, whatever the dependence between the $E_i$.
:::

::::

*Proof.* (a) The system is up on $E_1 \cap \dots \cap E_n$, whose probability is $\prod_i\mathbb P(E_i)$ by independence.
Each factor is at most $1$, so the product is at most any one of them.

(b) The system is down on $E_1^c \cap \dots \cap E_n^c$. Complements of independent events are independent, so this
event has probability $\prod_i(1 - A_i)$. Each factor is at most $1$, so $1 - A \leq 1 - A_i$ for every $i$.

(c) The number of components up is a sum of $n$ independent indicators, each $1$ with probability $a$, so it has the
binomial distribution $\operatorname{Bin}(n, a)$, and the system is up when it is at least $k$.

(d) In the series case the system is up on $\bigcap_iE_i \subseteq E_j$ for each $j$, so $A \leq A_j$; and it is down on
$\bigcup_iE_i^c$, whose probability is at most $\sum_i(1 - A_i)$ by the union bound. In the parallel case the system is
up on $\bigcup_iE_i \supseteq E_j$ for each $j$, so $A \geq A_j$. $\square$

Parts (a) and (b) are dual: a chain of components loses nines, a redundant group gains them. With $n$ components of
availability $a$, a series system has $1 - A = 1 - a^n \approx n(1 - a)$, so its unavailability grows linearly with $n$,
while a parallel group has $1 - A = (1 - a)^n$, so its number of nines is $n$ times that of one component.
The fourth example below plots both. Part (d) is the warning: redundancy helps only to the extent that the replicas fail
independently, and nothing about the parallel case can be proved without that.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest series system is a web server in front of a database. Its availability is the product of theirs, below
both.

::: {#exm-series-web-db}
#### A web server and a database

A web server and a database, each with $99.9\%$, in series give $0.999^2 = 99.80\%$ by part (a): twice the downtime of
either, $1.75$ hours a month instead of $43.8$ minutes.
:::

The simplest parallel system is two replicas of the same component, either of which can serve. Part (b) squares the
unavailability, which doubles the number of nines.

::: {#exm-parallel-two}
#### Two replicas

Two replicas of $99\%$ each, either of which can serve, give $1 - 0.01^2 = 99.99\%$ by part (b): two nines become four,
provided the replicas fail independently.
:::

Real systems are series chains of redundant groups. The two rules apply in turn, the parallel rule inside each group and
the series rule between them.

::: {#exm-series-of-parallel}
#### Tiers of replicas

A feed request needs a load balancer (two in parallel, $99.9\%$ each), an application server (three in parallel, $99\%$
each) and the database (a primary and a standby, $99.9\%$ each). The groups have $1 - 10^{-6}$, $1 - 10^{-6}$ and $1 -
10^{-6}$, and in series $A = (1 - 10^{-6})^3 \approx 1 - 3 \times 10^{-6}$: five nines from components with two and three.
:::

@fig-availability-replicas plots the number of nines of $n$ components in series and in parallel for three component
availabilities. The parallel lines are straight, as part (b) predicts, and the series lines fall slowly.

::: {#exm-availability-figure}
#### Nines against the number of components

In parallel, $n$ components of $a = 0.99$ have $2n$ nines; in series, the nines fall from $2$ for one component to $1.2$
for six. Adding a replica adds as many nines as one component has; adding a component in series loses a fraction of a
nine.

![Number of nines of $n$ components in parallel (solid) and in series (dashed), for component availabilities $0.9$,
$0.99$ and $0.999$.](figures/availability_replicas.svg){#fig-availability-replicas width=65%}
:::

A quorum is up when a majority of its replicas is. Part (c) gives its availability, which lies between the series and
parallel cases.

::: {#exm-quorum}
#### Two out of three

Three replicas of availability $a$, of which two must be up, give $A = 3a^2(1 - a) + a^3 = 3a^2 - 2a^3$. For $a = 0.99$
this is $0.999702$, three and a half nines; a single replica has two and three in parallel six. A majority quorum buys
consistency (two replicas always share at least one member) at the price of availability.
:::

Long chains are the hidden cost of splitting a system into many services. Part (a) says how fast the availability falls.

::: {#exm-series-many}
#### Thirty services in a chain

A request that passes through $30$ services, each with three nines, succeeds with $0.999^{30} = 97.0\%$, about one failure
in thirty-four requests, and the bound of part (d) gives $97\%$ even without independence. A design with many synchronous
dependencies must make each of them far better than the target for the whole.
:::

Independence is the assumption most likely to fail. A shared component, such as the power supply of a rack, is in series
with every replica that depends on it.

::: {#exm-common-mode}
#### A shared rack

Two replicas of $99\%$ in the same rack, whose power is up $99.9\%$ of the time, are not independent. Modelling the rack as
a component in series with the redundant pair gives $A = 0.999 \times (1 - 0.01^2) = 99.89\%$, not $99.99\%$: the rack
caps the pair. Placing the replicas in different racks or zones restores the independence that part (b) needs.
:::

Failover is not instantaneous or certain. If switching to the standby succeeds only with some probability, the parallel
rule must be corrected.

::: {#exm-failover-coverage}
#### Imperfect failover

A primary of availability $a_1$ fails over to a standby of availability $a_2$ with success probability $s$. Under
independence the pair is up when the primary is up, or when it is down, the standby is up and the switch worked: $A = a_1
+ (1 - a_1)a_2s$. For $a_1 = a_2 = 0.999$ and $s = 0.9$, $A = 0.999899$: an unavailability of $1.0 \times 10^{-4}$, a
hundred times the $10^{-6}$ of perfect failover. The switch, not the standby, limits the pair.
:::

A synchronous call to an external system puts it in series with the service. This is the general form of
@exr-req-dependency-cap.

::: {#exm-third-party}
#### An external dependency

A checkout service with its own availability $99.99\%$ that calls a payment provider of $99.9\%$ synchronously has $A
\leq 0.999$ by part (d), whatever its own design. Calling two providers, either of which can process the payment, puts
them in parallel: $1 - 0.001^2$, and the service's own $99.99\%$ becomes the limit again.
:::

The last example reduces the whole of @fig-three-tier to one number, applying the two rules group by group. It is the
availability estimate of the high-level design.

::: {#exm-three-tier-availability}
#### The availability of the container diagram

For a feed request in @fig-three-tier, take the load balancer pair at $99.9\%$ each, $146$ application servers of $99\%$ of
which any $97$ suffice for the peak, the cache (two replicas of $99.9\%$, a miss falling back to the database) and the
database (a primary and two read replicas, $99.9\%$ each, any one of which can serve a read). The load balancers give $1 -
10^{-6}$; the application tier, by part (c), is up with probability indistinguishable from $1$; the database group gives
$1 - 10^{-9}$. The cache is not needed for availability, only for load, so the feed's availability is about $1 - 10^{-6}$,
limited by the load balancers. In practice shared failures (deployments, configuration, the network) dominate such
numbers, which is the content of part (d).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise applies parts (a) and (b) directly to three components. It compares the two arrangements of the same
components, in a chain and as a redundant group.

::: {#exr-series-basic}
#### Series or parallel

Three components have availabilities $0.99$, $0.995$ and $0.999$. Give the availability of the three in series and in
parallel, and the number of nines of each.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

In series $0.99 \times 0.995 \times 0.999 = 0.98406$, $1.80$ nines; in parallel $1 - 0.01 \times 0.005 \times 0.001 = 1 -
5 \times 10^{-8}$, $7.3$ nines.

## Python

Both arrangements.

```{.python .run}
from math import log10, prod
a = [0.99, 0.995, 0.999]
series, parallel = prod(a), 1 - prod(1 - x for x in a)
print(f"series {series:.5f} ({-log10(1 - series):.2f} nines); parallel {parallel:.10f} ({-log10(1 - parallel):.2f} nines)")
```

```{.text .run-output}
series 0.98406 (1.80 nines); parallel 0.9999999500 (7.30 nines)
```
::::
:::

The second exercise inverts part (b) of the proposition. It asks how many independent replicas of a given quality reach a
target of five nines.

::: {#exr-parallel-replicas-needed}
#### How many replicas?

How many independent replicas of availability $0.99$ are needed for five nines? Of $0.95$? Of $0.9$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Part (b) needs $(1 - a)^n \leq 10^{-5}$, so $n \geq 5/(-\log_{10}(1 - a))$: $n = 3$ for $a = 0.99$ ($2.5$ rounded up), $n
= 4$ for $0.95$ ($3.84$) and $n = 5$ for $0.9$.

## Python

The smallest $n$ for each component availability.

```{.python .run}
from math import ceil, log10
for a in (0.99, 0.95, 0.9):
    print(f"a = {a}: n = {ceil(5 / -log10(1 - a))}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
a = 0.99: n = 3
a = 0.95: n = 4
a = 0.9: n = 5
```
::::
:::

The third exercise asks for a proof of the two inequalities of parts (a) and (b) from part (d) alone. They need no
independence.

::: {#exr-series-bounds-proof}
#### Bounds without independence

Prove that for any events, $\mathbb P(\bigcap_iE_i) \leq \min_i\mathbb P(E_i)$ and $\mathbb P(\bigcup_iE_i) \geq \max_i
\mathbb P(E_i)$, and show by an example with two components that the series availability can equal $\min_iA_i$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

For each $j$, $\bigcap_iE_i \subseteq E_j \subseteq \bigcup_iE_i$, so by monotonicity $\mathbb P(\bigcap_iE_i) \leq \mathbb
P(E_j) \leq \mathbb P(\bigcup_iE_i)$; taking the minimum and maximum over $j$ gives both inequalities. Equality in the
first: let component 2 be up whenever component 1 is ($E_1 \subseteq E_2$), for example a process and the machine it runs
on. Then $E_1 \cap E_2 = E_1$ and the series availability is $A_1 = \min(A_1, A_2)$, larger than the product $A_1A_2$.

## Python

Check on a simulated history: a machine up $99.9\%$ of the time and a process on it, up $99\%$ of the time and only when the
machine is.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(16)
machine = rng.random(10**6) < 0.999
process = machine & (rng.random(10**6) < 0.99 / 0.999)
print(f"A1 = {process.mean():.4f}, A2 = {machine.mean():.4f}, series = {(process & machine).mean():.4f}, "
      f"product = {process.mean() * machine.mean():.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
A1 = 0.9901, A2 = 0.9989, series = 0.9901, product = 0.9890
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise checks parts (b) and (c) by simulation, the "Monte Carlo check" the coverage of this chapter calls
for. It draws the states of the components at many random instants.

::: {#exr-kofn-monte-carlo}
#### A Monte Carlo check

Simulate $10^6$ instants for five independent replicas of availability $0.9$ and estimate the availability of "at least
one up", "at least three up" and "all five up". Compare with parts (a)-(c).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Part (b) gives $1 - 0.1^5 = 0.99999$, part (c) with $k = 3$ gives $\sum_{j \geq 3}\binom5j0.9^j0.1^{5 - j} = 0.99144$, and
part (a) gives $0.9^5 = 0.59049$. The simulated frequencies agree to within their standard errors, at most
$5 \times 10^{-4}$.

## Python

The simulation and the formulas.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from math import comb
rng = np.random.default_rng(17)
up = (rng.random((10**6, 5)) < 0.9).sum(axis=1)
for k in (1, 3, 5):
    exact = sum(comb(5, j) * 0.9**j * 0.1**(5 - j) for j in range(k, 6))
    print(f"at least {k} up: simulated {np.mean(up >= k):.5f}, exact {exact:.5f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
at least 1 up: simulated 0.99999, exact 0.99999
at least 3 up: simulated 0.99147, exact 0.99144
at least 5 up: simulated 0.59107, exact 0.59049
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise shows that the lower bound of part (d) for series systems is attained. The components must fail at
different times, never together.

::: {#exr-series-union-tight}
#### When failures never overlap

Three components are each down $1\%$ of the time, and their downtimes never overlap (they share a maintenance schedule that
takes them down one at a time). Give the series availability and compare it with the independent case.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The events $E_i^c$ are disjoint, so the system is down with probability $\sum_i\mathbb P(E_i^c) = 0.03$ exactly: $A = 0.97$,
the lower bound of part (d). Independent components would give $0.99^3 = 0.970299$; non-overlapping downtimes are the worst
arrangement for a series system, and the best for a parallel one, which is never down.

## Python

A schedule of $300$ time slots in which each component is down in its own $3$ slots.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
slots = 300
down = np.zeros((3, slots), bool)
for i in range(3):
    down[i, 3 * i:3 * i + 3] = True
print(f"each down {down.mean(axis=1)}; series A = {1 - down.any(axis=0).mean():.4f}; "
      f"parallel A = {1 - down.all(axis=0).mean():.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
each down [0.01 0.01 0.01]; series A = 0.9700; parallel A = 1.0000
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise quantifies the warning of part (d) for parallel systems. A common cause that takes both replicas down
together breaks the squaring of part (b).

::: {#exr-parallel-correlated}
#### A common cause

Two replicas are each down $1\%$ of the time. A fraction $f$ of each replica's downtime is caused by a shared event that
takes both down together; the rest is independent. Give the pair's availability for $f = 0, 0.1, 0.5$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The shared event occurs with probability $0.01f$, and each replica's own failures, independent of the shared event and of
each other, have probability $u$ with $0.01f + (1 - 0.01f)u = 0.01$. The pair is down when the shared event occurs or both
own failures do: $1 - A = 0.01f + (1 - 0.01f)u^2$. For $f = 0$ this is $10^{-4}$; for $f = 0.1$, $1.08 \times 10^{-3}$;
for $f = 0.5$, $5.03 \times 10^{-3}$. A tenth of shared downtime costs a factor of ten.

## Python

The formula and a simulation.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(18)
for f in (0.0, 0.1, 0.5):
    c = 0.01 * f
    u = (0.01 - c) / (1 - c)
    shared = rng.random(2 * 10**6) < c
    own = rng.random((2, 2 * 10**6)) < u
    down = shared | (own[0] & own[1])
    print(f"f = {f}: 1 - A = {c + (1 - c) * u**2:.6f}, simulated {down.mean():.6f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
f = 0.0: 1 - A = 0.000100, simulated 0.000096
f = 0.1: 1 - A = 0.001081, simulated 0.001069
f = 0.5: 1 - A = 0.005025, simulated 0.004933
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise splits an availability target across a chain. It is the availability counterpart of the latency
budgets of @exr-budget-allocate.

::: {#exr-series-allocate}
#### Availability budgets

A request crosses five services in series and must succeed $99.9\%$ of the time. If all five get the same target, what
must it be? If one of them is an external service with $99.95\%$, what must each of the other four reach?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

By part (a), $a^5 \geq 0.999$ gives $a \geq 0.999^{1/5} = 0.99980$. With the external service fixed, $a^4 \times 0.9995
\geq 0.999$ gives $a \geq (0.999/0.9995)^{1/4} = 0.999875$. The union bound of part (d) gives almost the same targets,
$1 - 0.0002$ and $1 - 0.000125$, without independence.

## Python

Both targets, by part (a) and by the union bound.

```{.python .run}
print(f"equal: {0.999 ** (1 / 5):.6f} (union bound {1 - 0.001 / 5:.6f})")
print(f"with the external service: {(0.999 / 0.9995) ** (1 / 4):.6f} (union bound {1 - 0.0005 / 4:.6f})")
```

```{.text .run-output}
equal: 0.999800 (union bound 0.999800)
with the external service: 0.999875 (union bound 0.999875)
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise weighs the cost of a replica against the cost of downtime. The optimum number of replicas is where an
extra replica saves less than it costs.

::: {#exr-parallel-cost}
#### The cheapest number of replicas

A replica costs $500$ a month and is up $99\%$ of the time, independently of the others. Each hour of downtime costs
$20\,000$. How many replicas minimise the expected monthly cost?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

With $n$ replicas the expected downtime is $0.01^n \times 720$ hours, so the cost is $500n + 20\,000 \times 720 \times
0.01^n$: $144\,500$ for $n = 1$, $2440$ for $n = 2$, $1514$ for $n = 3$ and $2000$ for $n = 4$. Three replicas are
cheapest; the fourth saves $14$ and costs $500$.

## Python

The cost for one to five replicas.

```{.python .run}
for n in range(1, 6):
    print(f"n = {n}: {500 * n + 20000 * 720 * 0.01**n:10.1f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
n = 1:   144500.0
n = 2:     2440.0
n = 3:     1514.4
n = 4:     2000.1
n = 5:     2500.0
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise compares majority quorums of different sizes with part (c). Larger quorums tolerate more failures,
but only if the replicas are good enough.

::: {#exr-kofn-majority}
#### Majorities of three and five

Give the availability of a majority quorum of $3$ and of $5$ replicas for $a = 0.99$, $0.9$ and $0.6$. When is the larger
quorum worse?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Part (c) with $k = 2, n = 3$ and $k = 3, n = 5$ gives, for $a = 0.99$: $0.999702$ and $0.99999$; for $0.9$: $0.972$ and
$0.99144$; for $0.6$: $0.648$ and $0.68256$. The five-replica majority is better in every case; it is worse only when $a <
\frac12$, where both are below $a$ and larger majorities are less likely to form (the binomial tail moves the wrong way).

## Python

The six values, and one case below a half.

```{.python .run}
from math import comb
def quorum(n, a):
    k = n // 2 + 1
    return sum(comb(n, j) * a**j * (1 - a)**(n - j) for j in range(k, n + 1))
for a in (0.99, 0.9, 0.6, 0.4):
    print(f"a = {a}: 2 of 3 {quorum(3, a):.6f}, 3 of 5 {quorum(5, a):.6f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
a = 0.99: 2 of 3 0.999702, 3 of 5 0.999990
a = 0.9: 2 of 3 0.972000, 3 of 5 0.991440
a = 0.6: 2 of 3 0.648000, 3 of 5 0.682560
a = 0.4: 2 of 3 0.352000, 3 of 5 0.317440
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise is a small design problem solved by enumeration. It chooses the number of replicas of each tier to meet
a target at least cost.

::: {#exr-series-parallel-design}
#### Designing for four nines

A request needs a load balancer, an application server and a database, in series. Load balancers cost $1$ unit and are up
$99.9\%$; application servers cost $2$ and are up $99\%$; databases cost $5$ and are up $99.5\%$. Replicas within a tier are
in parallel and independent. Find the cheapest numbers of replicas, up to four per tier, for $A \geq 99.99\%$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A single replica of any tier is down at least $10^{-3}$ of the time, ten times the whole allowance, so each tier needs at
least two. Two of each give $(1 - 10^{-6})(1 - 10^{-4})(1 - 2.5 \times 10^{-5}) = 0.999874$, just short of the target:
the application pair alone uses the whole allowance of $10^{-4}$. A third application server makes that tier $1 - 10^{-6}$
and $A = 0.999973$, at cost $2 + 6 + 10 = 18$, and no design of cost $16$ or $17$ meets the target. The enumeration confirms
it and lists the next options.

## Python

All $4^3$ designs, sorted by cost among those that meet the target.

```{.python .run}
from itertools import product
tiers = [(1, 0.999), (2, 0.99), (5, 0.995)]
ok = []
for counts in product(range(1, 5), repeat=3):
    A, cost = 1.0, 0
    for n, (c, a) in zip(counts, tiers):
        A *= 1 - (1 - a) ** n
        cost += n * c
    if A >= 0.9999:
        ok.append((cost, counts, A))
for cost, counts, A in sorted(ok)[:3]:
    print(f"cost {cost}: replicas {counts}, A = {A:.6f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
cost 18: replicas (2, 3, 2), A = 0.999973
cost 19: replicas (3, 3, 2), A = 0.999974
cost 20: replicas (2, 4, 2), A = 0.999974
```
::::
:::
::::

### Fan-out and the latency tail

A search, a feed assembled from many shards, or any query over partitioned data sends one request to many servers and
waits for all of them. Dean and Barroso observed that this turns rare slowness of single servers into common slowness of
requests: "if a user request must collect responses from 100 such servers in parallel, then 63% of user requests will take
more than one second" when each server is that slow for one request in a hundred [@dean2013tail, p. 76]. The proposition
below proves the rule behind the observation. It is part (a) of @prp-series-parallel-availability with "up" replaced by
"fast": a request is fast only if every call is fast.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-fan-out-tail}
#### Fan-out amplifies the tail

Let a request be sent in parallel to $n$ servers and complete when the last response arrives, so that its latency is $T =
\max(T_1, \dots, T_n)$, where $T_1, \dots, T_n$ are independent with common distribution function $F(t) = \mathbb P(T_i \leq
t)$.

(a) $\mathbb P(T > t) = 1 - F(t)^n$. In particular, if each call exceeds $t$ with probability $p$, the request exceeds it with
probability $1 - (1 - p)^n$, and
$$
1 - e^{-np} \leq 1 - (1 - p)^n \leq np .
$$

(b) For every $q \in (0, 1)$, $t_q(T) = t_{q^{1/n}}(T_1)$: the $q$-quantile of the request is the $q^{1/n}$-quantile of
one call.

(c) The request exceeds $t$ with probability at most $\varepsilon$ if and only if each call does so with probability $p
\leq 1 - (1 - \varepsilon)^{1/n}$, and this threshold is at least $\varepsilon/n$.
:::

::::

*Proof.* (a) $T \leq t$ exactly when $T_i \leq t$ for every $i$, so by independence $\mathbb P(T \leq t) = F(t)^n$. With
$F(t) = 1 - p$: since $1 - p \leq e^{-p}$, $(1 - p)^n \leq e^{-np}$, which gives the left inequality. For the right one,
$(1 - p)^n \geq 1 - np$ (Bernoulli's inequality) holds for $n = 1$, and if it holds for $n$ then $(1 - p)^{n + 1} \geq (1 -
np)(1 - p) = 1 - (n + 1)p + np^2 \geq 1 - (n + 1)p$ when $1 - np \geq 0$, while for $1 - np < 0$ the claim is trivial.

(b) By (a), $\mathbb P(T \leq t) \geq q$ if and only if $F(t)^n \geq q$, that is $F(t) \geq q^{1/n}$. The two sets of $t$
coincide, so their infima, $t_q(T)$ and $t_{q^{1/n}}(T_1)$, are equal.

(c) By (a), $1 - (1 - p)^n \leq \varepsilon$ if and only if $1 - p \geq (1 - \varepsilon)^{1/n}$. The function $g(x) = (1 -
x)^{1/n}$ is concave on $[0, 1]$, so it lies below its tangent at $0$: $(1 - \varepsilon)^{1/n} \leq 1 - \varepsilon/n$,
and therefore $1 - (1 - \varepsilon)^{1/n} \geq \varepsilon/n$. $\square$

Part (a) explains the figure in Dean and Barroso's paper, which the third example below redraws; part (b) says that a fan-out
of $100$ makes the $99.99$th percentile of a server the $99$th percentile of the request; part (c) says that each server
must be about $n$ times better than the target for the request. Dean and Barroso's conclusion is that the tail cannot be
eliminated at scale, only tolerated by techniques such as hedged requests [@dean2013tail, pp. 76-77].

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example is Dean and Barroso's own illustration of the effect. It is part (a) of the proposition with their
numbers.

::: {#exm-fanout-hundred}
#### One hundred servers

Each server answers in $10\,\mathrm{ms}$ typically but takes a second for one request in a hundred. A request that waits for
$100$ servers is slow with probability $1 - 0.99^{100} = 0.634$, the "63%" of the paper [@dean2013tail, p. 76]. The bounds of
part (a) are $1 - e^{-1} = 0.632$ and $1$.
:::

The second case in the paper has rarer slowness and more servers. The product of the two is what matters, as the bounds
of part (a) show.

::: {#exm-fanout-two-thousand}
#### Two thousand servers

"Even for services with only one in 10,000 requests experiencing more than one-second latencies at the single-server level,
a service with 2,000 such servers will see almost one in five user requests taking more than one second" [@dean2013tail,
p. 76]: $1 - 0.9999^{2000} = 0.181$, between $1 - e^{-0.2} = 0.181$ and $0.2$.
:::

@fig-fan-out-tail draws part (a) as a function of $n$ for three values of $p$. Each curve rises from $p$ to almost $1$ as $n$
passes $1/p$.

::: {#exm-fanout-figure}
#### The amplification curve

The curves are $1 - (1 - p)^n$ for $p = 10^{-2}, 10^{-3}, 10^{-4}$, with Dean and Barroso's two cases marked. On the
logarithmic axis they are the same curve shifted, since $1 - (1 - p)^n \approx 1 - e^{-np}$ depends on $np$ only.

![Probability that a request waiting for $n$ servers is slow when each server is slow with probability $p$, with the two
cases of Dean and Barroso marked.](figures/fan_out_tail.svg){#fig-fan-out-tail width=65%}
:::

Part (b) translates request percentiles into server percentiles. It is the form in which the proposition is used to set
server targets.

::: {#exm-fanout-quantile}
#### Which server percentile matters

With $n = 100$, the request's $99$th percentile is the servers' $0.99^{1/100} = 0.9998995$ quantile, essentially the
$99.99$th percentile. A server team that reports its $99$th percentile is reporting a number that the users of a fan-out
of $100$ never see.
:::

For exponential call latencies part (b) has a closed form. The request percentile grows only logarithmically in $n$, but
it grows.

::: {#exm-fanout-exponential}
#### Exponential calls

If each call is exponential with mean $m$, $t_q(T_1) = -m\ln(1 - q)$, so $t_q(T) = -m\ln(1 - q^{1/n}) \approx m\ln(n/(1 -
q))$ for large $n$. With $m = 10\,\mathrm{ms}$, the $99$th percentile is $46\,\mathrm{ms}$ for one call and about $92$,
$115$ and $138\,\mathrm{ms}$ for $100$, $1000$ and $10\,000$ calls.
:::

Part (c) is the budget a server team receives from the team that owns the fan-out. It is about $n$ times stricter than the
request's own target.

::: {#exm-fanout-budget}
#### A target for each server

For a request over $100$ servers to exceed $200\,\mathrm{ms}$ at most $1\%$ of the time, each server may exceed it with
probability at most $1 - 0.99^{1/100} = 1.005 \times 10^{-4}$, just above $\varepsilon/n = 10^{-4}$.
:::

Dean and Barroso's measured service shows a related trade-off: waiting for most rather than all responses. The
probability of collecting $k$ of $n$ responses in time is the $k$-out-of-$n$ formula of
@prp-series-parallel-availability.

::: {#exm-fanout-partial}
#### Waiting for most of the servers

In the measured service of Dean and Barroso, the $99$th-percentile latency at the root was $10\,\mathrm{ms}$ for one leaf,
$140\,\mathrm{ms}$ for all leaves and $70\,\mathrm{ms}$ for $95\%$ of them, so "waiting for the slowest 5% of the requests
to complete is responsible for half of the total 99%-percentile latency" [@dean2013tail, p. 76, Table 1]. A service that
may answer from $95$ of $100$ leaves needs, at each $t$, only $\mathbb P(\operatorname{Bin}(100, F(t)) \geq 95)$ to be
large, which happens at much smaller $t$ than $F(t)^{100}$.
:::

Hedged requests use redundancy against the tail: a second copy of a call is sent to another replica if the first has not
answered after a delay. Dean and Barroso report the effect on a real system.

::: {#exm-fanout-hedged}
#### Hedged requests

"Sending a hedging request after a 10ms delay reduces the 99.9th-percentile latency for retrieving all 1,000 values from
1,800ms to 74ms while sending just 2% more requests" [@dean2013tail, p. 77]. In the model of part (a), if a call is slow
with probability $p$ and the hedge is independent, the call is slow only if both copies are, so $p$ becomes roughly $p^2$:
for $p = 0.01$ and $n = 100$, the request is slow with probability $1 - (1 - 10^{-4})^{100} = 0.01$ instead of $0.63$.
:::

The proposition is the series rule of the previous unit applied to latency. The analogy makes it easy to carry results
from one to the other.

::: {#exm-fanout-series-analogy}
#### Fan-out as a series system

Let $E_i = \{T_i \leq t\}$, the event that call $i$ is fast. The request is fast on $E_1 \cap \dots \cap E_n$, as a series
system is up, and part (a) of @prp-series-parallel-availability gives $\mathbb P(T \leq t) = F(t)^n$. Hedging is the
parallel rule for one call; waiting for $k$ of $n$ is the quorum rule.
:::

The last example checks part (a) on a simulated service, with the slowness produced by background work on the servers
rather than assumed. It uses SimPy to run a root that fans out to twenty leaf servers.

::: {#exm-fanout-simulation}
#### A simulated fan-out

Twenty leaves each serve calls one at a time, with exponential service times of mean $5\,\mathrm{ms}$, and each runs a
background task of $40\,\mathrm{ms}$ at random times, on average every two seconds, as the daemons and maintenance tasks
of Dean and Barroso do [@dean2013tail, p. 75]. Requests arrive at $10$ per second and wait for all twenty calls. The
simulation measures the probability $p$ that one call exceeds $30\,\mathrm{ms}$ and the probability that a request does,
and compares the latter with $1 - (1 - p)^{20}$:

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
import simpy
rng = np.random.default_rng(19)
env = simpy.Environment()
n, slow = 20, 0.030
leaves = [simpy.Resource(env, capacity=1) for _ in range(n)]
calls, requests = [], []
def hold(leaf, duration):
    with leaf.request() as r:
        yield r
        yield env.timeout(duration)
def daemon(leaf):
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(rng.exponential(2.0))
        env.process(hold(leaf, 0.040))
def call(leaf):
    start = env.now
    yield env.process(hold(leaf, rng.exponential(0.005)))
    calls.append(env.now - start)
def request():
    start = env.now
    yield simpy.AllOf(env, [env.process(call(leaf)) for leaf in leaves])
    requests.append(env.now - start)
def arrivals():
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(rng.exponential(0.1))
        env.process(request())
for leaf in leaves:
    env.process(daemon(leaf))
env.process(arrivals())
env.run(until=600)
p = np.mean(np.array(calls) > slow)
print(f"{len(requests)} requests; P(call > 30 ms) = {p:.4f}")
print(f"P(request > 30 ms) = {np.mean(np.array(requests) > slow):.4f}; 1 - (1 - p)^20 = {1 - (1 - p)**n:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
6091 requests; P(call > 30 ms) = 0.0118
P(request > 30 ms) = 0.2110; 1 - (1 - p)^20 = 0.2115
```

The two probabilities of the request agree closely: the leaves' background tasks are independent, so their calls are
nearly independent, as part (a) assumes.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise applies part (a) to a few fan-outs. It shows how quickly a small per-call probability becomes a large
per-request one.

::: {#exr-fanout-basic}
#### Small fan-outs

Each call is slow with probability $0.01$. Give the probability that a request is slow for $n = 5, 10, 50$, with the two
bounds of part (a).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$1 - 0.99^n$ is $0.049$, $0.096$ and $0.395$; the lower bounds $1 - e^{-0.01n}$ are $0.049$, $0.095$ and $0.393$, and the
upper bounds $0.01n$ are $0.05$, $0.1$ and $0.5$. For $np$ small the union bound $np$ is nearly exact.

## Python

The probability and its bounds.

```{.python .run}
from math import exp
p = 0.01
for n in (5, 10, 50):
    print(f"n = {n:2d}: {1 - (1 - p)**n:.4f}  bounds [{1 - exp(-n * p):.4f}, {n * p:.2f}]")
```

```{.text .run-output}
n =  5: 0.0490  bounds [0.0488, 0.05]
n = 10: 0.0956  bounds [0.0952, 0.10]
n = 50: 0.3950  bounds [0.3935, 0.50]
```
::::
:::

The second exercise asks for the proof of the two bounds in part (a) by another route. The check evaluates them on a grid.

::: {#exr-fanout-bounds-proof}
#### The bounds from the union bound

Prove the upper bound $1 - (1 - p)^n \leq np$ from the union bound, without induction, and the lower bound from $\ln(1 - p)
\leq -p$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The request is slow on $\bigcup_i\{T_i > t\}$, whose probability is at most $\sum_i\mathbb P(T_i > t) = np$ by the union bound;
no independence is needed for this half. For the lower bound, $\ln(1 - p) \leq -p$ for $p \in [0, 1)$ because $\ln$ is
concave and $-p$ is its tangent at $1$; multiplying by $n$ and exponentiating gives $(1 - p)^n \leq e^{-np}$. (For $p = 1$
both sides are $0$.)

## Python

Check on a grid of $p$ and $n$: the largest violation of either bound, which should be at most rounding error.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
p = np.linspace(0, 1, 1001)[:, None]
n = np.arange(1, 501)[None, :]
v = 1 - (1 - p) ** n
print(f"max of (lower - value): {np.max(1 - np.exp(-n * p) - v):.2e}; max of (value - upper): {np.max(v - n * p):.2e}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
max of (lower - value): 0.00e+00; max of (value - upper): 5.55e-17
```
::::
:::

The third exercise asks for a proof of part (b) in the continuous case, together with a numerical check. The check uses
exponential calls, for which the quantiles are explicit.

::: {#exr-fanout-quantile-proof}
#### Quantiles of a maximum

For continuous, strictly increasing $F$, show directly that $F_T(t_{q^{1/n}}(T_1)) = q$, where $F_T = F^n$ is the
distribution function of $T$. Check it on exponential calls of mean $1$ with $n = 50$ and $q = 0.99$ by simulation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

For continuous strictly increasing $F$, $t_r(T_1) = F^{-1}(r)$, so $F_T(t_{q^{1/n}}(T_1)) = F(F^{-1}(q^{1/n}))^n = (q^{1/n})^n =
q$, and since $F_T$ is also continuous and strictly increasing, $t_q(T) = t_{q^{1/n}}(T_1)$.

## Python

Check on exponential calls of mean $1$, $n = 50$: the formula $-\ln(1 - q^{1/n})$ against the empirical $99$th percentile of
$10^5$ simulated maxima.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(20)
n, q = 50, 0.99
T = rng.exponential(1.0, (10**5, n)).max(axis=1)
print(f"formula {-np.log(1 - q ** (1 / n)):.4f}; simulated {np.quantile(T, q):.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
formula 8.5123; simulated 8.5666
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise inverts part (a) for the fan-out. It asks how wide a request may fan out before it misses a target.

::: {#exr-fanout-max-n}
#### The widest fan-out

Each call is slow with probability $10^{-3}$. What is the largest $n$ for which at most $5\%$ of requests are slow? And at
most $1\%$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$1 - 0.999^n \leq \varepsilon$ means $n \leq \ln(1 - \varepsilon)/\ln 0.999$: $n \leq 51.27$, so $51$, for $\varepsilon =
0.05$, and $n \leq 10.05$, so $10$, for $\varepsilon = 0.01$.

## Python

The two thresholds.

```{.python .run}
from math import floor, log
for eps in (0.05, 0.01):
    print(f"eps = {eps}: n <= {log(1 - eps) / log(0.999):.2f}, so n = {floor(log(1 - eps) / log(0.999))}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
eps = 0.05: n <= 51.27, so n = 51
eps = 0.01: n <= 10.05, so n = 10
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise evaluates the closed form of @exm-fanout-exponential for fan-outs from one to ten thousand. It shows
the logarithmic growth of the request percentile.

::: {#exr-fanout-exponential-growth}
#### How the percentile grows

For exponential calls of mean $10\,\mathrm{ms}$, give $t_{0.99}(T)$ for $n = 1, 10, 100, 1000, 10\,000$, and the increase per
factor of ten in $n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$t_{0.99}(T) = -10\ln(1 - 0.99^{1/n})$ ms: $46.1$, $69.0$, $92.1$, $115.1$ and $138.1\,\mathrm{ms}$. Each factor of ten adds
about $10\ln 10 = 23\,\mathrm{ms}$, the mean times $\ln 10$.

## Python

The five percentiles.

```{.python .run}
from math import log
for n in (1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000):
    print(f"n = {n:5d}: t_0.99 = {-10 * log(1 - 0.99 ** (1 / n)):6.1f} ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
n =     1: t_0.99 =   46.1 ms
n =    10: t_0.99 =   69.0 ms
n =   100: t_0.99 =   92.1 ms
n =  1000: t_0.99 =  115.1 ms
n = 10000: t_0.99 =  138.1 ms
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise tests hedging by simulation, with the delay before the hedge set at a percentile, as Dean and Barroso
suggest. It measures both the gain and the extra load.

::: {#exr-fanout-hedge}
#### Hedging after the 95th percentile

Calls take $10\,\mathrm{ms}$ on average (exponential) but, with probability $0.01$, an extra second. A hedge is sent to an
independent replica after $d$, the $95$th percentile of a call, and the call completes when either copy answers. For a
fan-out of $100$, estimate the share of requests that take more than $100\,\mathrm{ms}$ with and without hedging, and the
share of extra calls.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Without hedging, $1 - 0.99^{100} = 63\%$ of requests include a one-second call. With a hedge after $d \approx
30\,\mathrm{ms}$, a call takes a second only if both copies do, with probability about $10^{-4}$, so about $1 - (1 -
10^{-4})^{100} = 1\%$ of requests are still slow, while $5\%$ more calls are sent: Dean and Barroso's trade-off
[@dean2013tail, p. 77]. The hedge moves the slow requests from two in three to one in a hundred, but at a fan-out of $100$
that one in a hundred still sits at the request's $99$th percentile.

## Python

$10^4$ requests of $100$ calls each, with and without hedges.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(21)
def call_times(shape):
    return rng.exponential(0.010, shape) + np.where(rng.random(shape) < 0.01, 1.0, 0.0)
shape = (10**4, 100)
first = call_times(shape)
d = np.quantile(call_times(10**6), 0.95)
hedged = np.where(first > d, np.minimum(first, d + call_times(shape)), first)
print(f"d = {d * 1e3:.1f} ms; extra calls {np.mean(first > d):.3f}")
print(f"share of requests over 100 ms: without hedging {np.mean(first.max(1) > 0.1):.3f}, "
      f"with hedging {np.mean(hedged.max(1) > 0.1):.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
d = 32.0 ms; extra calls 0.050
share of requests over 100 ms: without hedging 0.638, with hedging 0.0122
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise computes the partial-results probability of @exm-fanout-partial. It quantifies how much is gained by
not waiting for the last few servers.

::: {#exr-fanout-partial}
#### Ninety-five of a hundred

Each of $100$ independent calls is late with probability $0.01$. What is the probability that at least $95$ arrive in time?
That all $100$ do?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The number in time is $\operatorname{Bin}(100, 0.99)$. All arrive with probability $0.99^{100} = 0.366$; at least $95$ arrive
with probability $\sum_{j \geq 95}\binom{100}j0.99^j0.01^{100 - j} = 0.99947$. A service that can answer from $95\%$ of its
shards is late for one request in two thousand instead of for two in three.

## Python

The binomial tail.

```{.python .run}
from math import comb
P = lambda j: comb(100, j) * 0.99**j * 0.01**(100 - j)
print(f"all 100: {P(100):.4f}; at least 95: {sum(P(j) for j in range(95, 101)):.5f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
all 100: 0.3660; at least 95: 0.99947
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise applies part (a) twice, to a two-level tree. Dean and Barroso's root servers distribute requests
"through intermediate servers" to many leaves [@dean2013tail, p. 76].

::: {#exr-fanout-tree}
#### A two-level tree

A root sends a request to $10$ intermediate servers, each of which sends it to $10$ leaves. An intermediate server is slow
with probability $0.005$ and a leaf with $0.001$, independently. What is the probability that the request is slow? Compare
with a flat fan-out to $100$ leaves.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

An intermediate branch is fast when it and its $10$ leaves are: $0.995 \times 0.999^{10}$. The request is fast when all ten
branches are: $(0.995 \times 0.999^{10})^{10} = 0.995^{10} \times 0.999^{100} = 0.8606$, so it is slow with probability
$0.139$. The flat fan-out is slow with probability $1 - 0.999^{100} = 0.095$: the extra level adds ten more servers in series.

## Python

Both probabilities.

```{.python .run}
tree = 1 - (0.995 * 0.999**10) ** 10
flat = 1 - 0.999**100
print(f"two-level tree: {tree:.4f}; flat: {flat:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
two-level tree: 0.1394; flat: 0.0952
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise drops independence, the hypothesis that part (a) cannot do without. If slowness is shared between servers,
the amplification shrinks.

::: {#exr-fanout-dependent}
#### Shared slowness

Each of $100$ servers is slow with probability $0.01$. In model A the servers are independent. In model B a shared event of
probability $0.01$ makes all of them slow at once and nothing else does. In model C a shared event of probability $0.005$ makes
all slow, and each is otherwise slow independently with probability $u$, chosen so that each is still slow with probability
$0.01$. Give the probability that a request is slow in each model.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A: $1 - 0.99^{100} = 0.634$. B: the request is slow exactly when the shared event occurs, $0.01$. C: $0.005 + 0.995u = 0.01$
gives $u = 0.005025$, and the request is fast only without the shared event and with every server's own slowness absent:
$1 - 0.995 \times (1 - u)^{100} = 0.399$. The same per-server rate gives anything between $0.01$ and $0.63$, depending on how
much of it is shared; this is why Dean and Barroso suggest synchronising background activity across machines [@dean2013tail,
p. 76].

## Python

The three probabilities.

```{.python .run}
u = (0.01 - 0.005) / 0.995
print(f"A {1 - 0.99**100:.4f}; B {0.01:.4f}; C {1 - 0.995 * (1 - u)**100:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
A 0.6340; B 0.0100; C 0.3988
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise tests the suggestion of @exr-fanout-dependent on the simulated service of @exm-fanout-simulation. The
background tasks are run either independently on each leaf, or on all leaves at the same moments.

::: {#exr-fanout-synchronised}
#### Synchronised background work

Run the simulation of @exm-fanout-simulation twice, once with each leaf's background tasks at independent random times and once
with all leaves running their tasks at the same random times (same mean interval). Compare the probability that a call exceeds
$30\,\mathrm{ms}$ and the probability that a request does.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Each leaf does the same amount of background work in both runs, so the per-call probability is about the same. With
independent tasks the request probability is close to $1 - (1 - p)^{20}$, as in @exm-fanout-simulation. With synchronised tasks
the slow calls of one request coincide: a request is slow only if it overlaps the common task, and the output shows its
probability falling from about $0.21$ to about $0.07$, a factor of three, although no leaf does less background work. It does
not fall all the way to the per-call probability, because a request also waits for the backlog that the common task leaves
on every leaf. Dean and Barroso's remark that synchronisation "enforces a brief burst of activity on each machine
simultaneously, slowing only those interactive requests being handled during the brief period" [@dean2013tail, p. 76] is the
model's prediction.

## Python

The same model as in the example, with a flag for synchronised background tasks.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
import simpy
def run(synchronised, seed=22, n=20, until=600):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    env = simpy.Environment()
    leaves = [simpy.Resource(env, capacity=1) for _ in range(n)]
    calls, requests = [], []
    def hold(leaf, duration):
        with leaf.request() as r:
            yield r
            yield env.timeout(duration)
    def daemon(targets):
        while True:
            yield env.timeout(rng.exponential(2.0))
            for leaf in targets:
                env.process(hold(leaf, 0.040))
    def call(leaf):
        start = env.now
        yield env.process(hold(leaf, rng.exponential(0.005)))
        calls.append(env.now - start)
    def request():
        start = env.now
        yield simpy.AllOf(env, [env.process(call(leaf)) for leaf in leaves])
        requests.append(env.now - start)
    def arrivals():
        while True:
            yield env.timeout(rng.exponential(0.1))
            env.process(request())
    if synchronised:
        env.process(daemon(leaves))
    else:
        for leaf in leaves:
            env.process(daemon([leaf]))
    env.process(arrivals())
    env.run(until=until)
    return np.mean(np.array(calls) > 0.030), np.mean(np.array(requests) > 0.030)
for flag in (False, True):
    p_call, p_request = run(flag)
    print(f"synchronised = {flag}: P(call > 30 ms) = {p_call:.4f}, P(request > 30 ms) = {p_request:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
synchronised = False: P(call > 30 ms) = 0.0120, P(request > 30 ms) = 0.2117
synchronised = True: P(call > 30 ms) = 0.0112, P(request > 30 ms) = 0.0735
```
::::
:::
::::

## Estimating cost {#sec-estimating-cost}

Cost is the characteristic that every other one is traded against, and Tan asks that a design discuss "the cost of
implementation, cost of monitoring, and cost of each non-functional requirement such as high availability"
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 3.8]. Xu ends the estimate of his video service with a cost line and draws a design
conclusion from it: "from the rough cost estimation, we know serving videos from the CDN costs lots of money"
[@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 14]. Reis and Housley give the vocabulary: total cost of ownership, capital and
operating expenses, the opportunity cost of a choice, and FinOps, the practice of monitoring spending as one monitors
load [@reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022, Ch. 4, pp. 118-120, and Ch. 3, pp. 85-86]. This section defines the total cost
of ownership and computes it with the arithmetic of the earlier sections: a cost estimate is a load estimate multiplied
by prices.

Prices in this section are round assumptions chosen for the arithmetic, of the order that cloud providers charged in the
2020s, and not quotations: $0.40$ per server-hour, $0.02$ per gigabyte-month of object storage and $0.02$ per gigabyte sent
through a content delivery network (the figure Xu uses [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 14]).

For more on this topic, see @reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022 [Ch. 4, "Cost Optimization and Business Value"],
@tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Sec. 3.8] and @SystemDesignInterview2021 [Ch. 14].

### Total cost of ownership

The definition follows Reis and Housley's distinctions between direct and indirect costs and between capital and
operating expenses. It adds the convention that makes the two kinds comparable over a period, amortisation, and the
unit cost, which is the number a business compares with its revenue per request.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-total-cost-of-ownership}
#### Total cost of ownership

The **total cost of ownership** $\mathrm{TCO}(\Delta)$ of a system over a period $\Delta$ is the sum, over $\Delta$, of its
**direct costs**, those attributable to it (the infrastructure it consumes and the people who build and run it), and the
share of **indirect costs** (overhead paid regardless of the system) allocated to it. Each cost is one of two kinds:

1. a **capital expense** ($\mathrm{CapEx}$), a price $P$ paid up front for an asset with useful life $L$, which contributes
   its amortised share $P\Delta/L$ to a period $\Delta \leq L$;
2. an **operating expense** ($\mathrm{OpEx}$), paid as a resource is consumed, which contributes its unit price times the
   quantity consumed during $\Delta$.

A **cost estimate** of a design multiplies each quantity of its load estimate (@def-load-estimate), such as server-hours,
bytes stored and bytes transferred, by its unit price, and adds the costs of people. The **unit cost** of an operation is
the part of $\mathrm{TCO}(\Delta)$ attributed to it divided by the number of its requests served during $\Delta$.
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Xu's video service gives the simplest cost estimate: one quantity of the load estimate times one price. It is an
operating expense.

::: {#exm-cost-xu-cdn}
#### Xu's delivery cost

"5 million * 5 videos * 0.3GB * $0.02 = $150,000 per day" [@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 14]: the bytes sent by the
content delivery network in a day, $7.5 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{GB}$, times its price per gigabyte. Over a 30-day month this is
$4.5$ million, which is why Xu's deep dive includes "cost-saving optimization".
:::

The storage of the running example is the second operating expense. A managed object store replicates internally and bills
one copy, so the replication factor of the load estimate does not enter its price.

::: {#exm-cost-storage}
#### Storage of the photo-sharing service

After one year the service stores $365 \times 40\,\mathrm{TB} = 14.6\,\mathrm{PB}$ of photos, one billed copy, which costs
$1.46 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{GB} \times 0.02 = 292\,000$ per month at the end of the year. Since the volume grows linearly, the
monthly bill grows linearly too, and the cost of the first year is about half of twelve times the final bill.
:::

Compute is billed by the server-hour, whether the server is busy or not. The number of servers comes from item 4 of the
load estimate of the running example.

::: {#exm-cost-compute}
#### Application servers

The $146$ servers of @exm-load-servers cost $146 \times 0.40 \times 730 = 42\,632$ per month if they run all the time. Running
only the number the load needs hour by hour, on average a third of the peak since the peak factor is $3$, would cost about a
third as much, a saving that depends on starting and stopping servers quickly.
:::

The outgoing traffic of the feed is the third operating expense, and the largest. It is computed from the bandwidth of
@exm-load-photoshare-bandwidth.

::: {#exm-cost-egress}
#### Delivering the feed

The feed sends $17.4\,\mathrm{GB/s}$ on average, $4.5 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{GB}$ in a month, which costs $900\,000$ at
$0.02$ per gigabyte: twenty times the compute and three times the storage after a year. As for Xu's video service, the cost
of the design is the cost of delivery.
:::

Buying hardware is a capital expense; renting it is an operating one. Reis and Housley recommend "an opex-first approach"
for flexibility [@reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022, Ch. 4, p. 119]; amortisation makes the two comparable.

::: {#exm-cost-capex-opex}
#### Buying or renting a server

A server bought for $8000$ with a useful life of $L = 48$ months contributes $8000/48 = 167$ per month, plus, say, $60$ a
month for power and space. Renting the same capacity at $0.40$ an hour costs $292$ a month if it runs all the time. Bought
hardware is cheaper only if it is busy at least $227/292 = 78\%$ of the time, which a service with a peak factor of $3$
never is on average.
:::

The unit cost is what a business compares with its revenue per request. For the running example it is a small number per
view, multiplied by a very large number of views.

::: {#exm-cost-unit}
#### Cost per thousand feed views

The feed's delivery and compute cost about $9.4 \times 10^5$ per month for $1.5 \times 10^{11}$ feed views, so $0.0063$ per
thousand views. If advertising brings $0.50$ per thousand views, delivery is about $1\%$ of revenue; the people who build and
run the service are then the larger cost.
:::

Tan's list of costs goes beyond infrastructure: maintenance, the "natural atrophy of software over time as libraries and
services are deprecated", and even "the costs to decommission the system" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 3.8]. These are
direct costs in the sense of the definition, paid in people.

::: {#exm-cost-people}
#### People are a direct cost

A team of eight engineers at $15\,000$ a month each costs $120\,000$ a month, three times the compute of
@exm-cost-compute. A design that saves ten servers but needs one more engineer to operate it raises the total cost of
ownership.
:::

Reis and Housley add a cost that no bill shows. Choosing one technology excludes the others and commits the team to it.

::: {#exm-cost-opportunity}
#### The opportunity cost of a choice

"Total opportunity cost of ownership (TOCO) is the cost of lost opportunities that we incur in choosing a technology, an
architecture, or a process" [@reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022, Ch. 4, p. 119]. Building the photo service on a database
that only one engineer knows makes the cost of moving away from it, if it proves unsuitable, a part of the decision; the
decision record of @exm-char-adr is where it belongs.
:::

Operating expenses grow with use, including use nobody intended. Reis and Housley warn that "excessive downloads from S3
buckets can drive spending through the roof" and recommend monitoring spending [@reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022, Ch. 3,
p. 86].

::: {#exm-cost-attack}
#### A cost attack

If a public photo link is fetched in a loop by a misbehaving client at $1\,\mathrm{Gb/s}$, it sends $324\,\mathrm{TB}$ in a
month, which costs $6480$ at $0.02$ per gigabyte. FinOps treats spending like load: an alert on the hourly egress of any
single object or client turns such a bill into an incident on its first day.
:::

The last example is Xu's cost-saving deep dive in numbers. Popularity is uneven, so a small share of the items carries most of
the delivery cost.

::: {#exm-cost-popular}
#### Serving only popular items from the edge

Xu proposes to "only serve the most popular videos from CDN and other videos from our high capacity storage video servers"
[@SystemDesignInterview2021, Ch. 14]. If the top $20\%$ of videos receive $90\%$ of the views and the origin servers deliver
the rest at a cost of $0.005$ per gigabyte, the daily delivery cost of @exm-cost-xu-cdn becomes $0.9 \times 150\,000 + 0.1
\times 150\,000 \times 0.25 = 138\,750$, a saving of $7.5\%$. The saving grows with the share of the long tail and the gap
between the two prices.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise recomputes Xu's estimate of @exm-cost-xu-cdn and extends it to a year. It is a direct use of the
definition.

::: {#exr-cost-xu-year}
#### Xu's delivery cost over a year

Recompute the daily delivery cost of Xu's video service, then the yearly cost, and the cost per video view.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$5 \times 10^6 \times 5 \times 0.3\,\mathrm{GB} = 7.5 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{GB}$ a day, $150\,000$ a day, $5.5 \times 10^7$ a
year; a view costs $0.3 \times 0.02 = 0.006$.

## Python

The three numbers.

```{.python .run}
gb_per_day = 5e6 * 5 * 0.3
print(f"per day {gb_per_day * 0.02:,.0f}; per year {gb_per_day * 0.02 * 365:,.0f}; per view {0.3 * 0.02:.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
per day 150,000; per year 54,750,000; per view 0.006
```
::::
:::

The second exercise moves old photos to a cheaper storage class, a standard saving for data that is rarely read. The
saving depends on how quickly photos stop being read.

::: {#exr-cost-tiers}
#### Cold storage

Photos older than $30$ days are moved to a cold storage class at $0.004$ per gigabyte-month. Give the monthly storage bill at
the end of the first year with and without the move, for $40\,\mathrm{TB}$ of new photos a day.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

At the end of the year $30 \times 40 = 1200\,\mathrm{TB}$ are hot and $335 \times 40 = 13\,400\,\mathrm{TB}$ cold. Without the
move the bill is $14.6 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{GB} \times 0.02 = 292\,000$; with it, $1.2 \times 10^6 \times 0.02 + 13.4 \times
10^6 \times 0.004 = 77\,600$, about a quarter. Reads of cold photos are slower and may cost more per request, which the
requirements must allow.

## Python

Both bills.

```{.python .run}
daily_gb = 40e3
hot, cold = 30 * daily_gb, 335 * daily_gb
```
