```{.python .run}
print(f"all hot: {(hot + cold) * 0.02:,.0f}; tiered: {hot * 0.02 + cold * 0.004:,.0f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
all hot: 292,000; tiered: 77,600
```
::::
:::

The third exercise finds the break-even utilisation of @exm-cost-capex-opex for other lifetimes. A longer life lowers the
amortised price but ties the money up longer.

::: {#exr-cost-buy-rent}
#### Break-even utilisation

With a purchase price of $8000$, running costs of $60$ a month and rent of $0.40$ an hour, give the break-even utilisation for
useful lives of $36$, $48$ and $60$ months.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The owned server costs $8000/L + 60$ a month whatever its use; rent costs $292u$ for utilisation $u$. They are equal at $u =
(8000/L + 60)/292$: $96.6\%$, $77.6\%$ and $66.2\%$. Owning pays only for steady, high load, and only if the hardware is still
useful at the end of its assumed life.

## Python

The three break-even points.

```{.python .run}
rent = 0.40 * 730
for L in (36, 48, 60):
    print(f"L = {L} months: break-even utilisation {(8000 / L + 60) / rent:.1%}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
L = 36 months: break-even utilisation 96.7%
L = 48 months: break-even utilisation 77.6%
L = 60 months: break-even utilisation 66.2%
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise mixes two ways of paying for compute. A commitment to a baseline buys a discount, and the peaks are paid at
the full price.

::: {#exr-cost-reserved}
#### Committed and on-demand capacity

The application tier needs $c(h) = 49 + 48\cos(2\pi(h - 20)/24)$ servers in hour $h$ (rounded up), between $1$ and $97$. Committed
servers cost $0.24$ an hour whether used or not; on-demand servers cost $0.40$ an hour when used. Which number of committed
servers minimises the daily cost, and what is the saving over all on-demand?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

With $b$ committed servers the daily cost is $24 \times 0.24b + 0.40\sum_h\max(c(h) - b, 0)$. Raising $b$ by one adds $5.76$ and
saves $0.40$ for each hour in which $c(h) > b$, so it pays while more than $14.4$ hours a day need more than $b$ servers. The search
gives $37$ committed servers, a level that the load exceeds for about fourteen hours of the day, and a saving of $10.8\%$
over paying for everything on demand.

## Python

The cost for every $b$, minimised by search.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
h = np.arange(24)
c = np.ceil(49 + 48 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * (h - 20) / 24))
cost = lambda b: 24 * 0.24 * b + 0.40 * np.maximum(c - b, 0).sum()
best = min(range(0, 98), key=cost)
print(f"best commitment {best} servers: {cost(best):.2f} per day; all on demand {cost(0):.2f}; "
      f"saving {1 - cost(best) / cost(0):.1%}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
best commitment 37 servers: 422.72 per day; all on demand 474.00; saving 10.8%
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise compares cost with revenue per user. It is the unit-cost question asked per user instead of per request.

::: {#exr-cost-per-user}
#### Cost per user

With the monthly delivery ($900\,000$), compute ($42\,632$), storage at the end of the first year ($292\,000$) and people
($120\,000$) of the examples, give the cost per daily active user per month. Which item would a $30\%$ reduction help most?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The total is $1\,354\,632$ a month for $10^8$ users, $0.0135$ per user per month. A reduction helps in proportion to the item's
share of the bill: delivery is $66\%$ of the total, so cutting it by $30\%$
saves $20\%$ of the bill, against $6.5\%$ for storage and $0.9\%$ for compute.

## Python

The total, the cost per user and the saving of each $30\%$ cut.

```{.python .run}
items = {"delivery": 900000, "compute": 42632, "storage": 292000, "people": 120000}
total = sum(items.values())
print(f"total {total:,}; per user per month {total / 1e8:.4f}")
for k, v in items.items():
    print(f"30% off {k:8s}: saves {0.3 * v / total:.1%} of the bill")
```

```{.text .run-output}
total 1,354,632; per user per month 0.0135
30% off delivery: saves 19.9% of the bill
30% off compute : saves 0.9% of the bill
30% off storage : saves 6.5% of the bill
30% off people  : saves 2.7% of the bill
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise asks whether compression pays when its cost is in compute and its saving in egress. Xu's lesson from the
latency numbers, to compress before sending, has a cost side too.

::: {#exr-cost-compression}
#### Does compression pay?

A better image encoding makes thumbnails $30\%$ smaller, but encoding costs $0.2$ CPU-seconds per photo, done once at upload,
on servers that cost $0.40$ an hour. With $2 \times 10^7$ uploads a day and the delivery bill of @exm-cost-egress, give the
monthly cost and saving.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Encoding takes $2 \times 10^7 \times 0.2 = 4 \times 10^6$ CPU-seconds a day, $1111$ CPU-hours, $444$ a day at $0.40$, about
$13\,300$ a month. The delivery bill falls by $30\%$ of $900\,000$, $270\,000$. Encoding once and delivering many times makes
the trade lopsided; the ratio of views to uploads, $250$, is the reason.

## Python

The cost and saving per month.

```{.python .run}
cpu_hours_per_day = 2e7 * 0.2 / 3600
cost = cpu_hours_per_day * 0.40 * 30
saving = 0.3 * 900000
print(f"encoding {cost:,.0f} per month; delivery saving {saving:,.0f} per month")
```

```{.text .run-output}
encoding 13,333 per month; delivery saving 270,000 per month
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise quantifies Xu's observation that views follow a long-tailed distribution. A Zipf law of popularity
gives the share of views carried by the most popular items.

::: {#exr-cost-zipf}
#### How much the popular items carry

Let the $i$-th most popular of $M = 10^6$ items receive views in proportion to $1/i$. What share of the views go to the top
$1\%$, $10\%$ and $20\%$ of the items?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The share of the top $m$ items is $H_m/H_M$, with $H_m = \sum_{i \leq m}1/i \approx \ln m + 0.5772$. For $M = 10^6$, $H_M =
14.39$; the top $10^4$, $10^5$ and $2 \times 10^5$ items have $H = 9.79$, $12.09$ and $12.78$, so shares of $68\%$, $84\%$ and
$89\%$. A content delivery network holding the top tenth of the catalogue serves most of the bytes.

## Python

The harmonic sums, computed exactly.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
M = 10**6
H = np.cumsum(1.0 / np.arange(1, M + 1))
for share in (0.01, 0.1, 0.2):
    m = int(share * M)
    print(f"top {share:.0%}: {H[m - 1] / H[-1]:.3f} of the views")
```

```{.text .run-output}
top 1%: 0.680 of the views
top 10%: 0.840 of the views
top 20%: 0.888 of the views
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise follows a storage bill over several years. Because the stored volume grows linearly, the bill grows
linearly and the cumulative cost quadratically.

::: {#exr-cost-growth}
#### Storage over three years

The service adds $1.2\,\mathrm{PB}$ a month of photos and never deletes them, at $0.02$ per gigabyte-month. Give the bill in
months $12$, $24$ and $36$ and the total over three years. How much does the third year cost compared with the first?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

In month $m$ the volume is $1.2m\,\mathrm{PB}$ and the bill $1.2 \times 10^6m \times 0.02 = 24\,000m$: $288\,000$, $576\,000$
and $864\,000$. The total is $24\,000\sum_{m \leq 36}m = 24\,000 \times 666 = 1.6 \times 10^7$. The first year costs $24\,000
\times 78 = 1.87 \times 10^6$ and the third $24\,000 \times (666 - 300) = 8.78 \times 10^6$, almost five times as much: a
retention period, or cold storage, is a cost decision.

## Python

The bills and the yearly totals.

```{.python .run}
bill = lambda m: 1.2e6 * m * 0.02
print([f"{bill(m):,.0f}" for m in (12, 24, 36)])
years = [sum(bill(m) for m in range(12 * y + 1, 12 * y + 13)) for y in range(3)]
print([f"{y:,.0f}" for y in years], f"ratio third/first {years[2] / years[0]:.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
['288,000', '576,000', '864,000']
['1,872,000', '5,328,000', '8,784,000'] ratio third/first 4.69
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise sets a spending alert for the cost attack of @exm-cost-attack. The alert must fire early without firing on
normal traffic.

::: {#exr-cost-alert}
#### A spending alert

Normal egress is $17.4\,\mathrm{GB/s}$ on average with a peak factor of $3$. A misbehaving client adds $1\,\mathrm{Gb/s}$.
Would an alert on total hourly egress above $1.2$ times the normal peak catch it? What would an alert on the egress of a
single client above $10\,\mathrm{GB}$ an hour catch, and how much would the attack have cost by then?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The attack adds $0.125\,\mathrm{GB/s}$, $0.24\%$ of the normal peak of $52.2\,\mathrm{GB/s}$, so a total-egress alert never sees
it. A per-client alert at $10\,\mathrm{GB}$ an hour fires in the first hour, when the client has fetched $450\,\mathrm{GB}$, a
cost of $9$. Alerts on spending need the same breakdown by source as alerts on load.

## Python

The share of the peak and the cost after one hour.

```{.python .run}
attack = 1e9 / 8 / 1e9
peak = 3 * 17.4
print(f"attack is {attack / peak:.2%} of the peak; one hour = {attack * 3600:.0f} GB = {attack * 3600 * 0.02:.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
attack is 0.24% of the peak; one hour = 450 GB = 9.00
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise puts an interval on a cost estimate with @prp-estimate-error. A total cost is a sum of products, so both
parts of the proposition are needed.

::: {#exr-cost-interval}
#### How certain is the bill?

The monthly bill of the photo-sharing service is delivery ($U \times \nu_{\text{feed}} \times$ page size $\times$ price),
compute (servers $\times$ hourly price $\times 730$) and storage (volume $\times$ price). Suppose $U$ is known within $1.3$,
$\nu_{\text{feed}}$ within $2$, the page size within $1.5$, the number of servers within $1.5$ and the volume within $1.3$, with
prices exact. Give the interval for each item and for the total, using the figures of @exr-cost-per-user without people.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

By part (a) of @prp-estimate-error, delivery is known within $1.3 \times 2 \times 1.5 = 3.9$, compute within $1.5$ and storage
within $1.3$. By part (b) the total, $1\,234\,632$, is known within the largest factor, $3.9$: between $3.2 \times 10^5$ and
$4.8 \times 10^6$. The bound is attained only if delivery is the whole bill; with these shares the worst cases of the sum are
the sums of the worst cases, between $4.8 \times 10^5$ and $4.0 \times 10^6$, factors of about $2.6$ and $3.2$. Delivery
dominates both the bill and its uncertainty, so the feed's page size and reading rate are the assumptions to measure first.

## Python

The intervals of the items and of the total.

```{.python .run}
items = {"delivery": (900000, 1.3 * 2 * 1.5), "compute": (42632, 1.5), "storage": (292000, 1.3)}
total = sum(v for v, _ in items.values())
low, high = sum(v / f for v, f in items.values()), sum(v * f for v, f in items.values())
for k, (v, f) in items.items():
    print(f"{k:8s}: {v:,} within {f:.2f}")
print(f"total {total:,}: worst cases [{low:,.0f}, {high:,.0f}], factors {total / low:.2f} and {high / total:.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
delivery: 900,000 within 3.90
compute : 42,632 within 1.50
storage : 292,000 within 1.30
total 1,234,632: worst cases [483,806, 3,953,548], factors 2.55 and 3.20
```
::::
:::
::::

## Exercises {#sec-estimation-and-the-design-process-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The three integrative exercises below combine the six sections. The first follows the upload path of the photo-sharing
service from its requirements to its cost.

::: {#exr-estimation-and-the-design-process-int-1}
#### The upload path, end to end

Uploads must have monthly availability at least $99.95\%$ and are stored for five years. (a) From the workload of
@exm-req-workload-assumptions, give the peak upload rate and the volume billed after one year by an object store that bills one
copy (@def-load-estimate). (b) An upload needs the load balancer pair ($99.9\%$ each), one of the application servers (three
or more, $99\%$ each), the object store ($99.99\%$) and the database pair ($99.9\%$ each), with independent failures. Does the
path meet its target, and which component limits it (@prp-series-parallel-availability)? (c) Give the monthly storage cost at
the end of the first year, and its interval if the photo size is known within $1.5$ and the number of uploads within $2$
(@def-total-cost-of-ownership, @prp-estimate-error).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

(a) $\lambda_{\text{up}} = 231$ per second, $694$ at peak; the store bills $365 \times 2 \times 10^7 \times 2\,\mathrm{MB} =
14.6\,\mathrm{PB}$ after a year.

(b) The groups have $1 - 10^{-6}$ (load balancers), at least $1 - 10^{-6}$ (three application servers), $0.9999$ (object
store) and $1 - 10^{-6}$ (database), so in series $A \approx 0.9999 - 3 \times 10^{-6} = 0.99990$, above $99.95\%$. The single
object store is the limit: its $10^{-4}$ is thirty times the rest together.

(c) $1.46 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{GB} \times 0.02 = 292\,000$ a month, known within $1.5 \times 2 = 3$ by part (a) of
@prp-estimate-error: between $97\,000$ and $876\,000$.

## Python

The three parts.

```{.python .run}
from math import prod
lam = 1e8 * 0.2 / 86400
volume_gb = 365 * 2e7 * 2e6 / 1e9
print(f"(a) peak {3 * lam:.0f}/s; volume after a year {volume_gb / 1e6:.1f} PB")
groups = {"load balancers": 1 - 0.001**2, "application": 1 - 0.01**3, "object store": 0.9999, "database": 1 - 0.001**2}
A = prod(groups.values())
print(f"(b) A = {A:.6f}; meets 99.95%: {A >= 0.9995}; largest unavailability: {min(groups, key=groups.get)}")
cost = volume_gb * 0.02
print(f"(c) {cost:,.0f} per month, interval [{cost / 3:,.0f}, {cost * 3:,.0f}]")
```

```{.text .run-output}
(a) peak 694/s; volume after a year 14.6 PB
(b) A = 0.999897; meets 99.95%: True; largest unavailability: object store
(c) 292,000 per month, interval [97,333, 876,000]
```
::::
:::

The second integrative exercise designs a search service that fans out to shards. It combines the latency budgets of
@sec-units-and-latency with the availability and fan-out rules of @sec-availability-arithmetic.

::: {#exr-estimation-and-the-design-process-int-2}
#### A sharded search service

A search request crosses the network ($\tau_1 = 60\,\mathrm{ms}$ at the $99.5$th percentile), a root server ($\tau_2 =
20\,\mathrm{ms}$ at the $99.9$th) and then waits for all $50$ shards. (a) What budget $\tau_3$ and what level must the shard
stage meet for $t_{0.99} \leq 200\,\mathrm{ms}$ by part (d) of @prp-latency-budget? (b) With independent shards, what
probability of exceeding $\tau_3$ may each shard have (@prp-fan-out-tail)? (c) Each shard has $r$ replicas of $99.5\%$, any one
of which can answer. How many replicas does each shard need for the search to be available $99.99\%$ of the time, with all
$50$ shards needed (@prp-series-parallel-availability)?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

(a) The first two stages use $0.005 + 0.001 = 0.006$ of the $0.01$ allowed, so the shard stage gets $\tau_3 = 200 - 80 =
120\,\mathrm{ms}$ at level $1 - 0.004 = 0.996$.

(b) By part (c) of @prp-fan-out-tail, each shard may exceed $120\,\mathrm{ms}$ with probability at most $1 - 0.996^{1/50} =
8.0 \times 10^{-5}$: the shards' $99.992$th percentile must be below $120\,\mathrm{ms}$.

(c) A shard is up with probability $1 - 0.005^r$ and the search with $(1 - 0.005^r)^{50}$. For $r = 2$ this is $0.99875$; for
$r = 3$, $0.9999938$. Three replicas per shard are needed.

## Python

The three answers.

```{.python .run}
level = 1 - (0.01 - 0.005 - 0.001)
print(f"(a) tau_3 = {200 - 60 - 20} ms at level {level:.3f}")
print(f"(b) per-shard exceedance <= {1 - level ** (1 / 50):.2e}")
for r in (1, 2, 3):
    print(f"(c) r = {r}: A = {(1 - 0.005**r) ** 50:.7f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
(a) tau_3 = 120 ms at level 0.996
(b) per-shard exceedance <= 8.02e-05
(c) r = 1: A = 0.7783126
(c) r = 2: A = 0.9987508
(c) r = 3: A = 0.9999938
```
::::
:::

The third integrative exercise starts from requirements and ends with a decision that survives the uncertainty of the
estimate. It uses the chat service of @exr-load-chat.

::: {#exr-estimation-and-the-design-process-int-3}
#### Requirements, estimate and a robust decision

(a) Write two non-functional requirements for the chat service as measurable triples (@def-requirements-specification), one on
delivery latency and one on monthly availability. (b) The number of connection servers was $17$; if the share of users
connected at the peak is known within $2$ and the number of users within $1.5$, give the interval (@prp-estimate-error) and
the number of servers that covers its upper end, with one spare zone of three (@exm-load-zone-headroom). (c) With the
availability requirement of (a) at $99.95\%$ and deployments that fail with probability $0.05$, causing $5$ minutes of downtime,
how many deployments a month keep the expected downtime within half the error budget (@def-availability)?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

(a) ($t_{0.99}$ of the time from send to delivery to a connected recipient, $\leq$, $500\,\mathrm{ms}$) and (monthly
availability of sending, $\geq$, $99.95\%$), at the workload of @exr-load-chat.

(b) The estimate $1.67 \times 10^7$ connections is known within $\Phi = 3$, so between $5.6 \times 10^6$ and $5 \times 10^7$,
which needs between $6$ and $50$ servers. Covering the upper end with three zones that survive the loss of one needs
$\lceil 50/2\rceil = 25$ per zone, $75$ in all; the decision to plan for $75$ servers is robust, while $17$ is only the central
estimate.

(c) The error budget is $21.6$ minutes, half of it $10.8$. Each deployment costs $0.05 \times 5 = 0.25$ minutes on average, so
at most $43$ deployments a month.

## Python

Parts (b) and (c).

```{.python .run}
from math import ceil
conns = 5e7 / 3
low, high = conns / 3, conns * 3
print(f"(b) connections in [{low:.2e}, {high:.2e}]; servers in [{ceil(low / 1e6)}, {ceil(high / 1e6)}]; "
      f"with a spare zone: {3 * ceil(ceil(high / 1e6) / 2)}")
budget = 0.0005 * 43200
print(f"(c) at most {int(budget / 2 / (0.05 * 5))} deployments a month")
```

```{.text .run-output}
(b) connections in [5.56e+06, 5.00e+07]; servers in [6, 50]; with a spare zone: 75
(c) at most 43 deployments a month
```

## References {#sec-estimation-and-the-design-process-references}

The chapter cites the following works, with the parts it uses.

- @SystemDesignInterview2021 [Chs. 2, 3, 8 and 14]: the power-of-two and latency tables, availability numbers, the Twitter
  estimate and the tips on rounding; the four-step design framework; the URL-shortener and video-service estimates, and the
  delivery cost and its savings.
- @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Secs. 1.1, 2.1-2.3, 3.1-3.4, 3.8 and App. C]: requirements with numbers, the draft API and the
  phases of a diagram; non-functional requirements, scaling, the table of nines, fault tolerance, latency and cost trade-offs;
  the C4 model.
- @liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 2, Ch. 5 and Apps. 1-3]: the six-step framework and its order; requirements on scale,
  latency, consistency and accuracy; the formulas and techniques of back-of-the-envelope estimates; conversion tables,
  machine capacities and latency numbers.
- @sinhaSystemDesignGuide2024 [Chs. 1-2]: system design as turning requirements into a blueprint; availability and latency as
  attributes of distributed systems.
- @gandhiHeadFirstSoftware2024 [Chs. 2-3, pp. 44-48, 70 and 90-97]: the three-part definition of architectural
  characteristics, limiting them, the two laws of software architecture and decision records.
- @reisFundamentalsDataEngineering2022 [Ch. 3, pp. 85-86, and Ch. 4, pp. 118-120]: FinOps, total cost of ownership, capital
  and operating expenses, and the opportunity cost of a choice.
- @dean2013tail [pp. 74-77]: fan-out amplification of rare slowness, the measured service of Table 1, synchronised background
  activity and hedged requests.
- @saltzer1984end ["End-to-end caretaking" and "Performance aspects"]: the end-to-end argument and the performance trade-off
  of reliability in lower layers.
